#6361. Capital One Venture Business Card Review

If you’re a traveler like me, chances are you’re always on the lookout for ways to make your trips more affordable. That’s why I collect points and miles: they help me lower my travel costs so I can spend my money on what’s actually important…which is usually booking more trips!

One card that can help you earn more points and miles — which translates to more free flights and free hotel stays — is the Capital One Venture Business card. It’s an easy-to-use card perfect for travels who want to simplify their points and miles collecting. Here’s everything you need to know about the card to help decide if it’s for you. It’s a solid business card for those who don’t want a high annaul fee card but want some added perks besides just getting miles when you spend money.

Table of ContentsWhat Is It?Rental Car PerksTravel PartnersWho Is This Card For?

The Capital One Venture Business card is the new rebranded version of Capital One’s Spark Miles. But it has some noteworthy improvements that I think make it worth adding to your wallet. Here’s a look at the card’s main perks:

The annual fee for the card is just $95, which means it’s effectively free once you factor in the two statement credits. With a default 2x miles for every dollar spent, that makes this card a solid choice for everyday spending. And without a ton of differing spending categories, the card is very easy to use, making it perfect for travelers new to the points and miles game.

In addition to giving you Hertz Five Star status, which lets you skip the counter at select locations while also offering a wider selection of cars, the card also offers rental car coverage when renting a car for business reasons. You’ll need to charge the full fee to your card and also decline the company’s collision damage waiver, but once you do that, you’ll be covered for damage due to both collisions and theft.

While I don’t often rent cars for work, I appreciate the free collision coverage and being able to skip the line (especially at busier rental locations).

With this card, you’ll earn Capital One miles. You can use them like you would any other rewards program: to get cash back, book travel directly, or transfer them to travel partners.

The easiest option is to redeem your miles for travel in the Capital One travel portal, which works like booking through Expedia or any other online travel agency. Doing so is very straightforward. You simply search for and book your flight, hotel, or rental car and choose “miles” as your payment method. It’s basically like using your miles as cash, at a value of one cent per mile.

Both options are super easy to implement, which is why this is a great card for newbies. And if this is the only way that you’ll use your miles, go for it! Using them is better than letting them sit around.

However, you can usually get more for your miles when you transfer them to Capital One’s transfer partners.

The ability to transfer to travel partners is what makes Capital One miles valuable. While the actual value varies based on what you book, you can usually find airline and hotel redemptions worth much more than the aforementioned 1 cent per mile.

Transferring to travel partners is a bit more work than using the portal, but there are more tools than ever to help you maximize your miles (such as point.me for finding flights and Awayz for finding award hotel stays).

Here are their current hotel and airline transfer partners:

This card is best for business travelers who are looking for an easy-to-use card to help them earn points and miles. While I personally think the Capital One Venture X Business card is a better card, it comes with a higher annual fee so, if you want a solid travel card for your business and don’t need the upgraded perks of the Capital One Venture X Business card, this is the Capital One card for you. And since the credits cover the annual fee, the card is essentially free!

The new Capital One Venture Business card has an amazing welcome offer, a respectable 2x on every purchase, and some solid perks for regular travelers. And with its low annual fee, this card is a no brainer for travelers looking for a new business card. I just wouldn’t wait too long — this huge welcome offer isn’t gonna last forever!

#6360. Best Day Trips from Toronto: Easy Escapes for 2026

Looking for the best day trips from Toronto? Whether you’re craving waterfalls, wineries, beaches, or small towns, Ontario is packed with incredible places to explore just a short drive from the city. The best day trips from Toronto include Niagara Falls, Elora, Blue Mountain, and Prince Edward County, all within 2 to 3 hours from the city.

We’ve lived in Toronto and traveled all around the province—and trust us, you don’t need to go far to find adventure. From hiking trails along the Niagara Escarpment to paddling the Grand River or sipping wine in Prince Edward County, there’s a day trip here for everyone.

Most of these destinations are within a 2-hour drive from Toronto, so you can head out in the morning and be back home in time for dinner. If you’re short on time but big on wanderlust, these are the top 25 Toronto day trips to add to your weekend plans in Ontario.

The best day trips from Toronto include Niagara Falls for first-time visitors, Hamilton for waterfalls and food, Elora for small-town charm and the gorge, Stratford for theatre, Blue Mountain for outdoor adventure, Prince Edward County for wineries and beaches, and the Toronto Islands for an easy car-free escape. Most are within 1 to 2.5 hours of the city, but places like Algonquin Park and Bruce Peninsula are better as long day trips or overnight getaways.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it combines history, nature, food, art, and outdoor adventure in one easy-to-reach city.

The best day trips from Toronto include popular destinations like Niagara Falls, Hamilton, Elora, and Prince Edward County, all within 2 to 3 hours of the city.Toronto Islands and Canada’s Wonderland offer easy escapes under an hour, perfect for families and low-stress outings.Elora and Stratford are ideal for those seeking small-town charm combined with nature and culture.Longer trips such as Muskoka and Algonquin Provincial Park provide stunning wilderness experiences but require more travel time.

Best for: skyline views, beaches, biking, picnics, and car-free exploringTravel time from Toronto: 10–15 minute ferry from downtownSuggested day: Take the ferry in the morning, explore Ward’s Island or Centre Island, rent bikes, have a picnic, and return near sunset for skyline views.

The Toronto Islands are the easiest day trip from Toronto because you don’t even need to leave the city. Once you step off the ferry, it feels like a completely different world, with beaches, bike paths, picnic areas, and one of the best views of the Toronto skyline.

This is a great option if you want a low-stress day trip without a long drive. You can spend the day walking, cycling, swimming in summer, or simply relaxing by the water.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Go late afternoon if you want the best skyline photos. The view of downtown Toronto from the islands is one of the classic shots of the city.

Best for: families, thrill rides, water park fun, and summer day tripsDrive from Toronto: about 30–45 minutesSuggested day: Arrive early, hit the big roller coasters first, cool off at Splash Works in the afternoon, and stay into the evening if the park has special events.

Canada’s Wonderland is one of the easiest family day trips from Toronto. It has roller coasters, kids’ areas, live entertainment, water rides, and Splash Works, which is perfect on a hot summer day.

This is a full-day outing, especially if you are visiting with kids or trying to ride the major coasters. It’s busy in summer, but that is part of the experience.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Buy tickets online and arrive before opening if you want to make the most of the day. The biggest rides get long lines quickly.

Best for: hiking, conservation areas, mountain biking, skiing, and quick nature escapesDrive from Toronto: about 40–60 minutesSuggested day: Start with a hike at Rattlesnake Point or Kelso, have lunch in town, then add Mount Nemo or Crawford Lake if you want a second outdoor stop.

Milton is one of the best quick nature escapes from Toronto. It sits along the Niagara Escarpment and gives you access to hiking trails, lookout points, conservation areas, and outdoor activities without committing to a long drive.

Kelso Conservation Area is great year-round, with hiking and mountain biking in warm weather and skiing or snowboarding in winter. Rattlesnake Point and Mount Nemo are also excellent for escarpment views.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Milton is ideal when you want a real outdoor day but don’t want to spend half the day in the car.

Best for: waterfalls, hiking, food, art, museums, and waterfront trailsDrive from Toronto: about 1 hourSuggested day: Visit a waterfall in the morning, explore Dundurn Castle or the waterfront in the afternoon, then head to James Street North for dinner or Art Crawl if it’s the second Friday of the month.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it combines nature and city energy in one easy trip. You can hike to waterfalls, visit museums, walk the waterfront, eat downtown, and still be back in Toronto by evening.

The waterfalls are the main draw, but Hamilton has become much more than an outdoor stop. James Street North, King William Street, the waterfront, and the city’s food scene make it worth a full day.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you want the full city-and-nature experience, see our guide to the best things to do in Hamilton, Ontario.

Best for: scenic drives, hiking, fall colours, cider, and countryside escapesDrive from Toronto: about 45–60 minutesSuggested day: Visit the Cheltenham Badlands, go for a hike, stop at a cidery or café, and enjoy a relaxed countryside drive.

Caledon is a great day trip when you want fresh air, rolling hills, and a slower pace. It’s close to Toronto but feels rural, making it perfect for a scenic drive or a low-key outdoor day.

The Cheltenham Badlands are the most famous stop, but Caledon also has trails, conservation areas, farm shops, and cideries that make it easy to turn a short drive into a full afternoon.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Caledon is especially beautiful in fall. Go early if you are visiting popular spots during peak colour season.

Best for: first-time visitors, waterfalls, wineries, romance, and classic Ontario sightseeingDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 to 2 hoursSuggested day: Visit Niagara Falls in the morning, then drive 20 minutes to Niagara-on-the-Lake for wineries, heritage streets, boutique shopping, or dinner.

Niagara Falls is one of the most famous day trips from Toronto, and it still delivers every time. Start with Horseshoe Falls, then add Journey Behind the Falls, the Niagara SkyWheel, Clifton Hill, or the Hornblower boat cruise if you want the full experience.

After the falls, slow the pace down in Niagara-on-the-Lake. The town is known for wineries, pretty streets, historic buildings, theatres, and one of the most charming main streets in Ontario.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If it is your first visit, do the falls first while you still have energy, then end the day with wine country and dinner in Niagara-on-the-Lake.

Things to do in Niagara Falls Where to Stay in Niagara FallsNiagara on the Lake Day Tours Niagara Day Tours from TorontoNiagara on the Lake

Best for: small-town charm, gorge views, tubing, kayaking, boutiques, and river adventuresDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 hoursSuggested day: Walk the town in the morning, hike along the Elora Gorge, have lunch downtown, then go tubing or kayaking if you are visiting in summer.

Elora is one of Ontario’s prettiest small towns and one of the best day trips from Toronto for people who want both nature and charm. The town has boutiques, bakeries, cafés, stone buildings, and a relaxed weekend feel.

The Elora Gorge is the highlight. The cliffs rise above the Grand River, and the trails offer beautiful views. In summer, tubing and kayaking add a little adventure to the day.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Elora gets busy on summer weekends, so arrive early if you want parking, lunch, and time on the river.

Best for: theatre, food, culture, gardens, romantic day trips, and small-town charmDrive from Toronto: about 2 hoursSuggested day: Explore downtown, walk along the Avon River, have lunch, browse the shops, and see a Stratford Festival performance if one fits your schedule.

Stratford is one of the best cultural day trips from Toronto. It’s known for the Stratford Festival, but even without a show, the town is worth visiting for its riverfront, restaurants, gardens, heritage buildings, and independent shops.

This is a slower, more polished day trip. It’s ideal for couples, theatre lovers, and anyone who wants a break from the city without heading into the wilderness.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you are seeing a show, build extra time into the day. Stratford is made for wandering before or after the theatre.

Best for: small towns, paddling, biking, river views, history, and easy food stopsDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 hoursSuggested day: Start in Paris for river views, shops, and lunch, then continue to Brantford for the Bell Homestead, Grand River trails, or a bike ride.

Paris is one of the prettiest small towns in Ontario, with the Grand River running through town, a compact downtown, cafés, bakeries, and great views from the riverfront. It’s a perfect low-key day trip when you want somewhere pretty but not overcomplicated.

Nearby Brantford adds history and trails to the day. The Bell Homestead tells the story of Alexander Graham Bell and the first long-distance telephone call, while the Grand River trails are excellent for walking, biking, and paddling.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Pairing Paris and Brantford makes the day feel more complete. Do Paris for the charm and Brantford for the history and trails.

Best for: markets, food, Mennonite culture, tech-meets-tradition, families, and easy wanderingDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 hoursSuggested day: Visit St. Jacobs Farmers’ Market in the morning, explore the village, then head into Kitchener-Waterloo or Cambridge for food, history, or the Butterfly Conservatory.

Kitchener-Waterloo and St. Jacobs make a great day trip because they offer such a mix of experiences. You can visit one of the best-known markets in Ontario, see Mennonite farms and horse-drawn buggies, then head into a modern university and tech region.

St. Jacobs is the classic stop, especially if you love markets, bakeries, crafts, and small-town shopping. Nearby Kitchener, Waterloo, Cambridge, and Galt add more food, history, and riverside exploring.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Go on a market day if you can. St. Jacobs Farmers’ Market is the anchor of this day trip.

Best for: beach-town nostalgia, Lake Erie, fish and chips, pier walks, and casual summer daysDrive from Toronto: about 2 hoursSuggested day: Walk the pier, have lunch at The Arbor or a local fish-and-chips spot, relax by the beach, then continue along Lake Erie if you want a mini road trip.

Port Dover is a classic Ontario beach town. It has a sandy beach, a pier, casual restaurants, shops, and that old-school summer feeling that makes you want to slow down.

This is not a polished luxury escape, and that is exactly the point. Port Dover is relaxed, nostalgic, and easy. It’s the kind of place where a hot dog, a walk by the water, and a sunset can be the whole plan.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Use Port Dover as the starting point for a Lake Erie mini road trip to Turkey Point, Port Rowan, or local wineries and breweries.

Best for: paddling, cottage-country scenery, lift locks, museums, Indigenous art, and relaxed exploringDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 to 2 hoursSuggested day: Visit the Peterborough Lift Lock, explore the Canadian Canoe Museum, paddle or walk along the water, then stop for food or local shopping before heading home.

Peterborough sits at the gateway to the Kawarthas and gives you a taste of cottage country without driving too far. It’s a good choice if you want water, history, culture, and a relaxed pace.

The Peterborough Lift Lock is the classic stop, and the Canadian Canoe Museum adds a meaningful look at paddling history and Indigenous craftsmanship. The area also has riverside trails, breweries, and access to the Trent-Severn Waterway.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Don’t treat Peterborough as just a place to pass through on the way to cottage country. It has enough to fill a full day.

Best for: skiing, hiking, biking, spa days, village atmosphere, and four-season adventureDrive from Toronto: about 2 to 2.5 hoursSuggested day: Spend the morning hiking, skiing, or visiting Scenic Caves, then explore Blue Mountain Village and finish with Scandinave Spa if you want a slower end to the day.

Blue Mountain and Collingwood are technically a longer day trip, but they are worth it if you start early. In winter, Blue Mountain is one of the most popular ski and snowboard areas near Toronto. In summer, it becomes a hub for hiking, biking, patios, and outdoor activities.

Scenic Caves, Blue Mountain Village, the waterfront in Collingwood, and Scandinave Spa all make this area easy to customize depending on your travel style.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you want the day to feel less rushed, pick one main activity. Don’t try to ski, spa, hike, shop, and eat your way through the whole region in one day.

Best for: beach days, families, swimming, paddleboarding, summer energy, and easy sand-and-sun escapesDrive from Toronto: about 2 hoursSuggested day: Arrive early, set up on the beach, swim or paddleboard, grab lunch nearby, and stay for sunset if traffic is manageable.

Wasaga Beach is one of Ontario’s classic summer day trips. It is known for its long sandy shoreline, shallow water, and big beach-day energy.

This is a good choice when you want a simple day: cooler, towels, sunscreen, water, snacks, and sand. It can get very busy in summer, but that is part of the Wasaga experience.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Go early on hot weekends. Parking and prime beach spots fill up fast. Book ahead with Ontario Parks or you can pay at parking lots.

Best for: lakes, paddling, fall colours, cottage-country scenery, breweries, and small townsDrive from Toronto: about 2 to 2.5 hoursSuggested day: Pick one town as your base, such as Gravenhurst, Bracebridge, or Huntsville, then add a lake stop, short hike, brewery, or boat cruise.

Muskoka is one of Ontario’s most famous cottage-country regions, with lakes, forests, docks, small towns, and that unmistakable smell of pine trees and campfires.

It is a bit of a long day trip from Toronto, but it works if you choose one area instead of trying to see the entire region. Gravenhurst, Bracebridge, Huntsville, and Port Carling all make good anchors.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Muskoka is better when you slow down. Choose one town, one lake, and one great food stop instead of racing between too many places.

Best for: wineries, beaches, food, art, romantic getaways, and summer road tripsDrive from Toronto: about 2.5 hoursSuggested day: Visit a winery or two, explore Picton or Wellington, stop at Sandbanks or a beach, and have dinner before heading back.

Prince Edward County is one of the best food-and-wine day trips from Toronto, though it also works beautifully as an overnight getaway. It has boutique wineries, cideries, beaches, farm stands, restaurants, art galleries, and small towns.

Sandbanks Provincial Park is the major beach draw, but the whole county is made for slow exploring. It’s ideal for couples, food lovers, and anyone who wants a countryside escape.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: For a true day trip, don’t overbook tastings. Pick one area of the county and enjoy it properly.

Best for: wilderness, paddling, hiking, fall colours, wildlife, and big nature daysDrive from Toronto: about 3 hoursSuggested day: Leave before sunrise, choose one hiking trail or guided paddling experience, stop at a lookout or visitor centre, and head home before you are too tired.

Algonquin is a stretch as a day trip, but it can be done if you start early and keep the plan simple. This is one of Ontario’s most iconic wilderness areas, with forests, lakes, hiking trails, canoe routes, and wildlife.

You won’t see all of Algonquin in a day, and you shouldn’t try. But a single hike, paddle, or scenic drive can still give you a taste of why the park is so special.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Algonquin is much better as an overnight, but if you only have one day, choose one trail or activity and make that the focus. Algonquin Outfitters offers excellent one-day guided tours .

No car? Book this Toronto to Algonquin Provincial Park private Tour.

Best for: The Grotto, Georgian Bay, hiking, turquoise water, cliffs, shipwrecks, and big adventure daysDrive from Toronto: about 3.5 to 4 hoursSuggested day: Leave very early, visit the Grotto or hike a section of the Bruce Trail, stop in Tobermory if time allows, and expect a long drive home.

Bruce Peninsula National Park is one of the most spectacular places in Ontario, but it is a very long day trip from Toronto. The Grotto, Georgian Bay cliffs, turquoise water, and Bruce Trail scenery make it unforgettable.

This is best for travellers who do not mind a long drive and a full day outdoors. For most people, it works better as an overnight getaway, but it can be done in a single ambitious day.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Reservations and parking rules matter here. Plan ahead, start early, and don’t wing it on a summer weekend.

Hamilton, Elora, and Niagara Falls are the best day trips from Toronto for waterfalls. Niagara Falls is the most famous, Hamilton has the greatest variety, and Elora gives you dramatic gorge scenery along the Grand River.

Wasaga Beach, Port Dover, Sandbanks in Prince Edward County, and the Toronto Islands are the best beach day trips from Toronto. Wasaga is best for a classic summer beach day, while Sandbanks is better if you want dunes and a longer road trip.

Niagara-on-the-Lake and Prince Edward County are the best wine-focused day trips from Toronto. Niagara-on-the-Lake is easier for a one-day trip, while Prince Edward County feels more relaxed if you can stay overnight.

Canada’s Wonderland, Toronto Islands, Niagara Falls, the Toronto Zoo, and Wasaga Beach are some of the best family-friendly day trips from Toronto. They offer easy activities, food options, and enough to fill a full day without complicated planning.

Milton, Hamilton, Elora, Algonquin Provincial Park, and Bruce Peninsula National Park are the best hiking day trips from Toronto. For an easy hike close to the city, choose Milton or Hamilton. For a bigger adventure, choose Algonquin or Bruce Peninsula.

Stratford, Elora, Paris, and Niagara-on-the-Lake are the best small-town day trips from Toronto. Each has a walkable centre, good food, independent shops, and enough charm to fill a relaxed day.

The best day trips from Toronto under 2 hours include Hamilton, Niagara Falls, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Elora, Stratford, Paris, Caledon, Milton, Kitchener-Waterloo, and Wasaga Beach. These are the easiest options if you want to leave in the morning and be back home by dinner.

Yes, Niagara Falls is one of the easiest and most popular day trips from Toronto. It takes about 90 minutes by car, and you can visit the falls, Journey Behind the Falls, Clifton Hill, the Niagara SkyWheel, and the Hornblower boat cruise in a single day if you start early.

For nature close to the city, Hamilton’s waterfalls, Milton’s conservation areas, Elora Gorge, and Caledon are some of the best choices. For bigger wilderness, Algonquin Park and Bruce Peninsula are spectacular, but they work better as long day trips or overnight escapes.

Yes, but your options are more limited. Niagara Falls, Hamilton, Toronto Islands, and some towns along GO Transit or VIA Rail routes are possible without a car. For waterfalls, conservation areas, beaches, and rural towns, driving is usually much easier.

The next time you use Clear to get through airport security, it might be faster than you've come to expect.

Over the course of this year, Clear has been expanding its new “e-gates” to dozens of airports across the country.

It's a more streamlined setup that allows passengers to fly through without stopping at one of its famous blue kiosks.

As of this week, Clear had deployed its new automated gates to 53 airports across the country.

By the end of the year, the tech is expected to be in place at nearly all the airports where the company offers its flagship Clear Plus service.

That's certainly good news for travelers looking to speed through Transportation Security Administration checkpoints — especially as the busy holiday travel rush looms.

In the past, travelers hoping to use Clear at TSA would walk up to the checkpoint, then peel off to get their identity verified with a quick photo. Then, a Clear staffer would escort them to the front of the TSA line.

While it's obviously a shortcut, the service hasn't been without pain points.

Sometimes, flyers would arrive to find no open kiosks, or have to wait for Clear staffers to be free to assist them.

The new e-gate setup is intended to improve the flow of passengers.

I've used the Clear e-gates at a handful of airports this year, and am typically able to walk through pretty seamlessly — often pausing for just a few seconds to get my photo taken before the gates open.

The company touts identity verification in five seconds or less under the new design (but do let us know in the comments what your experience was like).

As of this week, Clear had installed e-gates at nearly 80% of the airports it serves — and noted the "vast majority" of its network would have the e-gates by the end of this year.

At those hubs, the company said 96% passengers were getting through in five minutes or less.

These improvements should make the service an even better shortcut at more airports.

Clear is a paid service that lets passengers effectively skip the TSA line and jump right to carry-on baggage screening. It’s typically maximized in tandem with TSA PreCheck access.

Clear’s flagship airport security service (known as Clear Plus) now costs $219 for an annual membership.

But some travel cards will offset the cost. For instance, I get a statement credit of up to $219 each year for my Clear+ membership fee by carrying the American Express Platinum Card®, which has an annual fee of $895 (see ). Enrollment required; subject to auto-renewal.

Plus, three major U.S. airlines partner with Clear to offer special pricing: Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and Alaska Airlines.

TPG Tip: If you want to try Clear and sign up using TPG's special offer, you can save $40 on the first year's membership.

Even as Clear expands its e-gates at TSA checkpoints, the program has also gotten some friendly competition from the TSA's newest security shortcut called TSA PreCheck Touchless ID.

That service, which allows members to pass through security without pulling out their ID or boarding pass, is now available at dozens of airports across the country. TSA Touchless has no extra cost for PreCheck (and Global Entry) members, though you have to opt in via your airline profile.

For rates and fees of the Amex Platinum, click .

#6358. Don’t Scan This Abroad: The QR Code Travel Scam Tourists Miss

QR codes are everywhere when we travel now, on restaurant tables, parking meters, hotel signs, airports, train stations, and transit machines. This travel scam known as Quishing or QR code phishing is becoming the fastest growing travel scam warning out there. Most QR codes are legitimate, but scammers are using fake QR code stickers and fake payment pages to catch travellers when they are tired, rushed, or distracted.

QR code travel scam happens when a fake QR code sends travellers to a fraudulent website. The code may be placed over a real QR code on a parking meter, restaurant table, hotel notice, airport sign, or transit machine, or it may arrive by text or email pretending to be a fine, toll, ticket, or check-in request. The safest rule is simple: Pause. Check. Then pay.Read out post: 20 Common Travel Scams and How to Avoid Them

A scammer does not always need to hack a system or damage a payment machine. Sometimes they print a fake QR code sticker and place it directly over a legitimate code.

From a quick glance, the sign still looks official. The logo may look familiar. The instructions may seem normal. The page that opens may copy the colours, layout, and branding of the real company.

You think you are paying for parking, ordering food, checking into a hotel, or settling a toll. Instead, criminals may be collecting your credit card number, password, phone number, licence plate, email address, or other personal information.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that begin with a QR code and try to scare people into paying a fake unpaid balance.

The FTC has warned that scammers hide harmful links in QR codes to steal personal information, including by placing fake QR codes over real ones on parking meters.

Many restaurants now use QR codes for menus, ordering, or payment. Most are legitimate, but travellers should still be cautious. This is the easiest travel scam for QR code phishing as everyone uses it.

A menu QR code should usually show a menu. Be careful if it asks for information it does not need, such as your passport number, banking details, hotel room number, or a password.

Before scanning a QR code on a restaurant table, look at the surface. Does it look printed into the menu or table sign, or does it look like a sticker placed on top? If it looks raised, crooked, bubbled, or mismatched, ask staff for a printed menu or the restaurant’s official website.

Parking is one of the easiest places for this scam to work because travellers are often rushed and confused.

You may not know the local parking app. You may be dealing with another language. You may be worried about getting a ticket. That pressure makes a “scan to pay” sticker feel helpful.

Before paying through a parking QR code, inspect the sticker, read the URL preview, and check whether the payment page matches the city, parking authority, or official app named on the machine.

If anything feels off, do not use the QR code. Type the official website yourself, use the official parking app, pay at the machine, or ask local staff for help.

Airports and transit stations are full of QR codes: Wi-Fi, directions, tickets, luggage storage, forms, lounge access, and service information. Travel scams often happen when travelers are in a hurry. If you need wifi, a taxi, some food, QR codes are often the easiest way to catch you off guard.

That does not mean every code is unsafe. It means you should slow down when a public QR code asks for payment, passwords, ID documents, or personal information.

The FBI warns that malicious QR codes can send people to fake sites, steal victim data, embed malware, or redirect payments. The FBI warns that criminals can tamper with QR codes to redirect payments, steal login and financial information, or send people to malicious websites.

The easiest way to avoid this scam is to build one habit before you scan a public QR code.

Do not scan just because a sign looks official. Public signs, parking meters, table cards, and posters can be tampered with.

If the message says you must pay immediately, avoid a fine, settle a toll, confirm a booking, or prevent a penalty, slow down. Urgency is one of the biggest warning signs.

Before your phone opens anything, look at the QR code itself.

We call this the scratch test. You are not damaging the sign. You are simply checking whether the QR code feels or looks different from the rest of the surface.

Canadian readers can also check the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security’s QR code safety guidance and report fraud through the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

Most phones show a preview of the website before opening the page. Read it.

Look for misspellings, extra words, strange endings, random letters, shortened links, or a domain that does not match the company, hotel, restaurant, city, or attraction.

Do not rely only on the padlock symbol. A secure connection does not automatically mean the site is legitimate. The real question is whether you are on the correct website.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that include a QR code and pressure people to pay a fake unpaid balance.

For payments, passwords, account logins, or identity information, the safest option is often to bypass the QR code.

Open your browser and type the official website yourself. Use an app you already installed from the official app store. Ask an employee for the correct payment method. Contact your hotel, airline, rental car company, or bank through the phone number on your booking or card — not through the number on a suspicious page.

First, do not panic. Scanning a QR code does not automatically mean your information has been stolen. The bigger risk usually begins when you enter payment information, type a password, download a file, or provide personal details.

Close the page immediately if the link looks wrong, the message creates urgency, or the site asks for information you did not expect to provide.

Do not download an unfamiliar app or file from a QR code.

If you entered credit card information, contact your bank or card issuer using the official number on the back of your card or through the official banking app.

If you entered a password, change it through the official website or app. If you reused that password anywhere else, change it there too.

Watch for follow-up messages. A scammer who has some of your information may later pretend to be your bank, hotel, airline, rental car company, or payment provider.

Report the fake QR code to the business, parking authority, hotel, airport, or local authority so they can remove it.

A QR code may be suspicious if it looks like a sticker placed over another code, has peeling edges, opens a strange URL, uses a shortened link, creates urgency, asks for information that does not make sense, or directs you away from the official website or app.

At a restaurant, a QR menu should not need your passport or banking password. At a parking meter, the payment page should match the city or parking authority. At a hotel, a check-in code should not send you to a random payment page outside the official booking system.

The BBB has also warned consumers to double-check QR codes before paying for parking.

No. QR codes are part of modern travel, and many are perfectly safe.

The goal is not to panic every time you see one. The goal is to stop treating every QR code as automatically trustworthy.

A few seconds of inspection can protect you from a much longer financial or account-recovery problem later.

QR codes are convenient, but convenience is exactly what scammers are using against travellers.

Before scanning a public QR code at a restaurant, parking meter, hotel, airport, train station, attraction, or transit stop, remember the rule:

Inspect the code. Read the link. Go directly to the official website or app when money, passwords, or personal information are involved.

That tiny pause may be the thing that saves your trip.

Scanning a QR code is not automatically dangerous. The danger usually begins when you open a suspicious page, enter payment details, type a password, download a file, or provide personal information without checking whether the site is legitimate.

Inspect the physical code for stickers, raised edges, bubbles, peeling corners, or anything placed over another code. Then check the URL preview before opening the page. If the link looks strange or does not match the official company, city, hotel, or attraction, do not use it.

Before entering payment information, make sure the website belongs to the official business or authority. When in doubt, use the official app, type the website manually, pay directly at the machine, or ask staff for the correct payment method.

Contact your bank or card issuer immediately using the official number on the back of your card or your banking app. Watch for suspicious charges, replace the card if needed, and do not use any contact information from the suspicious website.

#6357. Madrid 5-Day Itinerary: A Guide to Culture, Gastronomy, and Local Life

Home to some 3.5 million people, Madrid is the capital of Spain and the country’s largest city. Though it’s somewhat sprawling, the city boasts stunning architecture, incredible food, and an energetic nightlife that stretches until dawn. Over 10 million people visit the city each year, and the minute you step out to explore, you’ll understand why Madrid is one of Europe’s top destinations.

Like Barcelona, Madrid is a city that starts late and goes slow. It’s a city for night owls, where dinner starts late and the parties even later. But if you can embrace the laid-back pace of life, the slow meals, and the late-night vibes, you’ll have a more authentic visit and uncover the true beating heart of the city’s culture.

I love all my visits to Madrid. I’ve been a few times over the years and the city never ceases to amaze me. The food, the energy, the art (so much art!). Madrid is just cool.

Being such a big city, I know it can be easy to feel lost. Where do you start with what you want to do? Where do you go? It took me a few visits to figure it out.

In this post, I’ll help you plan an epic five-day visit to Madrid that will ensure you not only see the main sights but that you also get off the beaten path and see just what makes Madrid so popular — and all without breaking the bank either!

This first day focuses on a prestigious area designated as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2021. There are over 40 monuments and over 40 buildings on the site. It’s easily one of the most picturesque and historic areas of the city.

The route begins at the Prado Museum, one of the best museums on the planet. Here you’ll find works from El Greco, Velázquez, and Goya, as well as many other masters (such as Rubens, Botticelli, and Caravaggio to name a few). If you only visit one museum in Madrid, this is the one. It’s incredible and worth taking the time to explore. It’s one of the biggest museums in the world, too. Make sure you spend a few hours here at a minimum.

Just a 10-minute walk along the Paseo del Prado, the journey continues at the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum, a private collection spanning from the Renaissance to Pop Art, and culminates at the Reina Sofía Museum. The Reina Sofía National Art Center offers a fantastic collection of modern art. Works by masters like Picasso, Miró, Kandinsky, Dalí, and Bacon can all be found here. The centerpiece is Picasso’s famous Guernica, a 1937 oil painting considered the most moving anti-war painting in the world. While I don’t love modern art, even I enjoyed this museum.

After museum hopping, it’s time to dive into Madrid’s culinary scene. Try Taberna La Fragua de Vulcano for a rustic atmosphere perfect for sampling cocido madrileño. If you are near the Reina Sofía Museum, don’t miss the vibrant garden terrace at Arzábal, renowned for having some of the best croquetas in the city. Finally, for a unique setting, Bodega de los Secretos lets you dine in restored 17th-century wine caves, making it the most atmospheric choice near the Prado Museum.

After a late lunch, spend some time exploring Madrid’s unique ‘House Museums. These are former private palaces that preserve the intimate atmosphere of their original owners. The crown jewel of this collection is the Sorolla Museum, the sun-drenched former residence of ‘the painter of light.’ Following a major architectural renovation, this underrated museum is set to reopen its doors in 2026, offering a refreshed look at its stunning gardens and Mediterranean canvases.

Or if you want something else, there is also the nearby Museum of Romanticism, where you can enjoy a coffee in its secret garden, or visit the Lázaro Galdiano Museum to marvel at a private collection of Goya, Murillo, Velázquez, El Greco, or Bosch housed in a magnificent neo-Renaissance mansion.

In the evening, enjoy some food and relaxation.

The second day delves into the medieval and Renaissance layout of the city, famously known as Habsburg Madrid (Madrid de los Austrias). The central hub is Puerta del Sol, where a photo at Kilometer Zero and the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue are mandatory for a traveler’s geographic check-in. Kilometer Zero is the official starting point of all the highways and railways in the country, making this effectively the center of the entire country. There’s a small plaque you can snap a photo of.

Nearby is the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue (El Oso y el Madroño). The statue shows a bear reaching up to eat fruit from a madroño tree, symbols which come from Madrid’s coat of arms (the bear represents the city and the tree represents the land and nature surrounding it that has helped make it prosper).

From here, walk toward the iconic Plaza Mayor, highlighting its porticoed architecture and the Casa de la Panadería. Plaza Mayor once hosted bullfights, markets, symphonies, tournaments, and even executions. Now it’s ringed with tourist shops, cafés, and restaurants. It’s a good place from which to indulge in some people-watching, offers some good (though overpriced) bars, and occasionally has concerts and events.

For a true “Local Life” experience, stop for a calamari sandwich in the nearby alleys. Your taste buds will thank you.

After a relaxing lunch and some people watching, head to the Royal Palace of Madrid. The largest palace in Western Europe, the Baroque-style palace was built in the 18th century and is home to over 3,400 lavishly decorated rooms. It was originally built on a former 9th-century Muslim fort and today functions much like an art museum with numerous works, including pieces by Caravaggio, Juan de Flandes, and Francisco Goya. Though it’s the official residence of the royal family, they don’t actually live here anymore, and the palace is only used for official state functions. You can walk through the palace (both self-guided and guided tours are available), starting at the grand stairway, and wander through lavishly decorated staterooms. There’s also the Royal Armory, which houses a collection of medieval weapons and armor.

To end the day, head to the Almudena Cathedral. Unlike many of the famous medieval churches in Europe, this one was constructed in the late 19th century. It was finally completed in 1993 and was consecrated by Pope John Paul II. While the exterior has a Neo-Classical design (to match the nearby palace), the cathedral also has a Neo-Romanesque crypt with over 400 columns that you can explore. Be sure to head up to the dome for stunning views out over the city.

Madrid is a paradise for foodies. It’s one of the reasons I keep coming back. While there are plenty of food tours to take in Madrid, I suggest heading off on your own to explore. Begin at the city’s iconic gastronomic markets. The glass-walled Mercado de San Miguel is a must for gourmet tapas near Plaza Mayor. It’s popular with the after-work crowd and is a place I usually visit a few times on my trips. Additionally, local favorites like Mercado de San Antón in Chueca and Mercado de Vallehermoso offer a deeper dive into regional flavors. Just make sure to bring an appetite.

If you do want to take a food tour, consider doing a food tour. This post has more of my suggestions.

For dinner, head to Sobrino de Botín, officially recognized by the Guinness World Records as the world’s oldest restaurant. It was actually a favorite of Ernest Hemingway during his time in Madrid. For a more casual vibe, go ‘tapas crawling’ through the historic streets of La Latina or Barrio de las Letras.

As the sun sets, head to the Gran Vía to experience Madrid’s world-class rooftop culture. Venues like The Roof at Picalagartos or RIU, 360º sky bar offer signature cocktails and dinner with breathtaking 360-degree views of the skyline.

For those who don’t eat meat, Madrid has actually evolved into one of Europe’s best veg hubs, boasting a vibrant vegetarian and vegan scene in neighborhoods like Malasaña, where plant-based versions of traditional Spanish dishes are now a staple of the city’s diverse culinary identity.

Madrid is the only European capital where nature, science, and royal history converge in a UNESCO World Heritage oasis known as the ‘Paisaje de la Luz‘ (Landscape of Light). But this prestigious area, encompassing the iconic El Retiro Park and the Paseo del Prado, is just the beginning of Spain’s monumental legacy. For more UNESCO wonders, take a day trip out of the city.

One popular destination worth visiting is the Monastery of San Lorenzo de El Escorial, a sprawling imperial masterpiece recognized by UNESCO for its historical significance. El Escorial is located just one hour from the city by car and was commissioned by Philip II in the 16th century. It’s a massive palatial complex that includes a monastery, library, palace, basilica, and tomb for Spanish monarchs. Yet as massive as it is, it feels more austere than other palatial complexes, likely owing to its granite walls and symmetrical layout.

Another option for a day trip is the Royal Palace and Gardens of Aranjuez, a World Heritage Cultural Landscape that rivals the beauty of Versailles. Located just one hour south of the city, this was originally a hunting lodge, also commissioned in the 16th century by Philip II. It’s a blend of Renaissance and Baroque styles, with lavish rooms filled with tapestries, porcelain, and ornate decorations. There is lots of greenery and gardens here, which is partly why the royal family used this as their spring residence.

Lastly, there’s the historic university city of Alcalá de Henares, the birthplace of Spanish novelist, poet, and playwright Cervantes (he wrote Don Quixote). Just 45 minutes away by car, it also holds its own UNESCO World Heritage status, offering a perfectly preserved look into the Spanish Golden Age (1492–1659).

On your last day, it’s time to get further off the beaten path. Step back into the Golden Age at the Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales and the nearby Royal Monastery of La Encarnación, two hidden palaces that house breathtaking royal art collections behind their cloistered walls.

The Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales is a convent founded in 1559 by Joanna of Austria (sister of Philip II). The name “Descalzas Reales” (which means “Royal Barefoot Ladies”) refers to the Order of Saint Clare nuns who lived here in relative austerity. What makes this monastery unique is that many aristocratic women took refuge here, often bringing their artworks and other valuables. Over the years, this turned the convent into a veritable treasure trove of art.

The Royal Monastery of La Encarnación was founded in 1611 by the wife of Philip III, Margaret of Austria. It was a royal convent, meaning it had the direct support of the monarchy. While the exterior has an austere Baroque style, the interior is quite lavish, with ornate chapels, colorful frescoes, and lots of religious sculptures and paintings. It’s also home to several notable relics, including a vial said to contain the blood of Saint Januarius. While tours are available, it’s still an active convent so parts are not open to the public (which, honestly, makes it all the more interesting to see).

To end your day with a local touch, head to the vast Casa de Campo park. This is the largest public park in the city, created in 1931. It covers a whopping 17 square kilometers (6.5 square miles) and includes an artificial lake, lots of paths, a zoo, and even an amusement park. Here, you can enjoy a scenic lunch or dinner at one of the lakeside terraces, offering an unrivaled view of the Royal Palace and Almudena Cathedral across the skyline. It’s the perfect place to end your trip.

While Barcelona tends to get more attention, I think Madrid is one of the best cities in Europe. It boasts a mouthwatering culinary scene, a raucous nightlife, and tons of things to see and do — no matter your interest or budget. I’ve been visiting the city for almost two decades and never get tired of the tapas, architecture, and history. The city just packs so much in and there really is something for everyone here. By following the itinerary above, you’ll see all the main sights while also getting off the beaten path in Spain’s historic capital.

#6355. Cruising to Alaska? Check if Your Next Port, Bus, or Lodge is Indigenous-Owned

The Huna Totem Corporation was featured on Condé Nast Traveler's Bright Ideas in Travel 2026. Read the full list of winners here.

From April to October, cruise ships tower over downtown Juneau’s Marine Way, a coastal path that connects the port zone to downtown. Should a traveler pause for a moment between ship and souvenir store, they’ll notice Kaagwaantaan Kootéeyaa, a tall, intricately carved pole rising against a backdrop of forest and mountains. At its base, a panel explains that the cedar pole depicts five of the Kaagwaantaan Tlingit clan’s crests: a hat, person, orca, eagle and bear. It is an arresting introduction to the long-overlooked human history of this place.

Since 2023, totem poles have adorned this highly trafficked shoreline, part of Kootéeyaa Deiyí (“Totem Pole Trail”)—a city-wide project led by the Sealaska Heritage Institute (SHI) that represents the cultures of the Tlingit people who have inhabited Juneau for at least 10,000 years, as well as the Haida and Tsimshian who arrived a few hundred years ago. Visible evidence of the region’s Indigenous communities was previously limited, says SHI’s Ricardo Worl (Tlingit), who sees the trail as “an opportunity to reestablish our presence on our ancestral lands.” Noting that more than a million cruise ship passengers land in Juneau each year, Worl hopes the trail “is the beginning of their education about our culture.”

Alaska’s cruise industry has long invited travelers to experience the “Last Frontier” while relegating Indigenous peoples to the margins of the tourism economy. Now, a shift is occurring—one that goes beyond simply incorporating Indigenous culture into the cruise experience. Across Alaska, Native corporations are increasingly owning and shaping the tourism infrastructure itself, from cruise docks and terminals to ground transportation, giving them a greater stake in how destinations develop, and how visitors experience them.

I came to Alaska to see how Indigenous ownership is changing the experience on the ground, following a route that took me from whale watching at cruise ports on the coast to bear and moose spotting at a lodge deep in the Interior. At each stop, I saw how Alaska Native corporations are shaping the places that travelers pass through.

Created following passage of the 1971 Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, Alaska Native corporations are for-profit companies run by and for Alaska Native shareholders. For Huna Totem, a Tlingit village corporation representing shareholders with ties to Hoonah and Glacier Bay, tourism is an important part of its economic development strategy. Its best-known development, Icy Strait Point in Hoonah, is Alaska’s first private cruise destination and has become a model for Alaska Native-owned tourism—creating local jobs, keeping economic benefits within the community and making Tlingit culture part of the visitor experience.

When Icy Strait Point opened in 2004, Huna Totem leadership was focused on “providing economic stability for generations, so the culture can be perpetuated,” says Ruth Banaszak, director of marketing and communications. Icy Strait Point has two cruise ship piers located about a half-mile apart and activity areas for 30 different excursions to distribute visitor flow around the site so that it never becomes overwhelming. To get around the vast site, I made use of the forested walking trails and two gondola systems, one of which took me to the summit of Hoonah Mountain, which I quickly and thrillingly descended via the ZipRider, a six-cable zipline. Walking around the museum exhibits housed inside a 1912 salmon cannery that closed when the fishing industry declined, I could connect tourism's present and future with its economic history. The cannery was once a symbol of loss; now it provides new economic opportunities. “We hire around 350 people for the season,” says Banaszak. “So, in a town of 950, anybody who wants to have a job in the community has one.” The model has also allowed local residents to build businesses of their own, including boat tours to Point Adolphus where, in just two hours, I spotted dozens of orcas, a few humpback whales and uncountable numbers of sea lions and sea otters. In each place, instead of being whisked onto an excursion operated by an outside company, I was experiencing a destination that had been shaped by the community whose ancestral home I was visiting.

“We’ve done this for our own community in Hoonah,” says Banaszak, “so now [we’re asking] how can we take what we’ve learned here and help other rural communities do the same thing?”

That thinking has led Huna Totem around Southeast Alaska and beyond. In Whittier, the corporation opened Glacier Gateway cruise terminal in 2024. Huna Totem and Doyon, Limited, another Alaska Native corporation, have also acquired Portage Glacier Cruises and Alaska Coach Tours, creating Native-owned touchpoints that extend from ship to shore and beyond. In Klawock, on Prince of Wales Island, Huna Totem partnered with Doyon and the local Alaska Native village corporation Klawock Heenya to develop a new cruise port in 2024. The destination uses a single-ship model, with development focused on Tlingit culture, local involvement and community values.

Back in downtown Juneau, Huna Totem is developing Áak’w Landing, a cruise dock and waterfront development targeting its first full season in 2028. The project is designed to improve how cruise visitors move through the city—including eliminating the need for tender boats at the site—rather than simply bringing in more ships. Reflecting its approach of being “culturally driven, community-centric, [and] business-focused,” says Banaszak, Huna Totem sees the project as both infrastructure enhancement and an opportunity to incorporate Alaska Native culture into the visitor experience—two poles from SHI’s Kootéeyaa Deiyí will be raised at the site.

The broader ambition is to create a network of Native-owned tourism businesses across Alaska. “So that Alaska Native tourism grows: culturally-led tourism as it should be done, people telling their own story themselves,” Banaszak says.

The cruise industry may seem an odd venture for Doyon, Limited, which is based in Fairbanks and represents the largely Dene people of the Interior, but, says Jordan Sanford, president of Doyon Tourism, “more than 60% of visitors come to Alaska by cruise, so [we realized] if we wanted to grow, we needed to be involved.”

Deep in Denali National Park, Doyon has operated Kantishna Roadhouse, the park’s only Indigenous-owned lodge, for 30 years. Arriving via a small plane from the park entrance—road access, closed for five years due to a landslide, will return in 2027—I spent blissful days backcountry hiking free from cell service. Evenings were spent listening to presentations by staff, such as an introduction to Dene beadwork and regalia; spotting wildlife including grizzly bears, moose, and caribou, then watching the setting sun light up the slopes of mighty Denali. Since 2004, in partnership with Aramark, Doyon has also operated bus tours, transit services, and campgrounds in the park. The partnership with Huna Totem gives Doyon an opportunity to diversify and grow, while responding to a recent shift in cruise passengers’ expectations: “They’re looking for more authentic experiences,” she explains. “We see that as our advantage. We put shareholders to work, and they share their culture,” she says. “There's a lot of businesses here that have been sharing the culture for so long, but from non-Alaska Natives,” she adds.

Next up is the restoration of the 1925 Chatanika Gold Camp near Fairbanks, which is scheduled to open in 2028 as a northern lights experience center, filling a critical infrastructure gap. Aurora viewing in Alaska today typically means pulling off the side of the road and drinking a hot chocolate, says Sanford. With Chatanika, “we're creating a space [with] cultural programming to make it more of an experience.”

It’s another link in an emerging network of Native-owned businesses across the state. The ultimate goal is “an Alaska Native-owned corridor, where [travelers] are visiting Alaska Native-owned businesses along the way,” says Sanford. For cruise passengers, that means more opportunities to encounter Indigenous culture, while knowing that Indigenous people are benefiting from the industry. And it means that your next Alaska cruise itinerary might begin at a Native-owned port, continue aboard a Native-owned bus, lead to a Native-owned excursion, and end at a Native-owned lodge.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6353. The Very Best Thai Food in New York City

There are several ways to describe delicious food in Thai: Aroy means delicious, while aroy mak takes it a step further to very delicious. But my favorite word is zaab (also spelled zabb or zab; แซ่บ), a term rooted in the Isan region of northeastern Thailand that conveys a bold deliciousness, often associated with the heat. In New York City, we’re spoiled for choice when it comes to food that delivers true zaab.

I’ve spent my life immersed in the world of Thai food. One of the joys of growing up in a Thai restaurant family is participating in one of our favorite hobbies: scoping out other Thai restaurants to see what’s good. Most summers, my aunts would close down their restaurant in Royal Palm Beach for two weeks, and they’d road trip from South Florida up to New York City to check out casinos and taste Thai restaurants along the way—when I was lucky, I got to join them. My grandpa, for his part, used to drive to the city weekly to get products for his grocery store in Washington, DC, and through his firsthand research, old friends, and the Internet, he created detailed restaurant guides to help me find footing when I moved to the city almost five years ago.

As I continue to eat my way through the city’s Thai restaurants, I feel spoiled for choice. More and more chefs are serving regional specialties of their hometowns and maintaining Thai food’s great balancing act between the spice, acid, salt, sweetness, and umami, while incorporating their own signature flair.

While the city’s established Thai spots, particularly out in Elmhurst, Queens, remain beloved, plenty of the most compelling and exciting bites can be found in various parts of the city. There has never been a more exciting time to eat Thai food in NYC, and these 14 restaurants best embody its golden era.

If you want an overview of the best dishes across Thailand without leaving the city, let your first stop in Queen’s Little Thai Town be Ayada. The beloved restaurant has familiar favorites like pad thai and tom yum, but let its expertise in other regional favorites be an excuse to try my dad’s favorite Yen Ta Fo, a bubblegum-pink soup with soft rice noodles and a savory tomato and bean curd sauce.

364 Grand Street, Brooklyn, NY 11211 (Williamsburg)

Must-order dish: Any of the fiery curries on the rotating menu

When the news of Ugly Baby’s closure last year hit my WhatsApp chat with my Thai friends, you would’ve thought that someone had died. In a way, it felt like we lost a family member. Ugly Baby was one of the rare spots in the city that didn’t hold back on heat like many in America do to appease Western palates and milder heat tolerances. But all was saved when the beloved restaurant announced its reopening in Williamsburg earlier this fall. It’s now a fun, lively two-floor restaurant with eclectic dishware and recipes from various Thai provinces, including brutally hot curries from Southern Thailand and Northeastern Isan cuisine.

Its menu is sorted from least spicy to most spicy—written out as “the laughs” to “the ugly” (dishes toward the latter end consist of a few menu items that will make you feel like you’re breathing fire). Luckily, waiters are standing by with large jugs of water, ready to refill at the sight of sweat dripping down your forehead.

Bangkok Supper Club makes a convincing case for the arrival of upscale Thai dining.

Order a la carte, or do the $150 tasting menu at Bangkok Supper Club.

641 Hudson St, New York, NY 10014 (Meatpacking District)

With an award-winning cocktail program by Suwincha "Chacha" Singsuwan and a menu from executive chef Max Wittawat, Bangkok Supper Club makes a convincing case for the arrival of upscale Thai dining. The drinks are as much of a draw as the food. I like to start my meal with a fish sauce cocktail, a savory, umami-forward drink that captures the depth of fish sauce while balancing it with sweet notes of floral pear. It’s unexpected, but feels just right, and is a lovely accompaniment to my other must-order: the pork jowl. These deep-fried pork cheeks arrive atop a fragrant, garlic-baked rice.

One of the best parts about eating in Thailand is getting food from restaurants and stalls that specialize in one singular dish. As my dad says, that’s how you know it’s good. Eim Khao Mun Kai is one such place. Its one dish, khao mun gai, is the Thai version of Hainanese chicken rice, served with a spicy, fermented bean sauce.

The $12 set meal includes tender steamed chicken thighs made with halal meat and gizzards, fragrant ginger rice that’s cooked with chicken droppings, and a savory broth-based soup made from the bones, with sides of cilantro and cucumber plus plenty of sauce. It’s a tight shop and cash-only. When my dad comes into town, it’s the first place we go to.

Must-order dish: Northern-style curry noodles

Since 1990, this institution has been serving what my friend calls “old-school auntie energy” with wooden accents, white tablecloths, and a sprawling menu. When I say sprawling, I mean it. You can flip through pages at SriPraPhai and can eat all the fried meats, papaya salads, curries, and noodle dishes your heart desires.

Zaab Zaab specializes in Northeast Isan cuisine, repping where both owners are from.

76-04 Woodside Ave, Queens, NY 11373 (Elmhurst)

208 Grand St, Brooklyn, NY 11211 (Williamsburg)

Zaab Zaab has locations in both Elmhurst and Williamsburg, and specializes in Northeast Isan cuisine from where owner Bryan Chunton and chef Aniwat Khotsopa hail. The restaurant’s signature dish, an herb-packed larb ped udon, features cilantro- and mint-packed ground duck, fried liver, and crispy skin; it’s served with a plethora of fresh lettuce, cabbage, extra herbs, and sticky rice. When I go with a group, though, I also make sure we order the pla neung manow, which comes steamed with a chili, garlic, and lime sauce that’s so flavorful, you’ll want to drink it like soup (luckily it’s served with little bowls so you can).

800 Grand St, Brooklyn, NY 11211 (Williamsburg)

Must-order dish: Chor muang for an appetizer; pad kea mao seafood as a main

Focusing on 19th- century recipes from the royal consort court, Kaew Jao Jorm’s (named after the former King Rama V’s favorite flower) serves a regal menu in its intimate, 20-seat restaurant. The exterior is on an unassuming street in Williamsburg, but inside, it is the restaurant incarnation of Mary Poppins' bag: compact, but they manage to pack in far more than you’d expect.

Though the signature dumplings, chor muang—chicken and peanut filling encased in delicate butterfly pea flower dough—are the star, don’t overlook the noodle dishes, which are slurpable, expertly sauced, and so soft as to be almost buttery.

Thai Diner does diner favorites reimagined, like their beloved Thai Disco Fries.

Head to Thai Diner for brunch, lunch, or a vibey dinner.

If you have friends from out of town that you really want to impress and show how fun eating in New York City can be, go to Thai Diner and get an order of the Thai Disco Fries. I find that these crispy, crinkle-cut fries smothered in a peanutty massaman curry sauce are delicious enough to justify to out-of-towners how much you overspend on rent. Reservations can be hard to get, but they do take some walk-ins, so your best bet is to either arrive slightly before opening, or put your name down and wander around Nolita until your name is called.

The restaurant has a tropical dive bar feel, with plenty of diner favorites reimagined like a custardy Thai tea babka, French toast, and a signature Thai Diner egg sandwich made with Isan-style sausage wrapped in a plush roti. Co-owners Ann Redding and Matt Danzer also recently opened Mommy Pai’s, a fast Thai chicken takeout spot on the same block that’s a great lunch spot without the wait.

Dishes are meant to be shared family-style here—like a whole fish drenched in cliantro-lime broth.

661 Driggs Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11211 (Williamsburg)

Must-order dish: Steamed fish with Thai herbs

Specializing in seafood dishes, Fish Cheeks focuses on the bright flavors of southern coastal Thailand. Dishes are meant to be shared family-style here, and though the menu features a few poultry, pork, and beef options, your best bet is trusting the name and going straight for fish. I recommend getting a whole steamed fish for the table—your dinnermates will relish in sharing the communal centerpiece and drenching rice in its cilantro-lime broth, or the coconut crab curry, which comes with rice noodles for soaking up every last bit of the creamy sauce.

Though its flagship Noho location can book out quickly, its equally delicious (and newer) spot in Williamsburg is a bit easier to secure a reservation at, for now.

New Flatiron restaurant LenLen is definitively cool.

The menu at LenLen includes crowd-pleasers and bolder dishes like a durian crab curry.

40 E 20th St, New York, NY 10003 (Flatiron)

If I had to describe LenLen in one word, it would be cool. This relatively new spot hit Flatiron earlier this year, bringing a fresh excitement to the Thai food scene in midtown. For me, the standout of the menu is the love-it-or-loathe-it durian crab curry. It’s earthy, fruity, and well worth the visit alone. While you’re there, order the wagyu beef boat noodles, too, which are served in a rich, dark broth that reminds me of the ones I’ve had in Ayutthaya, one of my favorite cities in Thailand (and the birthplace of boat noodles).

There are whispers of a speakeasy opening downstairs in the coming months, which gives the restaurant extra potential to become a go-to dinner spot that seamlessly transitions into a night out.

Ler Lers does classic Bangkok-style fare right.

From pad thai to grilled meats, Ler Lers does it all.

417 Tompkins Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11216 (Bed-Stuy)

Not to be confused with LenLen, Ler Lers is a newer spot in Bed-Stuy and does classic Bangkok-style fare right. Its ambiance is stylish and warm, with a mix of rattan and earthy tones, for a setting that makes sipping on a sweet iced Thai tea feel right even on a cold rainy day.

I’m pretty weary of ordering pad thai out in restaurants, just because the cuisine has so much else to offer. But a friend promised me that the pad thai topped with crispy pork belly was “awesome,” and after trying it for myself, I’ve started saying the same to friends and family. The rest of the menu has a lot of other familiar favorites like fried rice and grilled meats, and if you’re someone who enjoys a sticky tamarind sauce as much as I do, try the branzino, too.

Hommali is stylish in every sense of the word, from the plating to the space.

The Hommali cocktail menu is also expansive—go for the signature tomato option.

28 7th Ave S, New York, NY 10014 (West Village)

A newcomer to the West Village restaurant scene, this design-forward space has some serious pedigree with a menu curated by Bangkok-native Chattchakorn “Benz” Khajornchaisan, formerly of Eleven Madison Park. The restaurant is stylish in every sense of the word, with sage green tiles, oak accents, and warm lighting.

You can’t customize spice level here, so expect to get a little red from dishes like the prik larb beef tartare that comes with crispy tripe chips and is fiery with northern larb spices. The Hommali Five Spice dry-aged duck is also a standout and comes with fragrant rice that’s cooked in duck drippings. My opinion? The best order is getting the panang curry with tender beef cheek. It’s spicy, nutty, and you’ll want to order a side (or two) of roti to soak up that sauce.

The cocktail menu is also expansive—go for the signature tomato cocktail, which is vodka and rice wine-based with tomato extract, poblanos, and tamarind.

Soothr in the East Village specializes in noodles from all across Thailand.

204 E 13th St, New York, NY 10003 (East Village)

25-20 43rd Ave, Long Island City, NY 11101

Must-order dish: Sukhothai-style tom yum noodle soup

Thai noodle shop Soothr specializes in noodles from all across Thailand, and though the stir-fried variety is delicious, the soup noodles are the real standout. The Sukhothai-style tom yum noodle soup is a must-order, and encapsulates the best of Thai noodle soups with a deeply savory-acidic broth topped with bouncy fish cakes, meatballs, and rice noodles. Soothr has a new-ish Long Island City location that’s got a more nightlife vibe to it (and just as great noodles).

Kru in Williamsburg draws on Thailand’s vast culinary history, reimaging regional traditions through a contemporary lens.

90 N 14 St, Brooklyn, NY 11249 (Williamsburg)

Must-order dish: Lamb massaman curry pot pie

Named after the Thai word for “mentor,” chef Ohm Suansilphong honors the many teachers in his life through Kru. Here, he draws on Thailand’s vast culinary history, reimaging regional traditions through a contemporary lens. This looks like a crispy, massaman curry pot pie sprinkled with slow-cooked, pull-apart jackfruit, and tender lamb or tamarind-chili coated calamari that’s sweet, salty, and a little spicy. Chef adds and tweaks the menu seasonally, but I suggest the first thing you eat is always the Ma Hor, a savory bite of seasoned meat atop fresh fruit. The word means galloping horse, and it has enough warmth to open your tastebuds for the rest of the meal. Pay attention to the wine list: the restaurant is just as thoughtful about its award-winning program as it is the rest of the menu. Consider this a go-to as worthy of casual weeknight dinners as it is of special occasions.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

On the first Wednesday of each month, Atmos Rewards unveils new Members Day offers, including new Global Getaways destinations. Here's a look at the best November Members Day offers.

Atmos Rewards just launched its November Global Getaways offers. Each destination has its own eligible travel dates, but you must book by Nov. 7.

*Blackout dates to Hawaii are Dec. 17 to Dec. 30, 2026, and Feb. 12 through Feb. 15, 2027, and from Hawaii are Dec. 27, 2026, to Jan. 4, 2027, and Feb. 19 to Feb. 21, 2027.

Related: Alaska and Hawaiian expand 'Atmos Communities' with 6 new options to save and earn

One example of a route covered by this month's promotion is the following itinerary from Seattle to Venice. It costs just 25,000 points and $48 in taxes and fees. While writing this story, we saw 25,000-point award options for this route on many dates.

If you are an Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card holder, the taxes and fees on this award are only $27.60.

Prefer a trip to Singapore? We found awards from Los Angeles to Singapore on many dates for 30,000 points and $49 in taxes and fees (or $29 if you are an Alaska Summit cardholder).

Meanwhile, you can fly from Seattle to Honolulu on many dates for 11,500 points and $6 in taxes and fees.

You'll want to book quickly, though, as availability at the lowest rates will likely decrease as other members book. To book, go to the Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines website, log in to your account, click the "Use points" box and enter your desired itinerary before clicking "Search flights."

Keep in mind that you can book many routes besides the ones discussed in this story as long as your award is between the U.S. and an eligible destination on eligible travel dates.

Related: Which credit card should you use for Alaska Airlines flights?

Atmos Rewards Unlocked is the rewards marketplace where Atmos Rewards members can redeem or bid points on experiences and partner offerings.

This month, Atmos Rewards is letting members redeem 65,000 Atmos Rewards points for a 2026-27 Ikon Base Pass and 100,000 points for an Ikon Pass with $100 of mountain credits for use at participating resorts. These redemptions include one free day of ski butler service during the season with an equipment rental of two days or more. Active Escapes community members save 20%; redemptions close Nov. 23.

You'll also find plenty of other opportunities to redeem Atmos Rewards points for unique experiences, including an Iditarod insider experience, special getaways and even a behind-the-scenes tour of the Alaska Airlines Global Training Center. Head to the Atmos Rewards Unlocked page to see all the options.

There are multiple ways to earn Atmos Rewards points. You can, of course, earn them by flying Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines. The carriers also partner with over 30 airlines, including (but not limited to) members of the Oneworld alliance.

The Atmos Rewards cobranded credit cards are also a good way to accumulate points. You can earn points on purchases with these cards, but their welcome offers are also a way to quickly boost your account balance.

You can also transfer Bilt Points to Atmos Rewards at a 1:1 ratio and Marriott Bonvoy points to Atmos Rewards at a 3:1 ratio. And through Nov. 7, you can buy up to 250,000 Atmos Rewards points with a bonus of up to 110%. The 110% bonus kicks in when you buy 30,000 points or more. So, you could buy 30,000 points and get 33,000 bonus points for $1,128.75 (a purchase rate of 1.79 cents per point).

Related: Atmos Ascent vs. Atmos Summit: The Summit is better — but not for everyone

The Atmos Rewards Unlocked program provides some interesting ways to redeem points, but the Atmos Rewards Global Getaways deals are the true star of each month's Members Day.

Global Getaways are an excellent opportunity for travelers who want to book travel to the highlighted destinations, can book their flights within a few days and can travel during the specified time period. And if you are striving for Atmos Rewards status, keep in mind that you'll earn status points on Atmos Rewards award tickets.
