#6333. There's a New Luxury Sleeper Train Route Coming to the French Riviera Next Spring

As someone who travels a lot for work, I would give anything to swap a flight for a train—even if that means spending eight hours on the rails.

Thankfully, it's easy to travel Europe by train at nearly any price point. And although I am a big fan of modern high-speed routes, the most romantic way to see the continent is certainly aboard one of Belmond's gorgeous luxury trains, which travel to destinations such as the British countryside, the Amalfi Coast, and the Scottish Highlands.

But in 2027, my bucket-list Belmond journey is a glamorous new addition to its already impressive collection of itineraries: the French Riviera.

The Venice Simplon-Orient-Express offers three cabin types: Historic Cabins, Suites, and Grand Suites.

On May 10, 2027, the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express is launching a new route from Paris to Monaco, traveling to Monte Carlo for the first time in its history.

The journey, which will become a regular addition to the train's annual schedule, will take passengers through some of the most spectacular scenery along the French Riviera before arriving in the glamorous principality.

The new route will take travelers to Monte Carlo for the first time in the train's history.

The experience begins in Paris, where passengers will board the train's distinctive midnight blue carriages before settling into their accommodation for the night. There are several options to choose from, including the classic Historic Cabins, Suites, and Grand Suites, each drawing inspiration from the train's Art Deco heritage.

For those looking to really splash out, there's also L'Observatoire, an exclusive carriage created in collaboration with French artist JR. Designed as a private sanctuary on the rails, it comes complete with a bedroom, an en-suite bathroom featuring a freestanding bathtub, a spacious living area, a library, and even a secret tearoom.

As evening approaches, guests can enjoy dinner in one of the train's two restaurant cars, Étoile du Nord and L'Oriental, before heading to the famous Bar Car 3674 for cocktails and live piano music.

But perhaps the most exciting part of the new journey comes the following morning. After waking up to breakfast served in their cabins, passengers will be treated to sweeping views of the Mediterranean as the train makes its way along the Côte d'Azur. The route passes the red cliffs of the Massif de l'Estérel and travels through Saint-Raphaël towards Cannes and Nice. The train will then continue towards Monaco before arriving at Monaco-Monte-Carlo station.

Breakfast served aboard the Venice-Simplon Orient Express.

Monte Carlo also has a surprising connection to the train's history. In 1977, two original train carriages were purchased at an auction in the principality, helping set in motion the project that would eventually become the luxury train we know today.

“Introducing the destination feels like a natural continuation for the Venice-Simplon Orient Express, bringing the romance of luxury rail travel to a locale that has always understood the art of arrival,” says Pascal Deyrolle, Belmond's Europe area managing director for trains. “There's also something rather special about coming back to Monte Carlo, given the role it played in the train's history.”

The new journey is part of Belmond's expanding collection of European rail experiences, alongside the second year of its “Villeggiatura by Train” itinerary, which connects the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express with Belmond hotels in Italy.

Of course, a journey this luxurious comes with a price tag to match. Tickets for the new Paris-to-Monte-Carlo route start from €4,870 (approximately $5,450) per person, based on two people sharing a Historic Cabin. The fare includes the overnight journey, all meals with sommelier-selected wines, unlimited soft drinks, transfers, and 24-hour steward service.

Good news for travelers who prefer vacation rentals over luxury hotels: Chase is giving select cardholders thousands of new ways to put their travel benefits to use.

Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, The Edit by Chase Travel℠ will include more than 10,000 curated vacation homes in addition to its existing collection of luxury hotels and resorts.

That means eligible Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees), Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ (see rates and fees) and J.P. Morgan Reserve® cardholders will soon be able to use their annual The Edit statement credits toward vacation home stays — and potentially enjoy additional perks as part of their stay (minimum four-night stay required).

The information for the J.P. Morgan Reserve card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

If you're unfamiliar, The Edit by Chase Travel is a curated collection of luxury hotels and resorts that offers eligible cardholders additional perks when booking through the Chase Travel portal (minimum two-night stay required).

Currently featuring more than 1,500 hotels and resorts, the collection will expand to include more than 10,000 vacation homes beginning Jan. 1.

The homes will be curated by Plum Guide, a luxury vacation rental platform that evaluates properties using "more than 150 criteria related to comfort, design and location".

This builds on Chase Travel's partnership with Plum Guide, announced in April 2026, which brought luxury vacation rentals to more Chase cardholders through the travel portal.

With the latest expansion, eligible Reserve cardholders will have access to a curated collection of vacation homes through The Edit, complete with premium benefits.

Cardholders will also have the flexibility to redeem Chase Ultimate Rewards points toward these stays through Chase Travel.

Additionally, Sapphire Reserve and Reserve Business cardholders will have access to Reserve Travel Designers, who can help match travelers with vacation homes and provide personalized concierge assistance before, during and after their stays.

Related: I’ve been using the Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business for a year — here’s why I’m keeping it

One of the biggest draws of booking a hotel through The Edit is the additional perks that come with a qualifying stay (minimum two-night stay required).

Depending on the property, these can include complimentary breakfast for two, a $100 property credit, room upgrades when available and early check-in and late checkout.

Vacation home bookings through The Edit will come with a different set of benefits.

There's an important catch, however: Vacation home stays must be at least four nights to qualify for these The Edit benefits. Some benefits are subject to availability and may vary by property.

Eligible cardholders will also be able to use their annual The Edit statement credits toward qualifying vacation home bookings.

As a refresher, here's how those credits break down:

Beginning on Jan. 1, 2027, the Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business will offer four statement credits of up to $250 each for The Edit stays that can be used throughout the year. That's up from two statement credits of up to $250 each available on the card in 2026.

Keep in mind that while a two-night prepaid booking may qualify for the statement credit, vacation home stays must be at least four nights to receive the additional The Edit benefits.

Also, be aware that while you can redeem Ultimate Rewards points for eligible bookings, stays paid entirely with points do not qualify for The Edit statement credits under Chase's current terms. If you want to use the statement credit, you'll need to make an eligible prepaid purchase with your card.

Related: How to stack Sapphire Reserve credits for up to $500 off

The addition of more than 10,000 vacation homes to The Edit is welcome news for eligible Chase cardholders, particularly those who prefer the space and flexibility of a vacation rental over a traditional luxury hotel.

It also gives cardholders more options for using their annual The Edit statement credits, while offering perks such as a $150 in-stay credit and early check-in and late checkout when available.

Just keep the minimum-stay requirements in mind, and compare prices before booking to make sure you're getting the best value.

#6331. This Is The Summer To Tick Santorini Off The Bucket List

It’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

In the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

But now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

And the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

The trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up quickly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

As an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

Naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.

#6330. American Airlines Dropped Trump’s Name From West Palm Beach Gate Screens Ahead Of Midterm Elections

American Airlines quietly removed the Trump reference from its gate monitors for flights to West Palm Beach. The timing will invite speculation, but the simpler destination label is an improvement regardless of what prompted the change, which does not appear politically-motivated to me.

JonNYC reports that American has changed its destination displays from “Pres DJT, W Palm Beach” back to “West Palm Beach, FL.”

That reverses a change introduced after Palm Beach International Airport was renamed President Donald J. Trump International Airport earlier this year.

so… has anyone noticed that AA has changed the gate monitors from “Pres DJT, W Palm Beach” back to “West Palm Beach, FL” ?

The change is likely not connected to this week’s election and occurred in August as part of a planned transition. The IATA code for the airport is still DJT after the July 9, 2026 change from PBI.

The original change was peculiar because American generally identifies destinations by city, adding airport names when useful to distinguish between airports serving the same destination.

American does not ordinarily add the presidential names associated with airports serving places like Little Rock (Bill Clinton) or Grand Rapids (Gerald Ford). The West Palm Beach label stood out. Then again, as I indicated above, other airports did not change their IATA code.

There is a very practical reason to distinguish New York JFK from New York LaGuardia or Washington Reagan (National) from Washington Dulles. Leading with presidential initials on a flight to West Palm Beach offers less obvious help to passengers.

There was no possibility of similar confusion when flying into West Palm Beach.

Of course people will notice that this reversal surfaced around the midterm elections, but as I mentioned this goes back to August. Even so, it is an irresistible invitation to speculate about corporate America adjusting to a changed political environment, which was becoming clear even over the summer.

But I think it’s safe to say that American’s leadership did not order a “political” retreat, no matter what some MAGA world may be suggesting this morning. This was more likely all part of the transition plan.

I would be equally cautious about declaring that the original wording was personally ordered by executives seeking favor with the administration, though that could well be the choice as well. It was an unusual choice. The reasoning behind it remains a separate question.

Still, American created an unnecessary distraction by departing from a straightforward city label in the first place. Once a company makes a conspicuous change involving a political figure, undoing it will inevitably attract attention too…especially now.

American Airlines has restored the West Palm Beach destination label on its gate monitors, removing the presidential reference it added earlier this year.

The timing will generate political interpretations. Without more information, I would leave those as speculation and it appears wholly unrelated. The practical result is easier to assess: passengers once again see the name of the place they are flying to. That works for me. Now it’s time to move DJT back to PBI…there was certainly no need for that change either, though that ship (plane?) has sailed.

#6329. On Location: How Coastal Newfoundland Set the Scene for Netflix's No. 1 Series ‘Below’

A mysterious sea creature is captivating audiences on Netflix as the Josh Hartnett-led series Below remains the No. 1 show in Netflix’s global rankings. The six-episode thriller paints an eerie image of small-town life in Newfoundland, and viewers are intrigued by the mystique of the striking Canadian backdrop.

Despite the fictional giant squid terrorizing Snook’s Arm, the show pulls on elements of reality, from climate change affecting the Atlantic Canadian sea life to the government-run resettling of remote fishing towns, which started in 1954 and continues to this day. It’s that history that drew production designer Emmanuel Fréchette into the project.

“When I found out that more than 300 towns in Newfoundland had been resettled, I was amazed,” he tells Traveler. “The script is very interesting, mixing that reality with the mundane life in Newfoundland—and this creature!” After all, creator Jesse McKeown (The Umbrella Academy) had frequented the region for years, inspired to bring an authentic depiction of its culture to the screen.

That started behind the scenes as the cast and crew engaged in Newfoundland and Labrador’s most famous tradition. Visitors, who they called CFAs (or Come from Aways—this is also where Broadway hit musical draws its name), get “screeched in” by kissing a cod to become honorary citizens. So they all went to St. John’s Christian’s Pub to pucker up. “The guy there is such a great character, and he has a routine and speech that’s very entertaining," Fréchette says.

When it came to filming locations, the remote regions posed practical challenges, so the majority of the sets were built by production, a joy for Fréchette, who was trained as an architect. “I was stunned by the humble architecture, built by boat owners and builders,” he says of the homes’ low ceilings. “The structures are very endearing and make you think of a boat, so I wanted to follow that thread.”

That’s also what helped root the fantastical storyline into reality. “This was vernacular architecture—architecture without architects—just following the needs of the people out of survival, and I found that so beautiful,” he says. “So I really tried to mimic what I was seeing all around me that survived the decades.”

And it’s clearly had an effect on audiences. According to data provided by Booking.com, not only have searches for the province’s capital of St. John’s risen 16.9% by Americans on the platform compared to last year, but the coastal town of Twillingate, home to the floating icebergs, has skyrocketed 123.7%.

Here, Fréchette shares the filming locations from the popular Netflix series Below.

The show is set in the actual resettled town of Snook’s Arm, which had a population of 10 when it was approved for resettlement in 2017, according to the CBC. But its remote location would have been difficult to film in with such a big crew, so Brigus South—a town with a population of about 700 at last count in 2021—stood in.

“We picked that place because it had a connection with the water,” Fréchette says of the inlet going deep into the land. “Lots of the characters are dragged into the water, so it was great to have this presence for the eeriness.”

But to get the cozy town ready for its close-up took work, as the crew designed and built about 80% of what appears in the series, including the fish plant, Fishermen’s Hall, and wharf. The Penneys home was an existing home they covered, and the church was also a house that they retrofitted, adding the bell tower.

When Fréchette was scouting locations, he stayed in a hostel by the sea in Twillingate, about 275 miles northwest of the capital. “We’d be having a coffee with the window open, and suddenly we were freezing,” he recalls of a sudden drop in temperature from 68 degrees Fahrenheit to 50 degrees Fahrenheit. That’s when they’d look up and see an iceberg floating their way. “It lowers the temperature all around the bay—it’s such an amazing phenomenon.”

As it turns out, the Atlantic town sits along Iceberg Alley, where from late April through July, the remnants of broken glaciers glide down the coast. Many of the shots of Calvin (Hartnett) harvesting icebergs were actual footage from these massive blocks of ice naturally floating along.

The capital served as the home base for the cast and crew, who were spread out across hotels and home rentals during filming. But its Ocean Sciences Centre, about 30 minutes north of downtown, found the spotlight as one of the most striking structures in the series, the marine research center where Dr. Fonda Howander (Mackenzie Davis) worked.

While Fréchette admits it took some work to convince the operating facility to shoot there, he’s excited it worked out because “it really adds production value and is a great location.” After all, the circular wooden structure reflects that government building architect of the 1960s and early 1970s, “at a time we were dreaming and imagining things beyond what was possible to build today.” Reminiscent of designs by Canadian architects like Arthur Erikson, he adds that “it was ambitious, but it had a vision—and is fantastic!”

About 20 miles north of St. John’s at the top of the Avalon Peninsula sits Pouch Cove, a town of about 2,000 residents. The art director told Fréchette about the Pouch Cove Heritage Society, a historical building that was closed since they were fundraising to preserve it, so one weekend, they went up to visit. “The floor was sunken in and it was structurally unsafe,” he says.

The show’s head carpenter and engineer got to work, fixing it up, temporarily transforming it into the interior of Below’s Fisherman’s Hall, while permanently restoring it for the community. “It was a win-win because they were happy to get the money from the location, but also the work we did on it was helpful for them.”

When Calvin returns to his abandoned childhood town of Little Pot Rock, that dilapidated setting was an actual resettled town, about a 30-minute drive down from Pouch Cove on a dirt road that the production had to grade in order to shoot there.

“It was quite tricky, but just stunning—really wild and rugged,” Fréchette says, calling it “the most amazing location.” All that was there was one tiny house, about 12 by 20 feet, but it never showed up on camera. Instead, the production custom built all of the Budgell family’s dwellings. But the area can be visited as part of a 4.3-mile hike along the East Coast Trail.

The fishing village of Bay Bulls is home to North America’s largest Atlantic puffin colony, as well as a prime whale watching destination. But for Below, it was all about the functional purpose of its Pennecon Marine Base. Though it never shows up on screen, its industrial harbor was essential in order to dock the boat used as the research vessel since it had a draft (depth) of nearly 10 feet, and they needed an appropriate spot that the cast and crew could board. Also shot here were the exterior scenes of the submersible, which was hung from the boat by a crane and lifted onto the dock.

Pittman’s fish farm played an integral part of the plot, as Calvin confirmed that the sea creature was real—but it turns out the location was landlocked. “It was very complicated to do this on the sea because we’d have to deal with tides and storms, so we decided to cheat it on a lake in Brigus,” he says of the town that’s actually about 60 miles northwest from Brigus South. There was no actual fish farm there, so they custom-built the floating dock and cabin.

While the outside of Linda’s Bar was filmed using a retrofitted Brigus South home, the interior was actually the Rising Tide Convenience shop in the town of Harbour Main, about 33 miles southwest of St. John’s. The local business, best known for its homemade ice cream, “looked great inside, so we dressed it up,” Fréchette says, taking extra care to ensure the exterior entrance they built flowed seamlessly between cuts. As for Noah (Kaleb Horn)’s on-screen screech-in? That was a prop, but an actual frozen fish to ensure the fish kiss was genuine.

#6328. Wander.com: Best Luxury Take On Airbnb (With Real Value Too?)

At first, the big hotel chains of the world laughed off Airbnb and vacation rentals. No seriously, they did. Now, they all compete in the vacation rental business and act like it was always the plan.

The problem for the traveler, is that almost all of the newer entrants just plug into a massive pipeline of already existing vacation homes and apartments and pop them on their own branded website with no added luxury, differentiation, amenity or expertise in curation.

There’s no huge unlock of new places or highly curated places that you could virtually always stamp as worth recommending to a friend, the way you’d rate an Aman, St. Regis, or Four Seasons hotel.

This is precisely where Wander.com comes in, and it’s by far my favorite luxe vacation rental platform to date. The fact that it’s boutique and limited is what makes it, at least for me. And, the $350 off Wander promo code doesn’t hurt either.

Wander is a vacation rental company which truly hand picks every property that it lists, and has the exclusive listing on. Crucially, each of the vacation properties undergoes a sort of ‘Wander’ transformation to conform with brand standards for wifi, amenity, style and vibe.

It’s above my pay-grade as a blogger on this topic, but it seems like Wander co-invests in the real estate portfolio’s, or partners with owners in a unique way that’s far more integrated than others.

Where are they? Most Wander.com properties are scattered across the US, from the shores of Malibu to the great National Parks in Wyoming and all along the Eastern seaboard too. Hawaii is also a recent addition. New destinations keep popping up!

Each of their properties feels uniquely wonderful and aspirational, and I’d say all have a very modern and contemporary slant to luxury. Grandma’s cabinets are not in any of these homes, but Tesla chargers are. One nice touch: each Wander offers a dedicated workspace with desk, chair, monitors and lightning fast wifi.

I completely respect that all tastes are individual, but the interiors and setups of these homes much more reflect my personal tastes, more minimalist chic, than many less curated vacation rental options.

Most Wander properties are around $1000 a night. Some will be half that, some will be double. On its face, that’s intimidating to many, but when you factor in the number of bedrooms and features it’s really reasonable. Families, or multi-family get togethers… amazing.

All Wander.com properties are at least two bedrooms and many are four, five or even twelve. One is an entire island with multiple residential complexes. For me, I love these sort of getaways for catching up with family or friends, and I never mind when other people are contributing too.

We’ve had some of our best ever vacations renting a house in Palm Springs for weeks or months at a time. Often, family or friends want in too, so we split the house and end up with two bedrooms each for under $500 per night.

We’ve used these bonus rooms and features to socialize or catch up with people in the serenity of the home, not annoyed by service, crowded pools or tight room setups. For a longer stay, I absolutely hate having to rely on a hotel kitchen for every meal. I love to hit a local market and grill with family or guests.

Wander is offering $350 off first bookings, which is a great way to get started. To browse the homes, you simply download the Wander app and start doom scrolling. When you find one you’re ready to book, the process is very self explanatory and easy to share with others.

I’m personally a fan of virtually California vacation and the properties offered on the platform cover everything from Palm Springs to Napa and all in between in stunning form. The $350 off is a solid discount and combined with new property discounts, which are frequent, there is a lot to love. You can browse Wander and download the app here.

If you don’t see the Wander.com discount in your account, you can add promo code AKFVDFD7 once the app is downloaded.

#6327. Why the Algerian Sahara Should Be Your Next Off-Grid Adventure

I woke up in the small hours of the night. Orion’s Belt was directly above where I lay on a thin roll-up mattress, zipped into a canvas sleeping bag. The hunter’s three luminous studs stood out in a canopy awash with stars from horizon to horizon, the Milky Way a glittery paint stroke across the scene. Aside from an occasional shuffle or snuffle from my fellow campers, the night was draped in a thick blanket of stress-shrinking quiet. It’d been days since I had cell reception. I could practically hear my nervous system thanking me.

A breathtaking canopy of stars illuminates the vast Algerian Sahara.

You don’t need to sleep al fresco while camping in the Sahara Desert—I could crawl back inside my own pop-up dome tent at any time—but I’d certainly recommend it. It was a highlight of my trip to Algeria’s tranche of this continent-spanning desert.

I was in the Sahara on a nine-day tour with Explore Worldwide, a UK-based small-group tour company, which began running trips to Algeria earlier this year, partly as a reaction to the country’s new, albeit cautious, encouragement of tourism. I wanted to find out what that development looked like on the ground and experience the desert region that hopes to attract new visitors.

Algeria is one of our Best Places to Go in Africa in 2026. Find our full guide here.

Africa’s largest country is hard to miss on a map, but all but one of the 10 well-traveled people in my group (mostly British and 60-years-plus) were first-timers in Algeria. Traditionally, the economy here has been driven by the oil and gas sector, and the development of tourism has been of little interest to the government. This has led to a fraction of the arriving tourists received by other North African countries such as Morocco or Egypt; roughly a third of its visitors are members of the diaspora coming to visit and stay with family. But recently, a push to diversify the economy has led to the launch of an ambitious “master plan” to increase arrivals four-fold by 2030, with a special focus on desert tourism.

Although the majority of projects (such as much-needed new hotels) remain in-progress, the government has introduced visas on arrival for people spending the majority of their time in the Sahara—an option taken by nearly 39,000 visitors since 2023, contributing to an uptick in arrivals. I took advantage of the scheme myself. After an hour or so in the capital Algiers’ Houari Boumediene International Airport—queuing, waiting, and nervously watching an official wander around with my passport—I paid my fee in cash ($150 for 10 days), my passport was stamped, and I was warmly welcomed to Algeria.

Algiers' iconic Casbah is the most ancient quarter of the city—and well worth exploring for its winding alleys and traditional Ottoman-style architecture.

The trip kicked off with an Algiers city tour, giving us a brief but necessary taste of the country’s culture and history before we flew into the desert. I arrived early for a little solo exploration, allowing me to wander the cool, peaceful paths of the lush Hamma Botanical Garden, and enjoy a bowl of rechta (thin noodles with chicken in a clear broth) in the intimate lounge of El Walima Restaurant.

With our tour guide Wassim Messgo, we walked through the narrow lanes of the Casbah—the UNESCO-listed historic center—past a smattering of souvenir stalls, and visited the hard-hitting National Museum of the Mujahid—dedicated to the bloody war for independence from France between 1954 and 1962. I could’ve spent longer in Algiers and want to return to see other cities in the north. Messgo recommended Constantine: “You get Roman ruins in other parts of the region,” he said, “but not in a city like this.”

But my focus for this trip was the Sahara.

The Algerian government has introduced visas on arrival for people spending the majority of their time in the Sahara.

Algiers to Djanet—a little oasis town in Algeria’s southeast near the Libya and Niger borders—is a two-hour flight, usually scheduled in the middle of the night (to avoid desert winds during the day, so I was told). On arrival, I was reminded of Algeria’s high levels of security, partly due to fluctuating tensions with neighboring countries, particularly Morocco at present. Our passports were collected and our names ticked off against a list that linked us with our guide: Aissa Khirani, a Djanet native who’s spent the past 20 years leading tours locally and across Africa. Khirani told me that guides have to submit their plans to the military, including the identities of guests and staff, along with car registration numbers.

In addition to being a military hub, Djanet is the tourism gateway to this swathe of the Sahara. Our flight was perhaps half tourists—but for the five days we were in the desert, we encountered only six other vehicles. This was a benefit of traveling with a guide who knew his way around, while having a flexible itinerary so we could avoid other travelers—and account for unexpected weather events.

Djanet is a little oasis town in Algeria’s southeast near the Libya and Niger borders, and a gateway to the Sahara.

As we drove around the Tassili n'Ajjer plateau over the following five days, the landscape varied with surprising frequency—Mars-like rocky flats; sandy canyons edged by colossal rock formations; sweeping seas of peachy dunes with crisp ridgelines and wind-rippled faces. Camels, many belonging to Touareg nomads, grazed on sparse patches of vegetation. Caves and overhangs here have protected at least 15,000 examples of rock art, some thought to be 10,000 years old, depicting people hunting or dancing, giraffes, cattle, and jars possibly for carrying water as the region dried up.

We eased into desert life with two nights at something close to a glamping site—shared with a couple of other guests—which had tents you could stand up in, thick mattresses, even charging units. For the following three nights, we camped among the dunes and at the base of hulking rockfaces that resembled elephant skin. Our mobile set-up consisted of basic tents, a dining table by the campfire, and a “bathroom”—a chair with a cut-out seat in a canvas cubicle.

Camping at the base of the hulking rockfaces of the Algerian Sahara

Tents come with comfortable mattresses, extra seating, even charging units

“To be honest, I don't want Algeria to be like Morocco or Tunisia or Egypt,” Khirani told me, as we drove out of Djanet in a convoy of four Toyota four-wheel-drives, echoing sentiments Messgo had also shared. Both guides spoke about how relaxed Algeria currently feels for visitors; when I visited Djanet’s market, for example, we’d been greeted but otherwise left alone to browse the stalls of jewelry and fabrics.

As for the desert, Khirani continued, it still feels remote. “The desert to me means peace of mind,” he said. “It’s a sensation like emptiness, but with it a kind of happiness that you cannot describe.” He hopes to protect that experience, while encouraging tourism “in a smart way.”

The shifting shades and surfaces of the desert dunes

Caves and overhangs in the region have protected at least 15,000 examples of rock art, some thought to be 10,000 years old.

While I had precious moments of solitude—sitting on a dune at sunrise, submerged in quietness as the sand turned cool beige to warm caramel—many of my favorite memories are of people: Hemaya baking bread in the sand under hot coals; driver Ali Lazghem playing the same four songs on repeat and letting other drivers know exactly how he felt when they stalled at the top of a dune he was powering up; the whole team excited to see a locally famous and yet unnamed rock formation that features on the cover of Lonely Planet’s latest Algeria guide for the first time.

Back in Djanet, at the end of our off-grid adventure, I was finally able to shower again. I knew one wash wouldn’t be enough to fully de-grit my hair—at that stage, almost solid with desert debris—and that I’d be tapping out orange sand from my shoes for days. But that’s the thing about time in the desert. It tends to stick with you, in more ways than one.

I traveled with Explore Worldwide on their nine-day Algeria’s Sahara Desert Adventure tour, which begins and ends in the capital Algiers. Prices start at $2,410 (excluding international flights, which are typically via hubs such as Paris or London). The package includes accommodation, most meals and activities, including a day-tour of Algiers and five nights camping in the Sahara Desert; don’t expect guides to keep strictly to the itinerary, but you’ll certainly spend plenty of time in scenic parts of the Sahara, see several examples of rock art, and be treated to warm hospitality and tasty food throughout. If you want to explore the northern cities too, you can do Explore’s two-week Ancient Algeria and the Sahara Desert tour. In Algiers, the comfortable El Aurassi is considered one of the best hotels, though service and style fall short of a standard five-star experience. For a visa on arrival, tour operators will provide the required authorization letter—otherwise you can apply for a visa from your nearest Algerian embassy. Bring dollars to exchange for Algerian dinars when you arrive (ATMs are unreliable), as cards aren’t commonly accepted. Exporting dinars is prohibited. Also note that it’s illegal to carry binoculars and drones into Algeria.

#6326. Why Your Seatback Screen May Be Dark On Your Next United Airlines Flight

If you board a United Airlines flight and find a placard covering an inoperative seatback screen, it may be a consequence of an upgrade rather than an unexpected malfunction. United is installing Starlink ahead of cabin renovations on some aircraft, leaving passengers with excellent Wi-Fi but no working seatback entertainment.

An internal United memo reviewed by Live And Let’s Fly, explains that a small number of Boeing 737-900 aircraft, identified internally as the 73C configuration, have received Starlink before their United Next interior refresh.

That installation has deactivated the existing DirecTV system. The result is that the old seatback monitors no longer function.

In other words, the screen in front of you is still there, but your entertainment will need to come from your own device…at least temporarily.

> Read More: United Airlines Will Modernize Mainline Jets With New Interiors

The memo identifies these five aircraft by United’s internal fleet numbers:

That is the list as of November 3, rather than a permanent or comprehensive list of aircraft that may undergo this transition.

United says affected screens carry placards explaining the entertainment upgrade and directing MileagePlus members to free Starlink Wi-Fi. The aircraft also have Starlink signage beside the boarding door.

With the screens disabled, flight attendants must perform a live safety demonstration instead of playing the safety video.

I’d trade Starlink for DirecTV any day of the week and twice on Sundays…

United’s Starlink rollout is accelerating. Speaking at the CyberSat conference this week, United Chief Information Security Officer Deneen DeFiore said the deployment timeline had been reduced from two to three years to 18 months.

As of November 5, United’s official Starlink tracker lists 677 equipped aircraft and says Starlink is available on 50% of its daily flights. The tracker continues to list completion by the end of 2027.

You can also use that tool to check an upcoming flight within three days of departure. Aircraft assignments can change, so check again closer to travel.

The five aircraft in the memo illustrate a consequence of moving the connectivity installation ahead of the interior work but considering you can stream TV from your phones or computers I don’t see it as a loss of any sort.

I would much rather have fast, reliable, free internet than an aging DirecTV system. For working onboard, Starlink is a far more useful amenity to me.

That calculus changes slightly when traveling with my children. They don’t have phones so the setback monitors are very helpful to keeping them occupied during the flight. Having internet on your phone also does not replace the convenience of watching something on the screen in front of you while using that phone for something else.

But there are just growing pains in the ex-DirecTV fleet and I would not want United to delay Starlink simply to keep the old television system running. Still, passengers should know what to expect. Bring a charged device and headphones if you plan to watch something.

Some United Boeing 737-900s now have Starlink but inoperative seatback screens because the connectivity installation preceded their United Next cabin refresh. The long-term improvement is welcome. In the meantime, enjoy the better Wi-Fi, but expect to supply your own screen on these aircraft.

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

Those five aircraft are part of United’s 737-900s (not the more popular -ERs and an aircraft type that Alaska has already retired). It’s not surprising United hasn’t invested the money into a full refresh on these planes – I’m curious how long they’ll stay around anyhow.

Well, that is ridiculous. I loved having DirectTV on the plane. When will the screens be re-activated?

Direct TV is going away. Bigger screens with ability to stream some content (few broadcast stations, NFL Network, etc) via Starlink replacing them.

That would be awesome. Nothing more annoying than these screens forcing ads on you while otherwise being completely useful.

First World problem. I know a lot of people cant go 5 minutes without some sort of mind numbing content (i do see the need if you have younger kids) I am the odd ball. I read a book or maybe a nap. I rarely watch anything on an airplane screen. Maybe they will let you open the window shade to actually see outside!

Bring your own screen AND charging device.

#6325. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

#6324. What Is the UNESCO Tentative List, and How Do You Get on It?

With a total of 27 UNESCO World Heritage Sites, the United States is peppered full of sites of wonder. There's the Statue of Liberty, the patinated icon that has served as the first face millions of immigrants saw once they reached the country's shores and the San Antonio Missions in Texas which were first constructed the 18th century. Beyond manmade wonders, UNESCO has also recognized natural sites such as the Florida Everglades and the Grand Canyon. There's no shortage of modern marvels and breathtaking landscapes to behold in the US, which leads us to ask, how does a destination gain recognition as a UNESCO World Heritage Site? The process begins with the UNESCO Tentative List, which puts the best of the best up for consideration.

The Tentative List, as the name suggests, comprises natural and cultural properties that a country considers to have the potential to be recognized as World Heritage. It is not a confirmation that a site has been selected for inscription, only the first step towards a formal nomination, which is drawn up subsequently in the process. To qualify for World Heritage status, a property must demonstrate Outstanding Universal Value (OUV), meaning its cultural or natural significance ought to be considered exceptional from an international perspective. A site’s inclusion on the Tentative List places it in the position to be examined further for its potential OUV. This process enables a stronger foundation of vetting for the final nominations that a country draws up.

Even if a site included in a Tentative List is not nominated during one evaluatory round, there’s always a chance in the future that it may be added back to the list and considered for a nomination. The list is updated at any time per the country’s discretion, but each included site must undergo a separate nomination and evaluation process before qualifying for the World Heritage List. Once a site is inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage, it is removed from the Tentative List.

At the heart of UNESCO’s World Heritage process is the concept of Outstanding Universal Value (OUV). In simple terms, this means a place must be significant beyond its own country, and its cultural or natural importance must be exceptional enough to matter to people around the world, including future generations. A site must demonstrate this value against at least one of UNESCO’s 10 selection criteria, whether for its contribution to human history and culture, its geological features, its ecological processes or its biodiversity.

The cultural criteria include sites that represent exceptional examples of human creativity, demonstrate an important exchange of human values, bear testimony to cultural traditions or civilizations, or illustrate significant stages in human history. They also cover traditional settlements and landscapes, as well as properties associated with events, living traditions, beliefs, and works of outstanding universal significance.

The natural criteria consider exceptional natural beauty, significant stages in the Earth’s geological history, ongoing ecological and biological processes, and habitats important for conserving biodiversity.

Meeting one or more criteria is not enough on its own. A proposed property must also satisfy the relevant conditions of authenticity and integrity, alongside requirements for protection and management. Its inclusion must make a case for why its significance is exceptional in a global context, including through comparisons with similar properties.

It’s important to note that UNESCO’s 10 criteria are regularly revised to reflect the evolving understanding of World Heritage.

Countries identify properties they consider to have potential OUV and may eventually nominate for World Heritage status. UNESCO encourages them to involve a broad range of stakeholders in preparing their Tentative Lists, including site managers, local communities, government bodies, and non-governmental organizations. The process is led by each country, so the extent and nature of consultation can vary.

Currently, the US has 17 sites on their Tentative List, with nominations dating from 2008 and 2017. The US has submitted both cultural and natural sites for consideration with locales raning from the country's Pacific territories to Alabama. Below are the current contenders on the Tentative List, according to the National Park Service.

The country must still decide whether to proceed with a formal nomination and prepare the documentation required to demonstrate the property’s OUV. This includes establishing how the site meets the relevant selection criteria, documenting its authenticity and integrity, outlining the measures in place to protect it, and presenting a management framework. The nomination must also explain how the property compares with other sites of similar significance.

The country, not UNESCO, decides which properties to nominate for World Heritage status. Once a site on the Tentative List is formally nominated, independent advisory bodies assess its significance and conservation measures. The UNESCO World Heritage Committee then makes the final decision on whether to inscribe it on the World Heritage List.

Here’s how to make the most of South Australia

It took me several trips to Australia to realize I’d been skipping one of its best parts.

It took me several trips to Australia to realize I’d been skipping one of its best parts.

I’d visited the country a handful of times before, but this was my first trip to Adelaide and my first time exploring South Australia. Within a few days, I was eating my way through a 150-year-old market, walking among kangaroos and wallabies, blending my own bottle of shiraz, kayaking alongside wild dolphins, and bopping between breathtaking beaches, rolling hills, and wine country.

And getting there from the U.S. is about to become considerably easier.

United is bringing back its seasonal service between San Francisco International Airport (SFO) and Adelaide Airport (ADL) beginning Dec. 17. The route, now entering its second season, gives travelers the only nonstop connection between the U.S. and Adelaide, with schedules subject to change. Service is scheduled to run through Feb. 10, 2027.

Adelaide turned out to be an ideal home base for seeing just how much variety South Australia packs into a relatively small radius.

The state capital and largest city in the region still manages to feel surprisingly approachable. Its central business district mixes modern towers with low-slung stone cottages and other remnants of its colonial-era architecture, while the entire city center is wrapped in parklands that date back to Adelaide’s original 1837 city plan.

From the center of town, I could be among the rolling hills and small villages of the Adelaide Hills, heading toward the coast, or making my way into wine country — all in roughly half an hour.

That is, assuming you are prepared to drive on the left. My first encounter with my Australian rental car began with me confidently getting into the wrong front seat and momentarily wondering where someone had put the steering wheel.

For my stay, I checked into Hotel Indigo Adelaide Markets. My suite had a separate living area and a large balcony with sweeping views across the city and toward the hills. The hotel also has Merrymaker, a lively rooftop bar 16 floors above the surrounding market district.

Before I could start bouncing between wineries, markets, and wildlife encounters, though, I first had to cross the Pacific. United’s San Francisco-to-Adelaide service is scheduled to operate on a Boeing 787-9, and I got to make the overnight journey in United Polaris business class. After spending some time in the Polaris Lounge at SFO, I boarded and settled into my lie-flat seat for what was essentially going to be an entire night in the air.

Dinner started with tomato tartare and crostini, followed by braised short rib with risotto Milanese, garlic green beans, and fresh gremolata. It was genuinely tasty, to the point that I could almost forget I was eating dinner at 35,000 feet.

Even more memorably, I got my first experience with United’s Polaris sundae service. My extremely attentive flight attendant recommended I simply go for all the fixings, and I took her advice. She was right.

From there, I put the lie-flat seat to good use and got a substantial stretch of sleep before waking for breakfast closer to Adelaide. I went with a mushroom omelet and chicken sausage, which provided a convenient marker that it was time to stop thinking in San Francisco time and get onto my new schedule.

That rhythm ended up being one of the biggest benefits of flying the route in Polaris. Dinner, a real block of sleep, and breakfast before landing gave the flight something resembling a normal overnight routine. By the time I arrived in Adelaide, I felt far more functional than I normally do after crossing that many time zones and was ready to start exploring almost immediately.

Over the next few days, I got to see several very different sides of the region. Looking back, most of what I loved about South Australia fell pretty neatly into one of three camps: adventure, indulgence, and culture.

I managed to sample a little of all three, but depending on how you like to travel, any one could easily become the backbone of a trip here.

My adventure itinerary began less than half a block from my hotel at Adelaide Central Market.

The market has been operating since 1869 and today packs more than 70 artisans under one roof. What struck me more than its age, though, was how much it still felt like a place Adelaide actually uses.

At lunchtime, workers from the surrounding central business district mixed with families, visitors, and people picking up groceries. Around them were rows of fresh produce, flowers, bakeries, bookstores, sweet shops, and food stalls representing cuisines from around the world.

I had some of the best paella I’ve had in a long time, worked my way through a few of the savory pies and rolls Australia does especially well, and found my favorite at Smiley’s: a hot chicken roll that I would have happily eaten again the next day.

Dessert sent me down another very Australian rabbit hole. Honeycomb is a flavor I encounter constantly here and almost never back home, and I found a honeycomb cornflake slice that was essentially the Australian cousin of a Rice Krispies treat.

The food scene spills beyond the market, too. Elsewhere in the central business district, streets like Peel and Leigh narrow into pedestrian-friendly laneways packed with wine bars, restaurants, cocktail spots, and cafes.

And if there is one thing I’m reminded of every time I return to Australia, it is that Australians take coffee very seriously. My favorite stop was Exchange Coffee, where the menu seemed capable of accommodating essentially any permutation of coffee I could come up with.

From there, I headed into the Adelaide Hills for Cleland Wildlife Park.

I have been to enough petting zoos in the U.S. to approach almost any animal experience with a little skepticism. Cleland was nothing like that.

The park centers on conservation and education, and many of its kangaroos and wallabies move freely through large natural areas where visitors can walk among them. Adult admission costs AU$35.80.

I spent much of my visit wandering between animals that seemed largely unconcerned by my presence. At one point, I spotted a baby wallaby riding in its mother’s pouch with just its little head poking out, which may have been the single cutest thing I saw on the entire trip.

I also paid extra for a koala encounter and met Tek, a 10-year-old male whose fur was far softer than I expected. A keeper remained beside him throughout the experience, supplying eucalyptus and making sure the interaction stayed very much on his terms.

The keeper also informed me that Tek might have better labor protections than most humans. After a 30-minute stretch of close-up visitor encounters, he gets two complete days off from that kind of work entirely, which made me both laugh and feel a little jealous.

For the final stop on my adventure itinerary, I traded ground-level bush walks for the roof of Adelaide Oval.

The stadium manages to feel both thoroughly modern and distinctly historic, with its grassy northern mound, enormous fig trees, and century-old scoreboard still intact amid the contemporary grandstands. Those trees also have a wonderfully petty backstory: They were planted, at least in part, to stop people on nearby Montefiore Hill from watching games inside the Oval for free.

For an even better view, I signed up for Adelaide Oval’s RoofClimb. After changing into a jumpsuit and clipping into a harness, I followed my guide onto a track running across the stadium roof. From the top, Adelaide suddenly made much more sense geographically. I could trace the river through the city, see the Adelaide Hills rising in one direction, and look toward the coastline in another.

At the turnaround point came the obligatory opportunity to lean backward over the edge, arms out, with my harness very much attached.

A standard daytime RoofClimb takes about two hours and starts at AU$125 for adults and AU$95 for children ages 8 to 15. By the time I unclipped, it had landed in a very specific sweet spot: scenic, informative, and just adrenaline-inducing enough to make me feel like I had earned the view.

My indulgence itinerary began with one of the most elaborate meals I have ever experienced.

Restaurant Aptos sits inside a converted church in Stirling, in the Adelaide Hills, and serves just 14 diners at a time. Its 16-course tasting menu unfolds progressively across three interconnected dining rooms.

From the moment I walked in, it felt like stepping into another world.

The first course made it abundantly clear what kind of evening I was in for. I was handed what was essentially a branch dotted with five native Australian fruits and instructed to lick each flavor directly off the wood.

I tried crocodile tongue for the first time, paired with Geraldton wax flavors, and kangaroo seasoned with native Australian ingredients. The latter was considerably more tender and less gamey than I expected.

Across the 16 courses, the flavor combinations were at times so layered that my first reaction was almost sensory overload. I would take a bite, spend a few seconds trying to work out what exactly I was tasting, and then suddenly everything would settle into place.

Each course also arrived with a beautifully designed card detailing the ingredients and preparation. By dessert, I had a stack of 16 that felt less like a menu and more like a collection of art prints I wanted to take home and frame.

The following day, I stayed in the Adelaide Hills but traded a tasting menu for a pair of walking shoes at Mount Lofty Botanic Garden.

Calling it a botanical garden almost undersells it.

Spread across 97 hectares, Mount Lofty showcases cool-climate plants from around the world, with sections devoted to flora from places including South America, Africa, and Asia.

The landscape felt closer to a nature preserve than a manicured city park. I wandered past ponds, streams, flowers, and dense pockets of forest, with the scenery seeming to change every few minutes.

The birdlife also made me stop more than once. One thing I never quite get over in Australia is how exotic even an everyday bird can look compared with what I am accustomed to seeing in New York. At home, my baseline is largely pigeons and crows. Here, seemingly commonplace birds can look like something escaped from an aviary.

Admission is free, making Mount Lofty an easy way to spend a few hours in the hills.

From there, I continued to Hahndorf, Australia’s oldest surviving German settlement. Its main street is lined with heritage buildings, bakeries, pubs, boutiques, and antique stores.

I stopped at Otto’s Bakery for a vanilla slice, one of those Australian desserts whose name does very little to explain what it actually is. Rather than cake, it is a thick layer of silky vanilla custard sandwiched between crisp sheets of puff pastry.

The final stop on my indulgence itinerary took me south to McLaren Vale and d’Arenberg, where the Osborn family has been growing grapes since 1912.

The first thing I noticed, though, had nothing to do with wine.

The five-story d’Arenberg Cube rises above the vineyards in a jumble of black, white, glass, and mirrors. Against the rolling countryside, it looks a little like a Rubik’s Cube Salvador Dalí might have designed himself. Fittingly, one floor houses an exhibition of Dalí sculptures and graphic works.

My main reason for visiting was the Blending Bench, a hands-on experience that lets you create and bottle your own wine.

By sheer luck, I was the only person booked for my session. In front of me were three shiraz samples made from vines planted in 1898, 1969, and 1999, and all three tasted remarkably different.

Using pipettes, a worksheet, and plenty of trial and error, I measured different percentages into my glass, tasted the result, and adjusted from there.

I went in convinced the 1898 sample, easily my favorite on its own, would make up most of my final bottle. But tiny changes in the proportions completely altered the flavor. Eventually, I settled on something I liked even more than any of the three components separately.

Then I got to bottle, name, and label a full 750-milliliter version to take home.

The Blending Bench costs AU$120 and takes about 75 minutes. Between the architecture, art, vineyards, and leaving with a bottle I had actually created myself, it was easily one of the more memorable winery visits I have had.

For the culture itinerary, I started with a restaurant I had been excited about well before I ever landed in Adelaide.

Africola has one of the most distinct visual identities I have ever seen from a restaurant, from its website and branding to the space itself.

Once inside, though, what stood out was how much it felt like a neighborhood institution.

More than once, I watched members of the staff greet diners with the easy familiarity of people who had clearly been coming back for years. I sat at the bar, which gave me a front-row view into the open kitchen and all of the plating and preparation happening behind it.

I started with the crispy chicken tea sandwich, one of Africola’s signatures. Soft white bread encloses crisp chicken skin, with peri-peri drippings served alongside for dipping. Think of it as a tiny, rich South African cousin of a French dip.

Then came the peri-peri chicken itself, smoky, spicy, and incredibly savory, along with salt-baked Dutch cream potatoes with labneh, za’atar, and chives that landed on my palette like an elegant twice-baked potato. I also ordered the cos lettuce with buttermilk, dill, and shallot, essentially Africola’s much more interesting answer to a wedge salad.

When everything was placed in front of me, I was mildly horrified by how much food I had ordered. About an hour later, I had eaten most of it and was contemplating whether I could simply roll myself through the central business district and back to my hotel.

It ended up being one of my favorite meals of the entire trip.

The next afternoon, I headed to Adelaide Botanic Garden on the eastern edge of the city center.

The 50-hectare garden is free to enter and mixes outdoor collections with ponds, shaded paths, historic buildings, museums, and glasshouses.

One of those spaces is the Palm House, a Victorian glasshouse from the 1870s that now holds plants from Madagascar, including species threatened or endangered in the wild.

Nearby, the Museum of Economic Botany ended up being one of my favorite stops. The collection includes enormous seeds, preserved plant specimens, and historical models centered on the many ways humans have used plants for food, medicine, textiles, inks, and other parts of everyday life.

Taken together, the garden felt less like simply spending an afternoon looking at pretty plants and more like a reminder of how deeply the natural world has shaped the way people eat, build, heal, create, and live.

Another way to dig deeper is through the garden’s Aboriginal Native Plant and Social History Tour. Led by an Aboriginal guide, the 90-minute experience explores traditional uses of native plants for food, medicine, and tools, along with Aboriginal social history, cultural practices, and relationships with the land. Tickets are currently AU$42 per person, plus booking fees.

For the final stop of my trip, I traded the central business district for a morning on the water at the Adelaide Dolphin Sanctuary near Garden Island.

I joined the three-hour Dolphin Sanctuary Kayak Tour, where my guide, Kendall, first walked us through the basics before leading our group onto the water.

We paddled between mangrove-lined creeks and the partially submerged remains of old ships. The Garden Island ships’ graveyard contains 25 known vessels abandoned between 1909 and 1945 after they became obsolete, damaged, or no longer economical to maintain.

Farther into the mangroves, I started getting serious Florida Everglades energy, only without quite as many things I was concerned might kill me.

Kendall, who happens to be an American from Florida herself, was equal parts kayak instructor and naturalist, filling us in on dolphin behavior, conservation efforts, and the maritime history behind the wrecks as we paddled.

Then came the moment I had convinced myself probably would not happen.

I am an eternal pessimist when it comes to any wildlife activity involving the phrase “possible sighting,” but we ended up spending several minutes alongside a mother dolphin and her calf.

The pair moved back and forth through the water together, surfacing side by side, disappearing beneath us, and then looping around again.

The tour costs AU$79 per adult, lasts about three hours, and includes the necessary kayaking gear.

Between the shipwrecks, ancient mangroves, and a wild dolphin sighting I had fully talked myself out of expecting, it was a fitting way to finish a trip that consistently surprised me.

In only a few days, Adelaide gave me a version of Australia I had not experienced on any of my previous visits.

I could spend the morning in the center of a major city, the afternoon walking through vineyards or alongside kangaroos, and the evening eating ingredients I had never heard of before the trip. More importantly, almost none of it required spending hours getting from one place to the next.

That is ultimately what made Adelaide work so well as a home base. Whether I leaned into adventure, indulgence, or culture, there was a different once-in-a-lifetime experience within easy reach.

Beginning Dec. 17, United’s returning seasonal San Francisco-to-Adelaide service will make it easier for U.S. travelers to arrive directly in South Australia and start exploring, with schedules subject to change. So take it from me — don’t sleep on South Australia, unless it’s from the comfort of a Polaris Business Class seat on the way there.

#6322. A Flight Only Bookable With Points Offers Amazing Winter Sun

I often tell people that the best unkept secret with Avios is, in fact, the Avios app. Separate to the British Airways app, the Avios app allows users to set flight alerts and goals, but also gives a heads up about opportunities before they appear anywhere else.

Case in point: before a press release had even hit my inbox, the Avios app alerted me that an ‘Avios only’ flight had just launched. This isn’t the first time Avios has launched a flight only bookable with points, but it is the first time they’ve done one to CAPE TOWN, during peak winter break time.

British Airways and Avios have collaborated on a flight only bookable with Avios, where every seat on the plane is available for sale with points. First, business, premium and economy, all available using Avios. The flights depart as follows…

As noted, these flights are now bookable and if history repeats itself, they won’t be available for long. This plane only has 8 seats in first, so get in quick! One amazing thing about Avios is that they aren’t just the currency of one airline, but a whopping seven. If you have any points with Finnair, Iberia, Qatar, Aer Lingus, Logainair, Vueling or British Airways you can pool points together to book these flights.

Avios is also a transfer partner of Amex, Bilt, Capital One, Chase and plenty of other global financial institutions, so there should be ample opportunity to convert bank points into Avios and get these booked. Hot tip though, ensure there are seats available before you make your transfer, since this will be a hot commodity.

I love any airline rewarding members with flights entirely bookable with points. What makes this one different is that it’s not some off peak, off season destination. It’s Cape Town, easily one of the toughest tickets with any currency, during peak time, perfect for people looking to ditch the weather for the holidays and catch NYE in one of the best cities on earth.

Yes, Cape Town is by far one of my favorites and for any oenophiles, a trip to nearby Stellenbosch or Franschoek is a must. Standard luggage limits apply, so definitely bring enough suitcases to haul back wine. Fin. Head to British Airways website to book.

#6321. Booked! SAS Business Class To Germany, Because My Wife Chose Horses Over The Caribbean

One beauty of sitting on all these SAS EuroBonus miles is that spur-of-the-moment trips are possible…like a trip to Germany for a few days.

My wife works very hard and rather unexpectedly was given five days, though without a lot of notice. Life is busy for all of us and of course the kids are in school, but as they quickly grow up Heidi and I have elected to take advantage of opportunities like this…for we will regret not doing so later.

Heidi initially suggested a “trip to the Caribbean…somewhere warm” and I thought it would be a good opportunity  to visit Saint Kitts and Nevis and check out the Park Hyatt there. I also suggested we could fly to Iceland with no set plan, get in the car, and drive. Wouldn’t that be fun? I’ve never done a trip around Iceland’s Ring Road.

Ultimately, though, Heidi spoke to her best friend in Germany and decided it would be a prefect opportunity to see her parents (remember, she did not join us on the summer trip) and ride horses with her friend in the Black Forest. I loved the idea and got to work on the flights.

There wasn’t business class from Los Angeles, but there was from Chicago exactly on our dates…five days, with four nights on the ground. Hardly long enough, but better than nothing? We’ll fly into Zurich, but I bought a separate ticket (on Norwegian!) to return from Basel to Copenhagen to catch the SAS connection to ORD…with a very tight connection.

So as I conclude my India Trip Report and move on to our summer trip to Europe, I’ll be sharing updates from this trip. We’ll be traveling in business class on the SAS A330, a product I’ve reviewed many times, though I may do so again if the situation warrants.

There’s never an ideal time to get away, but I really hope this will be a refreshing time for Heidi and indeed for all of us. And yes, even though it’s hardly something new or different, I get really excited ahead of an intercontinental trip, especially in a premium cabin.

You’re not missing anything at the PH St. Kitts. It’s a resort factory if there ever was one.

Eh, the view of Nevis is kinda cool, you know, for like, 1 night, and only if burning Hyatt points… Bah!

The beach sucks and the service is bad. And not just island time bad, but like really bad. I honestly prefer the villas at the Marriott, and since they’ve improved the breakfast benefit, it’s just as good.

Other than the Yucatan, you’re right that I cannot think of anywhere I’ve seen more sargassum (seaweed) than at this Park Hyatt in Saint Kitts. Even similar east-facing resorts elsewhere in the Caribbean (think, Ritz-Carlton on St. Thomas, USVI) handled it way better.

Nothing more fun than a “spur of the moment ” riding trip!

Looking forward to your report – our niece is a horse person and we’re taking her to southern Germany next summer.

Be careful with your stash! They go very quickly when you’re flying the full family. I’ve burnt through my American stash from the sale a few years ago
