Amazon has a new restaurant delivery partner for its Prime members: Uber Eats, which replaces the Grubhub+ benefit Prime members had until today.

To celebrate the new partnership, Amazon Prime members can get $20 off each of their first two eligible Uber Eats orders of $25 or more on linked accounts made via Amazon, as long as those orders are for U.S. restaurants and placed by Nov. 18.

Beyond the limited-time launch promotion, Prime members will get $0 delivery fees on eligible Uber Eats orders of $25 or more placed through the Amazon app or website. Interestingly, this appears to work separately from any existing Uber Eats account or benefits you may already have.

Related: Which is the best food delivery app?

There's no need to download another app or create a separate Uber Eats account to use this perk. When you opt in through Amazon, you can use your existing Prime account information, including linked payment methods.

Think of it almost like ordering a box of paper towels from Amazon with free Prime delivery, only this time it's a salad, burger, breakfast tacos or fries. You place the order via Uber Eats in your Amazon account, almost as you would any other Prime delivery, but this time it is fulfilled by Uber Eats instead of your friendly neighborhood Amazon delivery truck.

Amazon has also said that there will be additional Prime-exclusive offers available only on Amazon that could save you more than $175 per year, so we'll be sure to keep an eye out for those.

TPG tip: Amazon Prime Visa cardmembers earn 5% back on all Uber Eats orders through Dec. 5, 2026 with eligible Prime membership.

The information for the Prime Visa has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

This $20 introductory promo seems to apply whether you use pickup or delivery, which isn't always the case with Uber Eats promos. So, it is possible to truly save $20 on a $25 order if you select pickup. If you opt for delivery, you will likely have some service fees and a tip to factor into the equation.

One thing to remember: After the introductory promotion ends, you may want to compare the total cost of ordering through the Amazon-linked version of Uber Eats with any promotions, credit card benefits or discounts available through your regular Uber Eats account. The best deal may depend on which version of Uber Eats you're using.

#6308. Live: Singapore Airlines Unveils All-New First & Business Class Suites For Its Boeing 777-9

Last Updated: 06:50 AM EST November 6, 2026 by Jake Hardiman

Singapore Airlines has unveiled the next stage in its total refresh of the passenger experience. Today, the Asian airline revealed its new first-class and business-class seats to the world at an event held at the Marina Bay Sands Exhibition Centre in Singapore. The airline will spend more than $2bn SGD ($1.5bn) on the upgrade program.

Airlines around the world are constantly looking to innovate when it comes to passenger experience. With a trophy cabinet of awards, including 2026 SkyTrax Best Airline, Singapore Airlines is looking at the experience in more detail than some others. A cabin refresh that was initially planned to launch with the arrival of the Boeing 777-9 is now expected from H2 next year and will also apply to some of the airline’s Airbus A350-900s.

Simple Flying's Tom Boon has been able to sample the new seats in person at today's event, with the gallery above showing the center pair in the new first class cabin. As shown by Tom and our good friend Rhys Jones from Head For Points, passengers can sit opposite one another when dining for a more social experience. The gallery below shows the new business class seat.

Tom also had the chance to sample the new economy and premium economy seats. He had lots to say about business class in particular, noting that "it looks better in person, but the colour scheme still doesn't seem to make total sense. (...) It's a shame that it doesn't look more Singapore Airlines-y, but how many people book a business class for the colour or even to fly, in a particular seat?" He added that:

"There's a lot of thoughtful design to it. (...) The screen looks amazing, the wireless charging capabilities of the seat also look great. (...) Bed-wise, it's a huge improvement from the current product, and also the table works in a much nicer mechanism than the current table, and it folds away in a much nicer way, so, overall it's a solid product. (...) Color scheme aside, it's a great business class seat."

As Singapore Airlines brings its next-generation widebody passenger experience to life, inflight entertainment will be a key pillar of this strategy. The carrier plans to "offer a more immersive, cinematic, and tailored entertainment experience" with its updated KrisWorld IFE system, which will feature more than 2,500 entertainment options when all is said and done.

This updated offering features "4K high-resolution touchscreens, OLED displays on selected aircraft, spatial audio, Bluetooth pairing for personal headphones, a redesigned user interface, [and] wellness and personalisation features." The OLED displays will be present in "Business Class on the retrofitted A350-900, First Class and Business Class on the retrofitted A350-900 ULR, and Premium Economy Class and Economy Class on selected 777-9s."

With Singapore Airlines continuing to modernize its onboard experience as part of a wider rollout of improvements, it has also pledged to join the growing list of carriers worldwide offering high-speed Starlink WiFi. The technology will be rolled out on its Airbus A350-900, A350-900ULR, and A380 widebodies, with passengers on these aircraft able to stream content and stay in touch with friends and family.

With Simple Flying's Tom Boon on the ground in Singapore for the launch event, we've been able to take an in-person look at some dish samples for the new menu. As seen above, these include poached lobster with champagne sauce, beef short rib sambai percik with nasi kerabu, and cheng tng gelée tremblante, and they are certainly suitably luxurious dishes for Singapore Airlines' updated onboard offering.

Today's announcement of the new premium seats comes as part of a larger overall investment in the passenger experience from Singapore Airlines. The airline has already announced new onboard menu concepts and new amenities for the entire cabin. The new menu and amenities are gradually being rolled out across flights from the start of November. The airline has also been upgrading its lounge experience.

All classes of travel will benefit from these enhancements.

Singapore Airlines had initially planned to launch the new cabin experiences in the first half of 2027. Due to supply chain constraints, the launch of the new cabin on an aircraft will now come during the second half of 2027. Despite the delay, Chief Commercial Officer Lee Lik Hsin told assembled media that the rollout should be completed on time by the end of the decade.

As mentioned, the business class aesthetic is a huge departure from the Singapore Airlines design. The pattern on the back of the seats is inspired by the Juno Satellite launched by NASA in August 2011.

Singapore Airlines has shown more photos of the first-class seat. Simple Flying is scheduled to visit the business and first-class seats between 02:30 and 03:50 EST. We will provide first impressions and in person photos of the seats afterwards.

Singapore Airlines has revealed that the Boeing 777-9 will get 54 business-class seats, while the Airbus A350-900ULR will have 70. The standard long-range A350-900 will have 42 seats. The seats will have the following specifications:

Singapore Airlines has revealed that the Boeing 777-9 will get 6 first-class seats, while the Airbus A350-900ULR will have four. The seats will have the following specifications:

23 inches (30 inches with armrests lowered)

Singapore Airlines has confirmed that the new Boeing 777-9s will all be delivered with the new cabin experience. Additionally, 41 Airbus A350-900s will get the new cabin. The A350-900 long-haul and A350-900ULR aircraft will get the cabin. First class will only go on the 777-9 and the A350ULR. However, the A350-900 mid-range aircraft, Boeing 777-300s, Airbus A380s, and all other fleets will not receive the retrofit.

Singapore Airlines CEO, Goh Choon Phong, is welcoming the media and invited guests to Singapore ahead of the reveal of the new Singapore Airlines long-haul and ultra-long-haul cabins. He confirmed that Singapore Airlines will be bringing first class to the world's longest flight between Singapore and New York.

"The A350 ultra-long-range aircraft will also feature the new first-class cabin, and this will be the first time we're featuring first-class on the ultra-long-range planes. So, when you take our flight between Singapore and New York in the future, you will also have the option of going in a first-class cabin."

Singapore Airlines has taken a bold approach with its new business class cabin, designed in collaboration with BMW’s Design Works and RECARO. The new seats are incredibly well thought out from a passenger experience. However, the colour scheme is a departure from the usual Batik-inspired palette that the airline has become famous for.

When describing the new cabin, one of the features consistently pointed out by the Chief Commercial Officer, Lee Lik Hsin, was the fact that passengers sit and sleep facing forward. Work, sleep, dining, and relaxing have all been considered. The seat, for example, has a dedicated space to place your laptop during the meal service, a huge bugbear for many passengers during the meal service. Additionally, the airline will also be introducing doors to its business class seats for the first time.

Arguably the biggest upgrade that Boeing 777 and Airbus A350 passengers will see is the introduction of double beds in select business class seats. According to Singapore Airlines, the full-flat beds measure 79 inches in length and up to 24 inches in width, while a padded bedsheet with memory foam will provide "additional cushioning and support".

When it comes to first class, Singapore Airlines has another bespoke product. Designed with PriestmanGoode, each first class cabin will have six seats, each with a floor to ceiling enclosure. Unlike the business class, the first class cabin sticks to the established Singapore Airlines design language.

The highlight of the first class cabin is the two center seats. These can be combined to make a sofa or double bed. The seats can be synchronised and adjusted as one. Of course, if the passengers occupying these seats are unknown to each other, a full height wall is able to separate them.

Singapore Airlines says that combined, the center seats offer “The largest double bed in commercial aviation”, measuring 80 inches in length and 60 inches in width. Another particular highlight of the seat, built by Collins Aerospace, is the option for face to face dining at all seats, allowing up to four people to dine together in the center seats.

#6307. Flying Blue Delays SAF & Donation XP Changes Until December 2026

One unique aspect of the Air France-KLM Flying Blue program has long been how environmental contributions have contributed toward elite status, whether through the purchase of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), or through mileage donations to environmental causes.

A couple of days ago I covered how seemingly overnight, the Flying Blue program drastically decreased status qualification through these methods, requiring 50% larger contributions to earn the same number of XPs (experience points, the method by which one earns status). There’s now an update, and I’m pleased to see the way this is being handled.

Flying Blue has announced that it’s delaying the changes it’s making to the ability to earn XPs through SAF and mileage donations, and this will now be implemented as of December 1, 2026. Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, shared the following with me:

On Monday, we updated how many XP you earn on Sustainable Aviation Fuel and charitable contributions. We didn’t handle the rollout well, and the new rate went live with unclear messaging and without notice. While this affects a small share of our members, we recognize for those members it matters a great deal.

The update was part of a continuous review of our elite program. We want to ensure we can keep delivering the benefits and service you expect.

For now, we’re pressing pause. From tomorrow (4 November), SAF and charitable contributions will earn XP at the previous rate, and any contribution made since 2 November will be credited at the prior rate as well. The new rate of €15 per XP begins on 1 December 2026; even at the new rate, no program in the market will recognize SAF contributions more generously than Flying Blue, including on award tickets.

We want Flying Blue to be a program you build your life around. Many of you put a lot of care into planning your flights and status qualification, and we understand your need to have time to make adjustments.

And to everyone who told us why this matters to you: thank you for caring this much about Flying Blue.

I am happy to see how Flying Blue leadership is handling this situation. Let me share my take on this situation, broadly.

I don’t necessarily think Flying Blue had to make some big, public announcement about the change in advance. After all, this isn’t an official part of the program, and there has really never been any member communication about these opportunities.

I think what was frustrating is that the change was implemented before the website was even updated. So you had the higher pricing already showing, while the page about SAF and mileage donations still reflected the old cost, leaving many people wondering if the change was a glitch or intentional.

At a minimum, I think it’s appropriate to update the webpage before the changes go live, and ideally even give a little notice on the page dedicated to this, just so members aren’t caught off guard.

When it comes to the change as such, Flying Blue does indeed have the most generous opportunities to qualify for elite status through these types of contributions. Selfishly I love this option, but it’s not like members are “entitled” to a certain rate of qualification through this method, since there’s not actually any objectively “fair” way to reward elite qualification for contributions.

So for Flying Blue, it’s presumably about balancing environmental goals with elite ranks. I know with the 50% price hike, I’ll be much less likely to buy SAF, and that’s fine.

As of December 1, 2026, the Air France-KLM Flying Blue program will be decreasing the number of XPs that members earn for contributing toward sustainable aviation fuel and environmental causes. This was initially supposed to be implemented a couple of days ago, but members were caught off guard, so I appreciate that the implementation of this has been delayed.

Membership is free and takes no more information than commenting as a guest. Earn status points for good contributions, and see fewer ads as your status grows.

#6306. This Train Offers a Front-Row Seat to One of Colorado’s Greatest Natural Wonders

“Locomotives all have their own attitudes and personalities,” says Adam Clawson, the 24-year-old engineer at the helm of Royal Gorge Route Railroad, as our train winds along the Arkansas River. “They are their own living, breathing machines, and you have to learn their personalities.”

It’s a warm Saturday afternoon in October, and Clawson is at the controls of a locomotive he knows well: “Black Betty,” a jet-black, 3,000-horsepower diesel-electric unit that runs along a 12-mile stretch of tracks in Southern Colorado. Clawson is a third-generation railroader, following in the footsteps of his grandfather and great-grandfather, who both worked along this same route.

The Royal Gorge Route Railroad winds along the Arkansas River in Colorado.

As he eases the rumbling locomotive through the gorge, he offers a running commentary on the geology and history unfolding outside the window. Millions of years ago, he says, as the Rockies rose above the plains, the Arkansas River began carving its ancient path through the emerging peaks. Over time, the water wore away the hard granite, cutting a narrow, V-shaped gorge that plunges as deep as 1,250 feet in places.

The result is the Royal Gorge, a geological wonder nicknamed the “Grand Canyon of the Arkansas River.” Visitors can experience the dramatic 10-mile-long chasm from several perspectives: From above, while gazing down from the Royal Gorge Bridge, the tallest suspension bridge in the nation (or for more adventurous travelers, while rock climbing a 5-hour via ferrata); and from below, while paddling the Arkansas’s roaring rapids on a whitewater raft. But for travelers looking to sit back and savor the scenery passing by, there's no better viewpoint than the Royal Gorge Route Railroad's open-air car, standing face-to-face with the staggering canyon walls.

The writer's view aboard the Royal Gorge Route Railroad

This train line is as historic as it is scenic. Though the tourist train didn't launch until 1998, the route itself has been here for nearly 150 years—but it was close to never being built in the first place. In the late 1870s, a pair of competing railroad companies—the Denver & Rio Grande and the Santa Fe—duked it out for the chance to build tracks through this narrow canyon. Their two-year battle, which involved everything from court injunctions to sabotage to gun-slinging hired guards, became known as the “Royal Gorge War.” Eventually, the two companies signed a treaty and the Denver & Rio Grande prevailed, building tracks that eventually reached the lucrative mining hub of Leadville.

Decades later, the train still threads through the same Old West landscape, but the ride is decidedly more comfortable. Today passengers can choose from three classes: Vista Dome, which offers nearly unobstructed views of the gorge from glass-enclosed dome cars; Deluxe Class in the vintage dining car, where four-top tables with cushioned booth-style seats and a bar are nestled against the large windows; and Coach Class, with four-person table seating and the option to order food and drink from the casual grill menu and bar. On select dates, there are also First Class dining tickets available for lunch and dinner, with elevated menus and wine pairings. Regardless of where you sit, all ticket holders have access to the open-air car, which is standing-room only. With Clawson or one of his fellow engineers at the controls, all travelers have to do is sit back and let the scenery unfold.

The journey begins roughly an hour south of Colorado Springs in Cañon City at a historic depot originally completed in 1914. A few miles later, a dilapidated pipeline comes into view, running along the canyon wall just above the river. Completed in 1910, this eight-mile-long, mostly wooden structure provided water to Cañon City until 1973. As the train passes under the Royal Gorge Bridge, Clawson encourages me to open the cab window, lean back, and look up. The wind whips my hair as I stare at the bridge some 1,000 feet overhead. It’s 18 feet wide, according to Clawson, but from this vantage point, it looks like a thin wire that’s been strung across a gaping expanse.

As the train works its way through the river gorge, water rushes past and red rock walls tower on both sides.

Next, the train squeezes through the gorge’s narrowest and deepest section, the towering red granite walls growing taller and more imposing as they tighten around the tracks. Then we chug over the famous “Hanging Bridge,” which was an engineering marvel when it was completed in 1879—and remains one even today. At this point, the chasm narrows to just 30 feet wide, creating a bottleneck that required a little ingenuity to get a train through. Engineer C. Shallor Smith came up with a brilliant solution: He designed a 175-foot-long bridge that’s suspended above the rushing water by A-shaped supports anchored to the canyon wall.

Soon after, Clawson spots a pair of plastic kayaks hauled out on a small beach on the other side of the waterway. “We might get mooned,” he warns, referencing how paddlers traditionally greet the train when it passes. But when we spot the kayakers standing on the bank a few minutes later, they simply smile and wave. Clawson blares the train’s horn in response.

Eventually, the train reaches its western terminus, the town of Parkdale. Clawson hits the brakes and we jump down onto the tracks. Standing in front of the train up close, I’m struck by just how imposing she is. Thinking back to Clawson’s personality comment, I imagine her as fiercely independent—a self-assured, no-nonsense type of gal who’s not easily pushed around.

We clamber back into the cab and the train heads in reverse, retracing the route toward Cañon City. I relax back into my seat, letting the engine’s vibrations and the rhythmic drone of the wheels lull me into a pleasant daze. Outside, the rocky surfaces of the gorge’s walls alternate between light and shadow while the river glints in the midday sun. High overhead, I spot a turkey vulture circling on a thermal, its wings arching in a shallow V as it glides without flapping.

Clawson follows my gaze. “You can’t make this up,” he says. “Somebody might type into AI, ‘Take this picture of me and make it look like I’m in paradise.’ [But] all I gotta do is step outside."

We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6305. 5 Procedures Pilots Follow When Flying Through Polar Airspace

Ethan is an aviation professional with a degree in Aviation Management with Flight from the Florida Institute of Technology. He previously wrote aviation and tourism features for Florida Tech’s student newspaper, The Crimson, where he developed a clear, reader‑focused reporting style. Aviation journalism has remained a consistent priority throughout his career.

He currently holds a Restricted ATP and Commercial Multi‑Engine Pilot certificate and works in aviation supply chain and aircraft component repair. Alongside his industry role, he is pursuing his Certified Flight Instructor rating and actively building flight experience.

A lifelong aviation enthusiast, Ethan spent countless hours at Raleigh–Durham International Airport’s observation deck studying air traffic and practicing amateur photography and videography.

The curvature of the Earth: the main reason why pilots conduct polar operations within the Arctic Circle and, in some cases, the Antarctic continent; aircraft originating in North America with a destination in Asia are commonly routed direc tly over the Arctic Circle. Although rare, some routes, such as the Qantas 'Antarctica Flights' brand, conduct sightseeing flights of the continent. Several other flights operate near Antarctica, albeit not as a full transcontinental route.

Many operating limitations, such as the remote nature of the poles and harsh weather conditions, solicit special operating requirements and procedures for safe flight. While the South Pole is generally considered unsafe for full crossing, the North Pole is not subject to the same limitation. Canada, Greenland, Iceland, and Russia all provide acceptable diversion options and air traffic control services. Greenland in particular has experienced massive growth in the aviation sector, notably via the Nuuk Airport(GOH) runway extension. Subsequently, United Airlines began nonstop flights to Newark Liberty International Airport(EWR), and Air Greenland has launched services to Iqaluit (YFB), connecting Inuit communities by air for the very first time.

The Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) is a global navigation aid comprising four major navigation constellations, as well as several regional systems. While the Global Positioning System (GPS) is the household name in the United States, there are equivalent systems worldwide that serve the same primary function:

GNSS consists of three components: the Space Segment, the User Segment, and the Control Segment. How that manifests in flight operations is that it is a closed system, though not immune to anomalies: the Space Segment consists of the physical satellites orbiting Earth at all times. Per the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), 31 satellites are currently operational in their orbit, and GPS requires a baseline core of 24 operational satellites to function globally. The User Segment consists of the physical GPS receivers installed on the aircraft, with functionality extending to many "user" modalities: Wide Area Augmentation System (WAAS) and Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring (RAIM) are the two that apply to GNSS. Finally, the Control Segment is a series of ground-based monitoring stations that supervise the integrity of the satellite performance.

Some flights operate long distances from the nearest airport.

WAAS is not usable in polar regions because its geostationary satellites sit over the equator, leaving the high‑latitude areas with poor or no WAAS coverage, due to the curvature of the Earth. As a result, aircraft flying polar routes are not WAAS equipped, and rely on RAIM/ARAIM and true‑north navigation methods. RAIM remains fully usable in polar operations because it relies on GPS satellite geometry and onboard integrity algorithms rather than on equatorial geostationary augmentation such as WAAS. For polar flights, RAIM is the primary GPS integrity method.

However, while reliable, RAIM and the broader GNSS system are not foolproof in polar regions. While satellite-based navigation is highly reliable at lower latitudes, such as in the contiguous lower 48 United States, its reliability degrades toward the poles. Therefore, all flights operating polar routes are equipped with backup navigational aids (navaids) such as Inertial Reference System (IRS) navigation, ground-based navigation such as VOR/DME, or dead reckoning. Per FAA guidance (ENR 7.3), GNSS anomalies must be reported to ATC immediately, and the FAA offers an online report for a more detailed review once the flight is on the ground.

Contingency procedures from ENR 7.3 are critical when an aircraft cannot maintain its clearance. This is common in polar regions due to weather, system failures, or the aforementioned navigation degradation. Therefore, a standard maneuver is performed when an aircraft deviates from its course assigned by ATC: a pilot will turn at least 30° left or right, move onto a track that’s 5 miles parallel to the original one.

Maintain the assigned altitude if possible: otherwise, minimize the descent rate. Then, add a small vertical offset (500 ft, or 1000 ft above FL410). Lastly, broadcast intentions on 121.5 (colloquially known as 'guard, the emergency frequency) and 123.45, which is officially recognized by the ICAO as an air-to-air advisory frequency for aircraft operating over remote oceanic areas.

The standardized procedure primarily helps with collision avoidance and weather avoidance. ATC response can be delayed during flights over polar regions due to a lack of radar coverage. The procedure comes from ICAO, and the FAA adopted it into ENR 7.3. It was created over decades of international work on how to keep aircraft safely separated in places where ATC cannot see you, especially oceanic and polar airspace.

By having a standard operating procedure in the event of collision or weather avoidance, pilots can safely operate in polar regions with peace of mind. Finally, because GNSS failures and IRS drift are more likely at polar altitudes, the contingency maneuver helps mitigate the risk of two aircraft unknowingly converging when their navigation accuracy degrades.

By immediately turning 30°, shifting 5 NM off the track, and adding a vertical offset, the aircraft creates predictable, research-based, engineered separation even if its GPS position becomes unreliable or its IRS begins drifting. This standardized move ensures that even without radar, fast ATC response, or perfect navigation, every aircraft follows the same escape pattern, keeping them safely spaced until normal navigation can be restored.

Several commercial air routes exist over the Arctic, but none over the Antarctic - why is this the case?

To mitigate the risk of GNSS navigation leading to midair collisions and to avoid wake turbulence, crews use the Strategic Lateral Offset Procedure (SLOP). This allows pilots to offset up to 2.0 nautical miles right of their track, which is considered an SOP for all oceanic crossings, per FAA guidance (ENR 7.1).

"Along a route or track there will be 21 positions that an aircraft may fly: on centerline or at increments of ­0.1 NM (for example, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4...1.8, 1.9, 2.0) right of centerline out to a maximum offset of 2 NM. Offsets ­must not exceed 2 NM right of centerline. The intent of this procedure is to reduce risk (add safety margin) by ­distributing aircraft laterally across the 21 available positions."

Pilots who cannot program automatic offsets must stay on the centerline, or use the 1 NM or 2 NM right offsets when applying SLOP. Offsetting helps reduce wake turbulence, and pilots should choose the best available right‑of‑track position and coordinate on 123.45 if needed, especially when overtaking another aircraft. They must never offset left of the centerline or more than 2 NM to the right, ensuring all aircraft remain predictably separated.

High‑latitude flying squeezes aircraft closer together because the meridians converge, which reduces the natural sideways spacing between tracks. At the same time, navigation accuracy drops near the poles due to magnetic field unreliability and a higher likelihood of GNSS or IRS drift. SLOP spreads aircraft laterally to counter these risks, creating predictable right‑of‑track separation and lowering the chance of a head‑on conflict in non‑radar polar airspace. SLOPs are primarily used for aircraft traffic flow and spacing, rather than for weather; pilots should instead take a "see and avoid" approach in relation to weather, work with ATC, and the aforementioned contingency maneuver.

Polar Flights are placed on an ICAO flight plan. In Field 15, pilots or dispatchers are required to enter all intended waypoints for the planned route of flight. Of course, such flight plans are always subject to change due to weather, traffic, and other factors. Pilots will enter the flight plan with respective waypoints into the Flight Management System (FMS) or Multipurpose Control Display Unit (MCDU), which relays information to Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Contract (ADS-C):

With respect to how positioning is reported, ADS‑C should be used as the primary reporting method. According to SkyBrary, ADS-C is an air traffic control surveillance system used mainly in remote and oceanic areas. Note that while ADS-C is active, stop all voice position reports.

If ADS‑C drops, pilots should immediately revert to the next available method in this order: fall back to Controller–Pilot Data Link Communications (CPDLC) or High Frequency voice. Avoid Aeronautical Radio, Incorporated (ARINC) 424 5‑character lat/long entries; ATC will reject them, as they are nonstandard coordinate reporting formats. Instead, this example format is unambiguous and ICAO‑compliant:

Navigation reliability in polar regions depends on maintaining RNP capability and filing the correct ICAO codes. Because magnetic variation becomes unusable at extreme latitudes, aircraft must rely on true‑heading navigation and high‑integrity long‑range systems. Polar operations require PBN/A1 or PBN/L1, plus specific datalink codes like P2, D1, and J5/J7 for ATC surveillance.

These requirements ensure the aircraft can hold precise tracks where lateral separation is minimal and ground‑based navaids are nonexistent. Reliable datalink communication becomes essential because HF propagation degrades near the poles. ADS‑C and CPDLC provide continuous position monitoring, enabling controllers to maintain safe spacing in airspace with no radar coverage.

Ultimately, robust navigation capability protects against the unique risks of polar flying: magnetic unreliability, GNSS degradation, and increased IRS drift. By filing correct capabilities and ensuring all long‑range navigation systems are fully functional, pilots maintain compliance with FAA oceanic procedures and preserve the accuracy needed for safe polar route operations. An ICAO flight plan filed with precision and strong planning also helps mitigate flight disruptions over polar regions, whether by the pilot or a company dispatcher.

#6304. 10 Magical Christmas Traditions Around the World

Living far away from family is hard at the best of times, but it becomes particularly difficult around the holidays. If there's one thing that makes it a little easier for me, it's being able to mix and match festive traditions from different countries to create something that's uniquely ours. As an Italian living in France with a British husband, I love bringing together the best of each culture for a rather extravagant Christmas. On Christmas Eve, we have oysters and Champagne, as per French tradition, followed by an Italian feast and plenty of Christmas crackers—although I draw the line at Christmas pudding, preferring a simple pandoro over anything else.

Whether, like me, you spend Christmas far from your family, are planning to chase the sun this December or are driving home for the holidays, one of the great joys of Christmas is making memories and indulging in nostalgic traditions. All over the globe, different countries and cultures celebrate the season in different ways, marking the holiday with long-established rites and rituals or merging heritage to create beautiful new traditions. Below, we run through some of our favourite Christmas traditions around the world, and ask the Traveller editors about their own personal festive rituals. From seafood feasts on Christmas Day in Australia to surfing Santa’s taking to the waves in SoCal, these are the most wholesome traditions for some festive joy this season.

Christmas is not recognized as a national holiday in Japan, but the festive season is still celebrated—albeit slightly differently from how you’d expect. As part of a marketing campaign launched in 1974, a few years after KFC first opened in Japan, the brand came up with the slogan ‘Kentucky for Christmas’, and it stuck. On Christmas Day, many Japanese families tuck into a full feast of fried chicken—a tradition so popular that you often have to order weeks in advance to make sure you’ve got your bucket guaranteed for the big day. The original Christmas meal even came with a bottle of wine. Christmas cake is just as surprising in Japan, too—strawberry shortcake, made with layers of sponge, whipped cream and fresh strawberries, is a festive favourite.

As you might imagine, food is at the heart of Christmas celebrations in Italy. Every region has its own traditions and dishes, enjoyed on Christmas Eve, Christmas Day and throughout the festive season. While northern Italians might tuck into tortellini in broth and other comforting dishes, in the south we go all out. In my family, we have twelve different dishes—mostly fish-based—served for Christmas Eve dinner, before indulging in traditional desserts and an unholy amount of nuts while playing tombola. If there is one tradition that the whole country shares, it's the rather quirky tradition of La Befana – a witch-like old woman who flies through the skies on a broomstick on the night of January 5, leaving gifts for children to discover on the morning of 6 January, known as Epiphany (Epifania in Italian). Well-behaved children receive sweets and presents, while naughty ones get coal – although these days it's usually sweet, sugary charcoal, which is actually delicious.

The real difference between the Scottish festive season and that of much of the rest of the world is Hogmanay. Once Christmas Day is done and dusted, the focus is on New Year’s—or, as the Scots call it, Hogmanay. Street parties in cities such as Edinburgh roll on until the early hours, Robert Burns’ Auld Lang Syne is sung at midnight, and the ‘first-footing’ custom takes place—the first visitor to a home after midnight is believed to bring good luck for the year ahead (along with traditional gifts such as whisky, shortbread or a lump of coal, of course). Traditionally, a tall, dark-haired man is considered the luckiest first-footer.

While much of the Northern Hemisphere is wrapping up against the cold, Christmas in Australia falls in the middle of summer, meaning festive celebrations often revolve around the beach, sunshine and outdoor gatherings. "The traditional Christmas lunch in Australia is usually seafood, a roast ham served cold, lots of salads and then a pavlova for dessert," explains Lauren Burvill, CNT’s senior commerce writer and resident Aussie. "After lunch the classic traditions are to play cricket in the backyard, or if you're lucky, on the beach. It's not unusual to see Santa on the beaches as well, often riding on an inflatable rescue boat from the local surf club. On Boxing Day the country's favourite pastime is to watch the cricket or the Sydney to Hobart yacht race."

Forget snowy landscapes and cosy fireplaces—in Southern California, you might spot Santa Claus swapping his sleigh for a surfboard during the festive season. "I grew up in greater Los Angeles, and though December isn't typically beach weather, something uncanny almost always happens on Christmas," explains Megan Spurrell, Conde Nast Traveler US’s associate articles director. "The temperatures spike to the mid-70s Fahrenheit with shining sun and many families, including my own, end up at the beach. But we also go to look out for a very SoCal figure, known as Surfing Santa. We keep our eyes out at Manhattan and Hermosa Beach, especially near the piers, though I've heard of surfing santas in Malibu and Santa Monica, too. Most are just local dudes with a Santa suit who reliably hit the waves on Christmas morning to entertain their neighbours (and get a surf session in)."

While many Western traditions see Santa leaving lumps of coal in stockings for badly behaved children, in Austria it's the terrifying Krampus who comes to punish them. As the folklore goes, the Krampus is a fearsome horned figure with a long, snake-like tongue, who accompanies Saint Nicholas on 5 December, otherwise known as Krampusnacht, the eve of Saint Nicholas Day. While Saint Nicholas rewards well-behaved children with sweets and small gifts, Krampus is said to frighten or punish those who have been naughty. Today, the tradition is celebrated with Krampuslauf parades, during which people dressed in elaborate horned masks and furry costumes take to the streets, particularly in Alpine towns and villages. The folklore even inspired a Christmas comedy horror film in 2015, starring Adam Scott and Toni Collette.

In Peru, Christmas Eve, known as Nochebuena, is the main event, with families gathering for a festive dinner and celebrations that often continue well past midnight. "We alternate years of spending Christmas in Southern California with my mom and sisters, and going to Lima, Peru, with my husband's family" says Megan. "Though Peru has plenty of traditions tied to Christmas, perhaps my favourite is the sheer fact (shared in many Catholic and Latin American countries) that the whole affair begins at midnight on the 24th. It can be torture waiting until midnight proper to dig into the feast of turkey and arroz arabe that sits out waiting, but the entire city explodes in fireworks when the clock strikes 12. And then the party doesn't stop until the wee hours of the morning, sometimes at a family member's house or at the city's bars and clubs. It almost feels like a preview of New Year's Eve, just a few days earlier."

Dumplings are a major part of Polish cuisine day to day, and Christmas is no exception. The traditional Christmas Eve supper, known as Wigilia, begins when the first star appears in the sky, with families gathering around the Christmas table for a feast that traditionally includes 12 meatless dishes. "My favourite part of seasonal eating has never been the Great British Christmas Roast, but instead 'Polish Christmas', celebrated by my family on Christmas Eve, a haphazard tribute to the Polish side of my family tree," says Olivia Squire, Traveller's features editor. "When I was a child, my grandmother used to make pierogi (Polish dumplings filled with mashed potato and cottage cheese) from scratch, which in more recent years has been taken over by my mum and I and usually involves a lot of swearing and tears. It's all worth it when we sit down to eat them alongside a vegetarian version of bigos (hunter's stew—an insult to my meat-loving ancestors), breaded fish and holy wafers, soundtracked by Carol's at King's, my English dad's addition."

Forget spending a fortune on Christmas presents—in Germany, the tradition of Schrottwichteln puts a rather amusing twist on exchanging gifts, with friends and family swapping unwanted, bizarre, or downright useless objects instead.

"For gifts, we follow the German tradition of Schrottwichteln (literally 'junk Secret Santa'), where everyone brings something completely useless, unwanted or gloriously ridiculous, often something they were given once and never knew what to do with. The more pointless, tacky or absurd, the better," Karin Mueller, Traveller's visuals director, tells us. "Our children have grown up with this ritual, and what began as a cosy dinner has become the highlight of the year. They never miss it. Now that they’re young adults, they bring their partners along, and it’s turned into this wonderfully chaotic, joyful, very-London celebration that I’m pretty sure they’ll keep going long after we stop hosting."

Across England, Christmas is celebrated with familiar traditions, from exchanging gifts to tucking into mince pies and singing Christmas carols. But each county and neighbourhood has its own customs, too. In some seaside towns, brave locals take part in a Boxing Day dip—sprinting into the freezing sea to shake off the Christmas excesses, often while raising money for charity. There's also the age-old custom of burning a Yule log, traditionally associated with good fortune and protection from misfortune. In Cornwall, some communities gather in local pubs for a traditional Cornish ‘shout’, joining together to sing folk songs and sea shanties.

"In the hazy betwixmas period, the days of lounging on the sofa and gorging on Terry’s chocolate orange are punctuated by one magical evening at a local pub for a Cornish 'shout'", explains Lucy Bruton, CNT's social media manager. "A shout refers to the community coming together to sing sea shanties and folk songs in the pub, and the Lerryn (where my family live in Cornwall) shout is a particularly special one to me. The tiny pub feels packed to the eaves with people of all ages belting out some of my favourite Cornish songs – from "Trelawney" to "Lamorna" and, of course, “Cornwall My Home”. It’s dark, cosy and a real slice of the magic of Cornwall."

#6303. Transfer Citi ThankYou Points To Turkish Miles&Smiles With 40% Bonus: Worth It?

At the moment, it’s possible to earn up to a 40% bonus when you transfer Citi ThankYou points to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. However, the bonus isn’t being offered on Citi’s end, but instead, is being offered on Turkish Airlines’ end.

Between November 1 and November 30, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 40% bonus when you move points from the Citi ThankYou program in the United States to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. However, there are some important terms to be aware of:

Ordinarily points transfer at a 1:1 ratio (in 1,000 point increments), while through this promotion you’d get 1,400 Miles&Smiles miles for every 1,000 Citi ThankYou points transferred, though only after the fact.

There are several great cards earning Citi ThankYou points, including the Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more) and Citi Strata Elite℠ Card (learn more), and it’s easy to combine points between the cards.

Back in the day, the Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles program offered incredible redemption values across the board, but that’s no longer really the case. At this point, I’d say the sweet spot with the Miles&Smiles program is if you’re looking to travel on Turkish Airlines specifically to or from Istanbul.

That’s because the Miles&Smiles program now charges per segment for awards on Turkish Airlines metal. You can find the cost of one-way saver awards below, just to give you a sense of pricing.

So as an example, a one-way business class award between the United States and Istanbul will cost you 65,000 miles. In other words, with a 40% transfer bonus, you’d be paying around 47,000 Citi ThankYou points for a business class award, which is a pretty great deal.

If you know what you’re doing and have specific redemption plans in mind, this could be a great deal. Just be sure you understand the complexities of the program, and read my guide to the Turkish Miles&Smiles program. Also keep in mind the Miles&Smiles expiration policy, which is that miles expire at the end of the third year after which they’re earned, regardless of activity.

The other big restriction is that the bonus miles will only post after the campaign is done, so you couldn’t transfer points and then immediately redeem all of them (including the bonus). The cap on 50,000 bonus miles is also limiting. But hey, if you value Turkish miles, this could definitely offer some value.

Between November 1 and November 30, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 40% bonus when you move points from Citi ThankYou to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. The catch is that the bonus miles only post after the end of the campaign, and you can only earn 50,000 bonus miles with this offer.

If you’re looking to travel on Turkish Airlines to or from Istanbul, there are some good deals to be had by taking advantage of this.

#6302. The Best Airbnbs in Colorado, Including a Ski-In Chalet and a Cliffside Cabin

I’ve always found Colorado a little hard to resist. After a handful of trips, I’ve explored everything from Aspen’s glitzy streets to Denver’s spirited food and cocktail scene to the many smaller towns in between—and somehow, there’s still more to discover. With four national parks; miles of hiking and biking trails; world-class ski resorts; and cities brimming with independent shops, restaurants, and bars, Colorado is a year-round playground with plenty to keep you busy (and plenty of reasons to come back).

Finding the right Colorado Airbnb is part of the fun. Think tucked-away mountain cabins with front-row seats to the snow, sprawling homes made for group getaways, and character-filled apartments that put you right in the middle of the action. While there are plenty of gorgeous Colorado hotels, there's something pretty wonderful about having your own Airbnb to return to after a day of chasing fresh powder, hiking, or exploring a new town. Whether you're plotting a winter ski escape, a summer adventure, or a fall foliage getaway, these are the 13 best Airbnbs in Colorado to add to your wish list.

We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews.

Number of guests: 9Bed and bath: 5 bedrooms, 4.5 bathsWhy we love it: In-ground pool, firepit, outdoor shower, dedicated office space, rooftop with mountain views

Don’t let the university neighborhood fool you—this south-of-downtown oasis is ideal for a quieter, family-friendly stay. It's close to the light rail, making it easy to get around when you so choose. With succulent-filled rooms, large paintings, five cozy bedrooms, and two-story windows, there’s lots to love about this space.

Any kids you're traveling with will favor the foosball and ping-pong tables in the basement, while adults will enjoy lounging in the sunken family room. But perhaps the most lovable feature is the private backyard, which has a pool, firepit, and full dining table, all surrounded by lush greenery and sleek appliances.

City: DenverThings to do nearby: Observatory Park, The Robert and Judi Newman Center for the Performing Arts, University Hills Farmers Market, University of Denver

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: California king bed, flat-screen TV, immersive sound system, disco ball, LED lighting, faux-fire Malm fireplace, skyline views

Get groovy at this nostalgic studio apartment, which features an authentic disco ball and skyline views (including a peek at Coors Field, where the Colorado Rockies play) in the heart of Denver's Lower Downtown (LoDo) neighborhood. Lucky for its guests, this spot is within walking distance of downtown Denver’s hottest entertainment, shopping, and dining outposts for a day or night out on the town. Plus, it’s equipped with all the amenities of your dreams, including a spacious California king bed, a 13-foot vintage couch, and a fully equipped kitchen for whipping up meals.

City: DenverThings to do nearby: Coors Field, Commons Park, Little Man Ice Cream shop, Ball Arena, 16th Street Mall, Larimer Square, McGregor Square, Denver Union Station

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Central location, fully equipped kitchen, private backyard, in-unit washer and dryer, kid-friendly amenities

You and your crew are in for a treat when staying at this charming, historic Boulder home. With original woodwork, colorful wallpaper, a fenced backyard, and three spacious bedrooms, guests here will enjoy a stylish stay.

Its location is the true star of the show: Right off Pearl Street, Boulder's happening hub of art, food, and entertainment venues, you'll be within walking distance from it all. Previous guests have raved about not having to rent a car when booking this base; even the airport bus takes you within three blocks of the address.

City: BoulderThings to do nearby: The Museum of Boulder, Pearl Street Mall, Boulder Theater, Pearl Street

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Rocky Mountain views, hot tub, outdoor kitchen with gas grill, firepit, Dobsonian telescope

Tucked on five private acres, this is a true mountain retreat in Bailey—a Colorado town less than an hour outside Denver, known for its quirky roadside attractions, outdoor recreation, and historic mountain charm. Dubbed “Skytrail Lodge,” this cabin fits right into the neighborhood.

The main living area is bright and welcoming, with floor-to-ceiling windows that bring the outside in. A big, comfy sofa anchors the living room, complemented by green and black accents that create an upscale, modern feel. Outside, lounge about on the deck and take in the incredible view of the Rocky Mountains. What better place to sip on your morning cup of joe, read a book, or indulge in an evening glass of wine?

City: BaileyThings to do nearby: Mount Bailey, Pine Valley Ranch Park, Brookside-McCurdy Trailhead, Crooked Top Mountain, Shawnee

Number of guests: 12Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4.5 bathsWhy we love it: Walkable to ski resort, private hot tub, chef's kitchen, spacious design, smart TVs

Tucked in the storybook town of Cascade Village, you'll find a stay that exudes real mountain charm, with creature comforts to write home about. This Vail house is just a five-minute walk to Vail Ski Resort, with a free shuttle to Lionshead and Vail Village nearby. Meaning no matter the season—whether skiing or hiking—guests will have a convenient stay accompanied by the amenities that make an Airbnb great: a private, six-person hot tub; a fully equipped kitchen; en suite soaking tubs; private balcony access; and a laundry area.

Folks who stay here can cook up dinner on the grill or in the spacious kitchen, enjoy their meals in the eight-person dining area, play some groovy tunes on the Sonos speaker, and sip on a cup of coffee while looking out over the city and mountains. If you needed a sign to book a fun group adventure, consider this it.

City: VailThings to do nearby: Eagle Bahn Gondola, Lionshead Village, Vail Village, Ford Park, Betty Ford Alpine Gardens

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Central location, wood-burning fireplace, shared hot tubs and heated pool, private patio

If you're looking for a stay in a mountain city that's as convenient as it is cozy, this Breckenridge condo is your solution. The renovated two-bedroom town house is designed for folks interested in exploring the downtown pubs, restaurants, and art-filled spaces—as well as the mountain trails, ski resorts, and beautiful natural surroundings.

Back at the rental, use the space to “ski, stroll, soak, and repeat,” as stated in the listing. Unwind around the crackling wood-burning fireplace, enjoy a home-cooked meal around the big dining table, stay in for a round of board games, or indulge in one of the condo's shared amenities: the heated pool, sauna, or one of the four hot tubs.

City: BreckenridgeThings to do nearby: Illinois Creek Trailhead, Carter Park and Pavilion, Breckenridge Brewery & Pub, South Main Street, QuickSilver SuperChair

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Hot tub, wraparound deck, wood-burning fireplace, mountain views

Say hello to your next base for that upcoming group trip. This three-story timber lodge is all about space, convenience, and mountain fun. With a light-filled, open-concept kitchen and living room, you'll have some room to breathe. The floor-to-ceiling windows with sprawling mountain views and a wraparound deck make it even better. The home sits only 12 miles from Breckenridge, so it's drivable to the city's best hubs—from nature to dining—while also being tucked away enough to sprawl out and frolic.

Aside from the four queen bedrooms, there's a game room complete with a foosball table, vintage arcade games, table tennis, and more, making it a truly kid-friendly base.

City: AlmaThings to do nearby: Peaceful Valley Lodge, Wheeler Lake Winter Trailhead, Downtown Breckenridge, Montgomery Reservoir

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Slopeside location, heated pool, hot tub, private balcony

With its ski-in/ski-out location and proximity to one of the lifts on Aspen Mountain, this is a stellar booking for snow chasers. But it's also a fantastic base for those heading to Aspen in the warmer months, thanks to its swanky year-round amenities, like a sprawling pool and hot tub with lounge chairs for relaxing or soaking up the sun.

City: AspenThings to do nearby: Aspen Mountain Ski Resort (one block to Lift 1A), Aspen Art Museum, Main Street, John Denver Sanctuary, White House Tavern

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bedsWhy we love it: Private hot tub, sauna, mountain views, wood-burning stove, design-forward interiors

This swanky cabin is ideal for those in need of a restorative nature trip. The cool cabin aesthetic extends throughout the open-concept kitchen, big windows, hot tub, and sauna—and the view of the sprawling mountain range is well appreciated.

The biggest peak you can see from the living room is the region's iconic La Plata, which is the fifth-highest in the Rockies. Mount Elbert, Colorado's highest peak, is at the back of the home, with one of its trailheads a few minutes down the road. Another big plus? The home sits just over a two-hour drive from Denver—making it a sweet weekend trip for Mile High City locals and a good road trip stop for those heading onward.

City: Twin LakesThings to do nearby: Rinker Peak, Independence Pass, Mount Elbert, Twin Lakes Village, Colorado Trail, Continental Divide Trail, Leadville

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Sauna, firepit, hot tub, tasteful interior design, barbecue grill with outdoor seating

The lush Glenwood Springs is an underrated gem compared to its more frequented neighbors, Grand Junction and Moab. At this one-of-a-kind cabin, though, you'll likely question why it's taken you so long to plan a trip here in the first place.

Awe-inspiring canyon views await in every room through expansive windows, adding to the spot's light and airy feel. Each bedroom features a Tempur-Pedic bed and private deck access for true comfort and solitude. Indulge in the outdoor perks, too—there's a six-person hot tub, a firepit on the patio, and a four-person barrel sauna ready for post-adventure restoration. You'll also have prime access to the village's downtown square and its iconic hot springs.

City: Glenwood SpringsThings to do nearby: Colorado River, No Name Trailhead, Lookout Mountain, South Canyon Hot Springs, Horse Mountain, Hanging Lake Trailhead

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Mountain and forest views, private patio, bathtub, indoor fireplace, Wi-Fi

As one of Airbnb's most wishlisted properties, find this spruced-up, octagon-shaped tree house tucked away in the small mountain community of Cascade. It’s a scenic 15-minute drive from Colorado Springs, but you’ll find serenity easily among the tree house's natural surroundings. With floor-to-ceiling windows that look out to a little forest paradise, a wood-burning stove, a coffee and waffle maker, puzzles, games, and a smart TV, you'll never want to leave.

If you do plan to go out, you’re just five minutes away from Pikes Peak Highway, dotted with loads of gorgeous hiking trails, but you don’t have to leave your property to catch a glimpse of hummingbirds and other wildlife.

City: Cascade-Chipita ParkThings to do nearby: Ski and/or trails, scenic drives, Woodland Park, restaurants, reservoirs

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Pikes Peak views, convenient location, fully equipped kitchen, opt-in grocery delivery

This lofty town house—positioned (basically) right next to Garden of the Gods public park—is all about the views. The kitchen, living, and dining room all face the iconic Pikes Peak through a glass garage door. When open, it transforms the space into a picture-perfect indoor-outdoor area, complete with an overhanging balcony for taking it all in.

Two of the three spacious bedrooms sit on the home's ground level with shared bathroom space. There's also a separate “kids room,” complete with two twin beds—plus a trundle and space to hang out with a television (and a game system). You might not want to spend too much time at home, though: The home sits just a few blocks from Manitou Springs and Old Colorado City for sightseeing, restaurant trips, outdoor adventures, and more.

City: Colorado SpringsThings to do nearby: Manitou, Red Rocks, Garden of the Gods, Old Colorado City, Academy Riding Stables, The Incline, The Cog Railway

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Quirky design, infrared sauna, firepit, mountain and valley views

Just a one-hour drive from Great Sand Dunes National Park and Preserve, this otherworldly home deserves a spot on your Colorado bucket list. It sits at the base of the Sangre de Cristo range, with mountain views by day and dark skies for stargazing at night. As one of the quirkiest picks on this list, this hobbit home has more creature comforts than appear at first glance. There's a kitchenette for meals at home, a dining table that seats four, and an in-unit washer and dryer. You'll also find an infrared sauna to relax in, as well as a firepit to cozy up around. Do note, the home is most ideal for duos or small families, with its one queen bedroom and a double bed in the loft.

City: CrestoneThings to do nearby: Great Sand Dunes National Park, Blueberry Peak, Duncan, Eureka Mountain, Sangre de Cristo Mountain Range

#6301. Former China Eastern Chairman Jailed In $10+ Million Bribery Scandal

The former chairman of China Eastern Airlines has been sentenced to 14 years in jail, as he accepted more than $10 million in bribes in his official role. Yowzers!

A court in China’s Liaoning Province has sentenced former China Eastern chairman Liu Shaoyong to prison. The court ruled that he accepted over $10 million in bribes in his official capacity as chairman of one of China’s largest airlines.

The court found that between 2002 and 2023, Liu abused his position at the airline to provide assistance to companies and individuals in business operations, project contracts, and flight route management. Liu has been sentenced to 14 years in prison, and has been ordered to pay a fine of $600K, plus his illicit gains and related proceeds have to be recovered.

While the court ruled that his conduct constituted bribery “in an exceedingly large amount,” the sentence he got was actually lighter than it could’ve been, due to mitigating circumstances. These include his confession, voluntary disclosure of previously unknown offenses, and expression of remorse and cooperation in recovering illicit gains.

Make of this what you will, but it’s interesting to note that this is all part of China’s “anti-corruption campaign,” targeting officials at various levels, including executives of state-owned enterprises.

In June 2025, Liu had been placed under investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI) and the National Commission of Supervision, for violations of party discipline and state laws. In January 2026, he was expelled from the Communist Party of China (CPC), after investigators found that he had abused his authority for personal gain, and he was formally charged in May 2026.

China Eastern’s former chairman has been sentenced to 14 years in prison, after he admitted to taking over $10 million in bribes in his official role. This came as part of a larger crackdown by the government, which also saw the executive expelled from the Communist Party of China.

Over the years we’ve seen a decent number of airline executives charged with corruption — after all, they control a lot of spending, and in some cases, might get influenced for the wrong reasons.

What do you make of this punishment for China Eastern’s former chairman?

#6300. Ryanair Weighs Fare Hikes, Pay Freeze As Fuel Prices Soar

Irish discount carrier Ryanair is bracing for a difficult 2027 as jet fuel prices rise and European oil hedges expire.

In its most recent earnings report, the airline said it is considering temporarily freezing pay for workers, lowering crew ratios, and ramping up use of artificial intelligence. The company did not specify how long it would look to freeze wages, or how it would adjust staffing.

Ryanair has over 27,000 employees across its group.

Speaking to CNBC on Monday, Ryanair CEO Michael O’Leary said ticket prices will rise across Europe as lower-price oil hedges run out.

“The market customers have been insulated for the last 12 months,” O’Leary said. “But those hedges are rolling off. There’s still no resolution in the Middle East. Jet oil today is $170 a barrel. I mean, this is a very significant cost cliff we’re all facing next year. I believe you’re going to see air fares rise next year across Europe by 10 percent, maybe even 20 percent.”

In its earnings report, Ryanair said that while short-haul air fares will increase “materially,” it will not be enough to offset the expected €2 billion increase in fuel costs, necessitating the additional cost-saving measures.

Fuel prices have prompted several major European airlines and airline groups to cut capacity this fall and winter, and to retire some older, less efficient aircraft. Price volatility also pushed Lufthansa to accelerate the shutdown of Lufthansa CityLine, and made the U.K.’s EasyJet amenable to a roughly $7.7 billion takeover by Apollo Global Management.

The price shock has generally been worse in Europe and Asia than in North America, as those regions are more dependent on Gulf oil and lack domestic refining capacity.

One of my favorite things about World of Hyatt points is how much flexibility they offer. You could redeem just a few thousand points for a night at a Category 1 Hyatt hotel or use a larger stash to book a higher-category hotel or all-inclusive resort.

Since Hyatt still uses award charts for most of its properties, you can sometimes get outsize value by redeeming points when cash rates are high. But free nights aren't the only way to use your points. From room upgrades and dining experiences to airline miles and rental cars, here's how you can redeem World of Hyatt points, including which options offer the best value.

The best way to redeem Hyatt points is usually for free hotel nights. Hyatt has award charts for most free night awards, though some are dynamically priced. There are also ways to combine points with cash and free night certificates.

Hyatt publishes award charts for free night awards at Hyatt hotels and resorts, participating resorts within the Hyatt Inclusive Collection brands and Miraval resorts. Each of these charts has five award pricing tiers — Lowest, Low, Moderate, Upper and Top — for each category.

Here's the award chart for standard room award nights at Hyatt hotels and resorts.

Hyatt publishes separate award charts for Hyatt Inclusive Collection brands and Miraval resorts, as well as for club rooms, standard suites and premium suites. Check out our guide to the Hyatt award charts for all the charts.

You can click on "Points Calendar" on the results page for any particular property when searching for award stays to see how many points each night costs.

However, free night awards at Mr & Mrs Smith hotels and Homes & Hideaways by World of Hyatt are priced dynamically based on paid rates. For example, this night at a Homes & Hideaways property in Florida would cost 16,011 points or $192.13. This means you'd get 1.2 cents per point when redeeming Hyatt points for this night.

And this night at a Mr & Mrs Smith property in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, would cost 8,750 points or $58.91. This means you'd only get 0.67 cents per point when redeeming Hyatt points for this night.

TPG's November 2026 valuations peg Hyatt points at 1.65 cents each. As such, you'll generally want to get at least this much value when redeeming your Hyatt points.

Related: Best Hyatt hotels in the world to book with points

You can also book Points + Cash rates for some stays. When these rates are available for your chosen room type and property, you'll redeem 50% of the points required for a free night and get 50% to 70% off the standard rate (which may be higher than the best available rate).

For example, I could redeem 12,000 points, book a Points + Cash rate of 6,000 points plus $156.50 or book a paid rate of $220.16 for this night at the Hyatt Centric Rittenhouse Square Philadelphia.

When redeeming points, I'd get 1.83 cents per point. And when booking a Points + Cash rate, I'd get 1.06 cents per point.

Related: Which credit card should you use for Hyatt stays?

You can also combine Hyatt points with paid nights and even free night certificates when booking with the Hyatt Pay My Way feature. To use this feature, sign in to your Hyatt account, search for a paid stay, click on the property and room type of your choice and then click on rates until you see one with a Pay My Way option.

Click on the Pay My Way box, and then you can choose whether to use points, cash, Points + Cash or free night certificates for each night.

I often use Pay My Way when redeeming free night certificates, as this lets me book a multinight stay even if I only have one free night certificate. I've also used Pay My Way to redeem points for a stay with one particularly expensive night.

Related: The best Hyatt Category 4 hotels to maximize your free night award certificates

You can redeem points to upgrade eligible paid stays at many Hyatt hotels and resorts. Here's a look at the upgrade rate per night:

You can sometimes redeem points for an upgrade at the time of booking. In the following example, you could redeem 9,500 points for a premium suite free night, 4,750 points plus $158 for a premium suite Points + Cash booking or 9,000 points plus $152 to upgrade a paid night to a premium suite.

If you don't upgrade at the time of booking, you can call (800) 544-9288 in the U.S. and Canada or contact a Global Care Center to see if your existing stay is eligible for an upgrade with points.

Related: Your ultimate guide to Hyatt hotel brands

You can redeem Hyatt points for dining and spa experiences at participating locations even if you aren't spending the night. Plus, you can redeem points during stays at participating locations to pay for in-room movies, parking, transportation and more.

To redeem points, simply request to use Hyatt points at checkout and choose how many points to redeem. You should be able to redeem points at participating locations based on the following chart:

As you can see, the redemption rate you'll get ranges from 1 to 1.54 cents per point, which is below TPG's November 2026 valuation of 1.65 cents per point for Hyatt points. As such, you'll usually want to find higher-value ways to redeem your Hyatt points.

You can redeem Hyatt points for Find experiences. For example, you could pay $60 plus taxes or redeem 4,286 points for this one-hour aerial yoga and meditation class.

Or, you could redeem 5,357 points or pay $75 plus taxes for an e-bike tour of San Diego.

It's worth taking a look at Find experiences, especially if you select Find experience credits as Hyatt Milestone Rewards. But you usually won't get outsize value when redeeming points for these experiences.

Related: Why bidding on a Hyatt Find experience auction might be the most valuable way to redeem your World of Hyatt points

You can convert Hyatt points into airline miles with the following programs:

For most of the airline programs, you'll get 1 mile for every 2.5 Hyatt points you convert. However, Hyatt uses different conversion rates for Aeromexico Rewards, Air China PhoenixMiles, China Eastern Miles, Qantas Frequent Flyer, Southwest Rapid Rewards and Virgin Atlantic Flying Club.

You must convert at least 5,000 points at a time but can convert additional points in increments of 1,250. If you convert 50,000 points or more, you'll usually get an extra 5,000 bonus miles.

However, converting Hyatt points to airline miles will rarely make sense. Conversions can take six to eight weeks. Plus, at the usual 2.5:1 conversion ratio, transferring 5,000 Hyatt points yields 2,000 airline miles. Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, you'd be giving up approximately $82.50 in Hyatt points for those 2,000 miles.

You can redeem Hyatt points for Avis free day awards, which are valid at participating locations in the U.S. and Canada, by calling (800) 544-9288. When available, you can redeem 6,000 points per day for an intermediate-size car. However, there are blackout periods that you'll see on the redemption certificate once you redeem your points. Avis free day awards usually expire one year after they're issued.

World of Hyatt members can redeem points for an Aeroplan flight reward certificate valid on Air Canada flights. The 30,000-point certificate costs 50,000 Hyatt points, and you can apply it toward the base fare in points of an Aeroplan flight reward.

Given that TPG's November 2026 valuations peg Hyatt points at 1.65 cents each and Aeroplan points at 1.45 cents each, this won't be a good-value redemption for most travelers. However, if you were planning to convert Hyatt points to Aeroplan points, the flight reward certificate might provide better value.

Related: How to redeem Aeroplan points for maximum value

World of Hyatt and American Airlines AAdvantage are winding down their partnership. But eligible Explorist and Globalist members can redeem Hyatt points for AAdvantage Status for a Day until 1 a.m. EST on Nov. 16.

You can redeem 5,000 Hyatt points to get AAdvantage Gold status for a day, 8,000 points to get AAdvantage Platinum status for a day and 12,000 points to get AAdvantage Platinum Pro status for a day.

However, you can only use these awards on your own travel itineraries, and some fares aren't eligible.

Related: Why I rely on credit cards to earn American Airlines elite status

Finally, you can redeem Hyatt points for a future meeting credit to use for meetings and catered events at participating Hyatt hotels and resorts based on the following chart:

As you can see, the redemption rate is 1.33 cents per point regardless of how many points you redeem toward a future meeting credit. You must call a Hyatt Global Care Center to redeem points for a future meeting credit. You can't use future meeting credits at Hyatt Vacation Club, Bahia Principe and Destination by Hyatt Residences locations.

Redeeming World of Hyatt points for free nights is usually the best way to get good value from your points. I particularly like redeeming Hyatt points at hotels where cash rates are high, as I can often get outsize value. But I'll also redeem points on stays with resort fees, as Hyatt waives resort fees on free night awards.

Other redemption options, including room upgrades, Find experiences and airline miles, can make sense in certain situations. But I generally recommend saving your Hyatt points for free night awards, especially if you can be flexible about where and when you stay.

#6298. Every Airline Flying From The US To Australia & The Routes Served In 2026

The Global Guy & Kevin Hackert | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Nonstop travel between the US and Australia remains one of the most important long-haul markets across the Pacific, connecting major US gateways with Australia's largest cities and several destinations beyond its traditional east coast hubs. In 2026, airlines are operating an extensive selection of services, with the US gateways of Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), San Francisco International Airport (SFO), and Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) providing the majority of connections.

The market features a combination of established nonstop routes, competitive services, and newer connections designed to give travelers greater flexibility. There are four main airlines providing nonstop links between the two countries, with a total of 8,820 flights scheduled between them in 2026, according to the latest data from ch-aviation. This equates to a total of 2,610,162 seats, and more than 18 billion available seat miles across the various airline and route combinations. These totals illustrate the scale of the market, while individual routes reveal how airlines distribute capacity according to demand, network strategy, and the importance of their respective US gateways.

American Airlines serves Australia through a focused network linking Los Angeles International Airport and Dallas/Fort Worth International with Sydney Airport (SYD) and Brisbane Airport (BNE). The airline's scheduled services for 2026 include 365 flights between Los Angeles and Sydney, and 135 between Dallas/Fort Worth and Brisbane. The oneworld carrier also schedules 13 flights between Los Angeles and Brisbane, giving it a presence across several important transpacific city pairs rather than relying on a single gateway. Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport (SYD) is the most prominent Australian destination in American Airlines' published network, with the Los Angeles service offering a major link between Southern California and Australia's largest international aviation market.

The Dallas/Fort Worth to Brisbane route provides another important option, particularly for travelers originating in the central and eastern US who can connect through American Airlines' major Texas hub. These services complement the airline's broader domestic network, allowing passengers from numerous US cities to travel to Australia without necessarily beginning their journeys on the West Coast. The airline's schedule also demonstrates the different scales of its individual routes, with Los Angeles to Sydney recording 110,960 seats and Dallas/Fort Worth to Brisbane offering 35,031. Its Los Angeles to Brisbane operation is substantially smaller, with 3,705 seats. American Airlines' network between the US and Australia in 2026 is summarized in the table below:

Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport (DFW)

Delta Air Lines operates an extensive selection of services connecting Los Angeles with Sydney, Brisbane, and Melbourne. The schedule shows 418 flights between Los Angeles and Sydney and 182 between Los Angeles and Melbourne. The SkyTeam carrier's 65 flights between Los Angeles and Brisbane add another option for passengers traveling between the US and Australia's east coast. Los Angeles to Sydney is Delta Air Lines' largest Australian route, accounting for 114,981 seats and 860,862,747 available seat miles. The Los Angeles to Melbourne service adds 50,050 seats, creating a substantial second connection to Australia. These routes give Delta Air Lines a significant presence in the transpacific market, while its Los Angeles connections allow passengers from other parts of the US to access its long-haul services.

Delta Air Lines' network emphasizes established destinations with strong demand for business and leisure travel. Sydney provides access to Australia's largest metropolitan area, while Melbourne attracts visitors interested in its cultural attractions, sporting events, and business districts. Although the airline's Brisbane operation is smaller than its Sydney and Melbourne services, it broadens the available choices for travelers heading to Queensland. Together, these routes demonstrate how Delta Air Lines combines its US network with demand across Australia's principal international gateways.

The airport handles millions of passengers annually.

Qantas has a particularly important role in the US to Australia market as Australia's flag carrier, with services connecting several American cities to Sydney, Melbourne, and Brisbane. The carrier's operation include 353 flights between Los Angeles and Sydney, 357 between Los Angeles and Melbourne, and 336 between Los Angeles and Brisbane. Qantas also operates nonstop services between San Francisco and Sydney, demonstrating that its US network extends beyond its principal Los Angeles gateway. The carrier's Los Angeles to Melbourne route offers 105,666 seats, while Los Angeles to Brisbane offers 78,740 seats. Qantas' Los Angeles to Sydney service provides 170,458 seats, making it one of the most substantial individual routes between the two countries. The airline's San Francisco to Sydney operation adds another important connection for passengers traveling from Northern California, reducing the need to travel through Los Angeles before beginning a transpacific journey. The oneworld carrier's route network is outlined in the table below:
