#6274. Lockheed Built The Constellation’s Famous Triple Tail For One Key Reason - To Fit Inside An Airline’s Existing Hangars

Brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age. He became involved in the flight simulator and VATSIM communities, which sparked his interest in aviation and eventually led him to earn his private pilot license. Outside of work, he continues to build flight hours, explore new airports, and stay involved in the aviation community.

The Lockheed Constellation is one of the most recognizable aircraft ever built, and its most distinctive feature, the triple tail, was not an aesthetic choice. It was a solution to a hangar door. When TWA asked Lockheed to design a long-range pressurized airliner in 1939, one of the requirements was that the aircraft had to fit inside TWA's existing maintenance facilities. A single vertical stabilizer large enough to provide directional stability on a four-engine aircraft of the Constellation's size and speed would have made the tail too tall to clear the hangar doors.

Lockheed's engineers split the required fin area across three shorter vertical stabilizers, keeping the aircraft's overall height to 23 feet 8 inches (7.2 meters). The solution worked; TWA got an aircraft that fit its infrastructure, and Lockheed produced 856 Constellations across all variants before the jet age ended the propeller airliner era. Here is why the triple tail was necessary, how it worked aerodynamically, and what the aircraft contributed to commercial aviation beyond its silhouette.

In 1939, Trans World Airlines owner Howard Hughes approached Lockheed with a set of requirements for a new long-range airliner. Hughes wanted an aircraft that could carry a 6,000-lb (2,720 kg) payload, fly 3,500 miles (5,630 km) without payload, and cruise at more than 250 mph (402 km/h) at 20,000 feet (6,096 meters). Those were aggressive specifications for the era and would have produced a large, heavy, four-engine aircraft substantially bigger than anything TWA was operating. Hughes added one additional requirement: the aircraft had to fit inside TWA's existing maintenance hangars.

That constraint created a specific engineering problem. The Constellation's four Wright R-3350 engines drove large-diameter propellers that required tall landing gear to maintain ground clearance. The tall gear raised the fuselage, which in turn raised the tail. A conventional single vertical stabilizer providing enough area for directional stability on an aircraft of this size and speed would have pushed the total height well beyond what TWA's hangar doors could accommodate. Lockheed's engineers, led by chief engineer Hall Hibbard and chief aerodynamicist Kelly Johnson, needed to provide the required vertical stabilizer area without exceeding the hangar height limit.

The solution was to split the vertical stabilizer into three shorter fins mounted across the horizontal tailplane. Three fins provided the same total surface area as a single large fin while keeping each individual surface short enough to hold the aircraft's overall height to 23 feet 8 inches (7.2 meters). The design fit inside TWA's hangars.

The aerodynamic function of a vertical stabilizer is to provide directional stability by resisting unwanted yaw, keeping the tail of the aircraft tracking behind the nose in straight flight and during turns. The size of the fin determines how much yaw resistance it generates. A larger fin produces more stability. The total area required depends on the aircraft's size, weight, speed range, and the distance between the center of gravity and the tail surfaces. On the Constellation, splitting that area across three fins rather than concentrating it in one did not reduce the total stabilizer area. It redistributed it across three shorter surfaces.

The three-fin arrangement also produced a secondary aerodynamic benefit that a single center fin would not have provided. The two outboard fins sit in the slipstream of the inboard propellers, which means they receive accelerated airflow from the engines at all flight speeds. At low speeds, where a conventional vertical stabilizer is least effective because the airflow over it is slowest, the propeller wash over the outboard fins maintains a higher local airspeed across those surfaces. The result is improved directional stability during takeoff, landing, and low-speed flight, and better yaw authority during single-engine operations when the aircraft needs to counteract the asymmetric thrust of three operating engines against one failed engine.

The triple-tail configuration came with trade-offs. The horizontal stabilizer had to be structurally reinforced to support three fins and the associated loads, which added weight. The flight control system required three rudders instead of one, with corresponding control cables, hinges, and actuators that added mechanical complexity and maintenance requirements. The Douglas DC-6, which competed directly with the Constellation on the same routes, used a conventional single-fin tail and did not pay those weight and complexity penalties.

A nostalgic journey awaits as Lufthansa's iconic aircraft nears completion.

The Constellation was designed at Lockheed's Burbank, California facility under the leadership of two engineers whose careers extended well beyond the program. Hall Hibbard served as chief engineer and Kelly Johnson as chief aerodynamicist during the initial design phase, with project engineer Don Palmer managing the detailed engineering as the program progressed. Johnson, who was 29 when the Constellation project began, would later found Lockheed's Advanced Development Programs division, better known as Skunk Works, where he led the design of the P-80, U-2, and SR-71.

The Constellation's wing was derived from the Lockheed P-38 Lightning fighter, scaled up from a 52-foot (15.8 meters) span to 123 feet (37.5 meters). The structural approach and airfoil design carried over from the fighter program, which gave Lockheed's team a tested aerodynamic foundation to build on rather than starting from a clean sheet. The fuselage was a pressurized aluminum semi-monocoque structure with the distinctive curved dolphin shape that rose at the nose, dipped at the midsection, and rose again toward the tail. The pressurization system maintained a cabin altitude of approximately 8,000 feet (2,438 meters) while cruising at 20,000 feet (6,096 meters), making it one of the first large commercial airliners to offer pressurized flight as a standard feature.

Power came from four Wright R-3350 Duplex-Cyclone 18-cylinder radial engines, the same engine family that powered the Boeing B-29 Superfortress. Each engine produced approximately 2,200 horsepower in early variants, later increased to 2,700 and beyond in the Super Constellation series. The R-3350 was powerful but temperamental, prone to overheating issues that contributed to several incidents during the Constellation's early service years. The aircraft also introduced hydraulically boosted flight controls and a thermal deicing system on the wing and tail leading edges, features that were not standard on contemporary airliners.

The Constellation first flew on January 9, 1943, from Lockheed's Burbank field. It flew not as a TWA airliner but as a military transport designated C-69, requisitioned by the US Army Air Forces after the attack on Pearl Harbor redirected Lockheed's production priorities toward the war effort. The nine L-049 airframes originally ordered by TWA were purchased by the War Department, and 22 C-69s were built between 1943 and 1945. The aircraft spent the war years stateside, used primarily for long-range personnel transport while the Douglas C-54 Skymaster handled the higher-priority overseas airlift missions.

On April 17, 1944, Howard Hughes and TWA president Jack Frye flew the second production C-69 from Burbank to Washington National Airport in 6 hours and 57 minutes, averaging 331 mph (533 km/h) at 65% engine power. The aircraft was painted in full TWA livery despite carrying a military serial number, and the flight was a publicity exercise as much as a delivery. Hughes was required to hand the aircraft over to the Army Air Forces upon landing in Washington. On the return trip, the aircraft stopped at Wright Field in Ohio, where Orville Wright boarded for what would be his last flight, more than 40 years after his first at Kitty Hawk. Wright commented that the Constellation's wingspan was greater than the distance of that first flight.

When the war ended, TWA bought back every C-69 it could from the government and converted them to civilian configuration. Commercial Constellation service began in February 1946, and the aircraft immediately outperformed the Douglas DC-4, the airliner most carriers were using on long-haul domestic and early transatlantic routes. The DC-4 was unpressurized and cruised at approximately 227 mph (365 km/h). The pressurized Constellation cruised at 340 mph (547 km/h) at 20,000 feet (6,096 meters), above most weather. Douglas responded with the pressurized DC-6 in 1947, and later the DC-7, and the resulting competition between Lockheed and Douglas through the 1950s produced the most intensive period of propeller airliner development in aviation history. Lockheed built 856 Constellations across all variants before production ended in 1958, the same year the Boeing 707 entered service and rendered the entire category obsolete.

From the TriStar Stargazer to Buffalo’s Electras and Australia’s Connie — meet the oldest Lockheed commercial aircraft still flying today.

The Constellation introduced several technologies that became standard across commercial aviation. Cabin pressurization at the scale Lockheed implemented allowed airline passengers to fly above weather for the first time on a production airliner, establishing the principle that commercial aircraft should cruise at altitudes where turbulence and storms are below rather than around the aircraft.

Hydraulically boosted flight controls addressed the increasing force required to move control surfaces on larger, faster aircraft, a problem that would only grow as airliners became heavier through the 1950s and into the jet age. The thermal deicing system on wing and tail leading edges replaced the rubber boot deicing used on earlier aircraft with a more reliable heated-air approach. Triple tails disappeared from commercial aviation when jet airliners arrived.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

The Boeing 707, Douglas DC-8, and every subsequent commercial jet used a single vertical stabilizer. The hangars that had constrained the Constellation's designers were replaced or expanded to accommodate the new generation of aircraft, removing the height limitation that had created the three-fin design in the first place. By the time airports were building hangars for the 747 in the late 1960s, no vertical stabilizer height was too tall to accommodate. The engineering problem the triple tail solved ceased to exist.

Of the 856 Constellations built between 1943 and 1958, approximately 55 survive. As of 2026, only two are airworthy. VH-EAG, a C-121C Super Constellation operated by Australia's Historical Aircraft Restoration Society, flies from Illawarra Regional Airport in a restored Qantas livery and carries passengers on demonstration flights. N422NA, a VC-121A named Bataan that served as General Douglas MacArthur's personal transport and later flew for NASA during the Apollo program, is maintained by the Air Legends Foundation and appears at US airshows.

#6273. Emirates Profits Plunge Due To War… But The Airline Still Made Money?!

It goes without saying that it has been a tough year for airlines, due to the United States getting into a war with Iran. All airlines have been dealing with higher jet fuel prices, but airlines in the Gulf region have of course been dealing with additional issues, as all kinds of airports in the region have been attacked, making some people reconsider traveling through the region.

That’s why I think it’s interesting to note that Emirates has just released its financial results for the first half of the fiscal year (April 1 through September 30, 2026). Yes, Emirates’ profits decreased massively, but surprisingly, the airline still turned a healthy profit, and the numbers look much better than I would’ve guessed.

Prior to this year, Emirates was the world’s most profitable airline for two years in a row, as the carrier really is incredibly well run.

That’s why I think it’s interesting to note how the airline performed over the first six months of the current fiscal year, which coincides entirely with the current Iran conflict. While there are results for the overall Emirates Group (which also includes dnata, etc.), I’m focusing on the airline specifically, since I find that to be most telling.

Emirates reported a half-year profit of $1 billion, down 68% compared to the previous year. Interestingly, revenue was $15.5 billion, down “only” 13% compared to the same period the previous year. The airline didn’t actually cut back its total capacity that much — available seat kilometers (ASKM) decreased by 17% compared to the previous year, while the passenger load factor decreased to 72%, from 79.5% the previous year. Emirates carried 21.8 million passengers over the six months, down 22% from the same period last year.

As of September 30, 2026, Emirates is operating 91% of its pre-disruption network, with the passenger and cargo network spanning 150 airports in 78 countries. However, that reflects the number of destinations, rather than the total actual capacity (in other words, many destinations are being operated with reduced frequencies).

Emirates CEO Sheikh Ahmed bin Saeed Al Maktoum reflected on this as “a demanding six months,” and said that “once again our business model and our people stood up to the test.” He explained that the company is entering the second half of the fiscal year “with measured optimism,” “while keeping a close watch on costs and geopolitical developments.”

One would think that Gulf carriers are in the toughest spot of any airline, given that they’ve been so reliant on connecting people traveling between other regions, and at least among some people, their willingness to travel through the region has decreased, assuming it can be avoided.

Admittedly many people also just live in this region, so it’s not like there are endless options. But when you consider all factors, I’d say these are very encouraging results, much better than I would’ve expected.

I know there’s often a lot of skepticism when it comes to the reported financials of Gulf carriers. I do think at some Gulf carriers, there’s reason to be skeptical about the math, based on what is and isn’t reported.

In the case of Emirates, though, the airline is legitimately very profitable and well run. The airline has managed to efficiently scale its operation in a way that no other airline really has, and that’s where credit goes for the carrier’s success.

Of course we have to acknowledge that there’s a difference in underlying economics. Dubai (DXB) is much lower cost to operate out of than somewhere like London Heathrow (LHR) or New York Kennedy (JFK), and Emirates Group owns both the airline and the ground handling company. Furthermore, the cost of jet fuel is lower in Dubai than it is in somewhere like London, and I imagine the airline also has access to more attractive financing opportunities, given that it’s owned by the government.

However, that’s hardly anything that’s super hidden or secret. I mean, economics in US aviation are also sort of lopsided. Airline profits are largely reliant on everything except actually flying, which is a privilege and upside that most foreign carriers can’t fully unlock.

I think it’s also interesting to note how well Emirates’ yields have held up during this time. For example, just based on looking at fares through Google Flights, it seems like Etihad’s strategy has just been to publish incredibly low fares to fill seats, including in premium cabins. I haven’t found that to be the case with Emirates, though, as the airline has managed to maintain pricing power despite reduced demand.

Emirates has reported its financial results for the first half of the 2026-2027 fiscal year. As you’d expect, this was a generally tough time for a Gulf carrier, given the current war with Iran. While Emirates’ profits were cut by around two-thirds, the airline still turned a healthy profit of around $1 billion.

Honestly, the actual operating figures don’t at all reflect what you’d expect during a crisis, so it seems like the airline is weathering this story pretty well, all things considered. I do feel like Emirates is uniquely positioned among its competitive set, and I’d be shocked if the story is similar at Etihad or Qatar Airways.

What do you make of Emirates’ financial results?

#6272. Bizarre: Lufthansa Group Now Requires Travel ID For Online Check-In

Most airlines encourage travelers to check-in online, given that it’s mutually beneficial — it saves time for the traveler, and saves resources for the airline. Well, Lufthansa Group is implementing a new policy that makes it more difficult to check-in online, as flagged by aeroTELEGRAPH, and that strikes me as rather backwards.

Lufthansa Group has the concept of a Travel ID, whereby customers have an account they can use to log-in across digital platforms belonging to all carriers, including Lufthansa, SWISS, Austrian, Brussels Airlines, Edelweiss, Discover Airlines, etc. This is separate from the Miles & More program, as the idea is that it simply creates a unified log-in for digital services across the airlines.

So along those lines, Lufthansa Group is progressively rolling out an initiative whereby customers need to have a Travel ID account in order to check-in online via the website or app.

Lufthansa Group is rolling out this requirement gradually. The Travel ID is required to check-in online as follows:

There are a limited number of exceptions for the Travel ID requirement. Specifically, you don’t need a Travel ID if you’re a traveler checking in at the airport counter or machine, if you’re traveling on a ticket issued by another airline, or if you’re on a flight operated by another airline with a ticket issued by Lufthansa Group.

Airlines love data and being able to market to customers. It’s one of the reasons that airlines create such strong incentives to sign-up for their loyalty programs (or in this case, a log-in that allows the airline to market to you). We’ve seen countless airlines roll out free Wi-Fi for those who are loyalty program members, and the logic is easy enough to follow.

However, in this case we’re talking about online check-in, which is something that arguably helps the airline more than it helps the customer. I can understand an airline wanting to add a step for something that entirely benefits the customer (like free Wi-Fi), but doing it for a basic function that saves the airline money? Well, that’s quite the approach to take.

In fairness to Lufthansa, I’m not sure this is actually a bad idea, or will backfire that much. Yes, it’s a minor annoyance, but:

Now, it’s still rather customer unfriendly, in my opinion, but that’s not exactly the first time we’ve seen something like that in the airline industry…

Lufthansa Group will start requiring passengers to sign-up for a Travel ID in order to check-in online. This is progressively being rolled out through November 30, 2026. Making it more complicated to check-in online seems counterproductive.

At the same time, clearly this is intended to encourage travelers to register for a Travel ID, so that Lufthansa can better track customer data and market to travelers. Usually we see incentives created to encourage this kind of registration, but in the case of Lufthansa Group, the airline is instead threatening to take something away if you don’t register.

What do you make of Lufthansa Group’s new online check-in requirement?

#6271. This Swanky Service Lets Commercial Fliers Skip the Airport Entirely—And It's Now Available in Dallas and Miami

As my plane touched down in Dallas, I could already make out my chauffeur waiting on the apron, the jet-black SUV glimmering in the Texas sun. It wasn’t long before my luggage was whisked away and we were driving across the airfield, past rows of planes waiting at their gates—so close that I could read their tail numbers. Our destination? A new private terminal operated by the company PS, which offers a curious promise to commercial fliers: Travel with us, and you will never step foot in the airport.

The shared “Salon” area at the PS Dallas Terminal, included in the entry-level pricing. Access to private suites cost an additional fee based on membership status.

Ten minutes later, my driver dropped me off at PS’s sleek new 12,200-square-foot private terminal at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW), where I was greeted by caviar and Champagne and escorted to my own private suite. Between the goodie-filled drawers, marble sinks, and the rainfall shower, I could have spent my whole time in the bathroom, where I had my pick of Le Labo products, plush towels, and comfy robes. It wasn’t like any airport lounge I had ever been to, rivaling even first class. And yet, it's still a fraction of the cost of flying private.

Champagne and caviar at the PS private suite.

PS first launched at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) in 2017, then called “The Private Suite.” As the name implies, all PS terminals have their own private, line-free TSA security screenings and dedicated Customs and Immigration checkpoints separate from the crowds. While this has earned the brand a reputation of being a “celebrity terminal," PS CEO Amina Belouizdad Porter says public figures actually make up "a very, very small portion" of the customer base. The real clientele are premium business travelers, families, and travelers going for celebratory splurges, she says.

"If you fly from LA to New York and back in first class, these days, that's around $4,000. If you do that private, that's probably $100,000,” Porter explains. “The gap is so big, and there are many people that want to bridge that."

For the last decade, PS has continued to expand. After renaming itself to PS in 2020, it opened a terminal at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) in 2023. The PS terminal at DFW opened on June 1 and was quickly followed by another PS location at Miami International Airport (MIA) later that month. This October, I flew between the two new terminals to get a better idea of how the exclusive service works behind the scenes—and who it’s actually for.

Each private suite has a bathroom complete with Le Labo products, plush towels, and robes.

In Porter’s view, departing is the most stressful part of air travel. "That's when you're asking, 'Where am I going? What time is my plane? Where's my gate?'" she says. Arrivals or transfers can be just as confusing for many travelers: going through immigration and customs, dealing with heavy bags, finding the right taxi stand or connecting to the right terminal for the next flight. The point of PS is to make both legs of the airport journey as seamless as possible.

After I was welcomed at the PS facility at Dallas-Fort Worth and spent a night in the city, I experienced the departure product en route to Miami. I once again rolled up in a chauffeured car to the PS terminal, where caviar was (naturally) waiting for me. The Dallas terminal occupies a gated facility adjacent to Corporate Aviation at DFW and was designed by interior designer Jean Liu to feel residential, like a luxury hotel.

The 40-foot bar in “The Salon” at the Dallas PS terminal.

I spent much of my pre-flight time in the public lounge area dubbed “the Salon,” which had floor-to-ceiling windows looking out over the tarmac. This area hosts a stunning 40-foot bar, taking inspiration from an old-fashioned Southern saloon. Once I settled in, I ordered breakfast (in Dallas, PS executive chef Matt Roman's blue cornbread is a must), and then worked and read a magazine. My boarding pass came with a sheet telling me when to be ready to board, though the PS staff guides make sure you are always where you need to be regardless.

Behind the scenes, the Control Room tracks all flights, delays, arrivals, and departures. From there, PS coordinates with the airline, TSA, and Customs and Border Protection, and stays in direct contact with the flight crews, which is how they’ll know your flight is delayed before the passengers at the gate do.

When it was time for me to board, I went through security right inside the PS terminal. It's a real TSA checkpoint, because PS is the only company in the United States with a private partnership with both TSA and CBP. Guests go through one at a time, and if you check a bag, PS checks it in with the airline for you. Once again, a car drove me to my plane, and I walked up a set of steps outside the jet bridge, through a door, and straight to my seat.

The open-air courtyard at the Miami PS terminal, located in the historic Pan Am headquarters.

By the time I got to Miami, I knew the PS drill. A sign with my name on it waited at the jet bridge, and from the plane it was a 15-minute drive to the original Pan Am headquarters.

At 34,000 square feet, the PS terminal in Miami is nearly three times the size of the one in Dallas—and the design could not be more different. That’s because the Miami terminal is a loving restoration: the building once housed both Pan Am's former headquarters and its stewardess college, where flight attendants trained in the 1960s. In March 2026, the buildings were added to the National Register of Historic Places as part of the “Pan American Airways Historic District," making the terminal a stunning architectural gem.

Pan Am’s Miami headquarters first opened in 1964, sat empty for 15 years, and was slated for demolition before PS restored it. The restoration shows off the New Formalist style (the bold, geometric designs of Miami's postwar resort boom), with an exterior wrapped in a patterned concrete screen and a repeating trapezoid design that reappears in the planters and door handles. The original insignias and gold paneling are still there, and going up the stairs, the Pan Am logo is engraved over and over into the stone wall.

The Miami PS terminal is filled with playful vintage touches, including palm tree wallpaper and capiz shell chandeliers.

Within the terminal, each PS suite has a different vibe (mine was pink), complete with nods to the beach and vintage touches, including palm tree wallpaper and capiz shell chandeliers. The courtyard is open-air, with a decorative pool tiled by Miami artist Nina Surel in Art Deco pastels that's lined with pink-and-white striped loungers and fringed umbrellas. This time, my Private Suite opened onto a balcony overlooking the courtyard. Inside was the same selection of amenities as in Dallas, plus a fresh food menu that was fitting for glitzy Miami: sashimi with cilantro dust, the classic caviar and Champagne, and—for good measure—a cubano. I enjoyed a chair massage, one of the spa's 30-minute treatments (including reflexology, manicures, hair and beard trims, and full-body massages). As much as I would have liked to linger, when it was time to go I took a sandwich to-go for my next flight, and left in PS style: Another car. Another plane.

Of course, none of this comes cheap. PS operates on a tiered membership system: The entry-level Salon Membership costs $1,250 annually, puts access to the Salon at $995 per person, and allows a member to book a Private Suite (accommodating up to four travelers) for $4,950. The top-tier All Access Membership is priced at $4,850 per year, and lowers access rates to the Salon to $895 per person, and Private Suite rates to $3,650. Without a membership, entry to the Salon costs $1,295 per person, and a Private Suite booking costs $4,950. Notably, because the Salon has an age requirement (21 and over, there’s alcohol), parties traveling with those underage are required to book a Private Suite. Pets are welcome in all PS private terminals, and all PS reservations must be made at least 24 hours ahead of travelers’ departure times.

Access to the private suites starts at $4,950 for members, with room for four travelers.

How should you decide if it's a worthwhile purchase for your trip? Porter is honest about which travelers should skip the whole thing: “If you're on your own, with no checked bags, going on an hour flight for the weekend, then the airport is just fine,” she says. "It makes the most sense for long flights and complicated routings; and parties with a lot of checked bags, kids, and older parents who could use the assistance.”

Because the concept blends private and commercial aviation in a way that hasn't been done before, Porter believes it's hard for travelers to fully understand the value of PS—until they've experienced it themselves. "It's just complete peace of mind," she tells me in Dallas. “That's what we're selling.”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6270. Lufthansa Realizes 28 Business Class Seats Isn’t Enough For Boeing 787

In recent times, Lufthansa has started taking delivery of factory fresh Boeing 787s, featuring the carrier’s all-new Allegris cabins. Management at the airline has reportedly decided that the configuration of these planes isn’t quite right for many routes, so now it’s planning some updates.

That’s a sensible change, but it always just feels like Lufthansa is a step behind when it comes to acting logically and catching onto trends, no?

Lufthansa currently has a fleet of 20 Boeing 787-9s. Four of these were acquired secondhand (they were former Hainan Airlines jets), while 16 are brand new, and feature Allegris interiors. Not only that, but Lufthansa has at least another 22 of these planes on order, which will be delivered in the coming years.

In the long run, the Dreamliner is supposed to be the carrier’s primary long haul aircraft based in Frankfurt, complementing the Boeing 747-8s and Boeing 777-9s. Meanwhile Munich (MUC) is primarily getting Airbus A350s (including the A350-900 and A350-1000).

Lufthansa’s 787s are configured with 287 seats, including 28 business class seats, 28 premium economy seats, and 231 economy seats. Keep in mind that three of those seats aren’t even certified yet (but should be certified before the end of 2026), so actual business class capacity is currently just 25 seats.

Anyway, even with all seats certified, Lufthansa Group management has decided that the capacity doesn’t actually match demand on many routes, with CEO Carsten Spohr indicating that the airline is working on installing more business class and premium economy seats on upcoming Dreamliners.

Reportedly nothing has been finalized yet, as this is still in negotiations with suppliers, but the idea remains that the current configuration doesn’t offer enough premium seats.

Given the eventual size of Lufthansa’s Dreamliner fleet, it would also be reasonable to think the airline may have two configurations in the long run, to reflect the demand of different destinations. For example, one would assume that the potential customer demand profile would be different to New York (JFK) than to Columbus (CMH), both of which are going to be Dreamliner routes in the coming months.

I know ragging on Lufthansa is just too easy, from its challenging labor relations, to its botched Allegris rollout, and more. However, I can’t help but feel like the airline is a little behind on trends.

I mean, for how long have we been talking about the surge in premium travel demand? American is taking delivery of 787-9s with 51 business class seats, United is taking delivery of 787-9s with 64 business class seats, and British Airways is reconfiguring 787-9s with eight first class seats and 38 business class seats.

So Lufthansa just taking delivery of dozens of factory fresh 787s with just 28 business class seats seems a little off, especially since Lufthansa only recently started adding these planes to its fleet.

I get that demand differs between markets, and the 787 is actually supposed to be the less premium plane in the fleet, in the long run (with the Boeing 747s and 777Xs being the most premium Frankfurt-based planes), but still, 28 seats just doesn’t seem like a lot by any metric. Heck, the Airbus A330s that are slowly being retired have 42 business class seats, and that’s an overall smaller plane.

Of course the whole Lufthansa Allegris and SWISS Senses situation is just sort of messy, from the 3.5-seat first class cabin that makes no sense, to the need to install a weight on SWISS A330s to balance out the weight of first class, to the new Allegris seats delaying entry into service for planes by years, despite it not actually being that cutting edge at this point.

Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr has indicated that the airline is considering a new configuration for many upcoming Boeing 787s. Management has decided that 28 business class seats and 28 premium economy seats isn’t sufficient, which strikes me as a rather obvious, when you look at trends. Heck, these Dreamliners are partly replacing planes with 50% more business class seats.

I’m curious to see what Lufthansa eventually settles on for a premium Dreamliner configuration, because I agree, 28 business class seats isn’t a lot!

What do you make of Lufthansa reconsidering its 787 layout?

Your statement that ‘ragging on Lufthansa is almost too easy’ sums up the situation nicely. Can anyone really remember a time when this airline, and LH group in general, wasn’t a joke? Remember when Lufthansa itself could seriously claim to be among the most premium and reliable brands on earth? It’s long been a trope that British Airways is the airline that most severely shredded its premium image, especially under Cruz. But he lasted less than 5 years running BA, and they’ve spent the last 6 years doing (just) enough to recover some of that, and are arguably about halfway there at best in terms of repairing the damage. Spohr has had a dozen years to wreck Lufthansa, with no end in sight, and they clearly cannot start repairing the damage until he goes. The fact they continue to get the most basic planning wrong, misreading or ignoring clear industry trends, just underlines this. Among the flagship European carriers, LH is just so far behind Air France, and even BA as things stand, it’s hard to imagine when they can actually try to catch up, saddled with their current leadership.

How Sophr is still CEO just shows you how the LH board and management is clueless. Its one bad decision after another and they keep the guy on...

Nah they just knew all the premium travelers were going to spend their money elsewhere. Smart. :D

......yet still there is no accountability. Now that AA seem to have finally seen the light, LH must be out on their own as the most incompetant managemnt for a major airline

The whole Allegris philosophy was a gamble on one very specific aspect: segmenting customers with different seat types. The allegris business class seat is a very inefficient seat. It is essentially the same concept as united’s Polaris, except with more seat pitch, and every second row, just one middle seat instead of two. Lufthansa thought they could segment their business class customers, upsell certain seats (especially the throne seats, the long bed and the mini-first class at the bulkhead) and make up for the lost revenue of having such an inefficient layout and shrinking the size of the cabin (to maintain a large economy class cabin). But this gamble failed, because Lufthansa didn’t realise that by upcharging so many business class passengers even to simply select a window seat put a bad taste in many people’s mouths. Look at BA, AF and KL. all business class seats in their cabins are created more or less equal with the exception of the bulkheads. Furthermore, Frankfurt is a business heavy market, but has less point-to-point business traffic, and a lot of connecting traffic. It is easy for travellers who are not star-alliance loyal to simply connect elsewhere, or fly united across the Atlantic. Lufthansa wanted to create a segmented business class cabin, but instead created a business class “lite” and charged for extras after that. And now they’re stuck with a VERY expensive, delayed seat, which occupies way too much space on their aircraft, and as such they have had to make huge compromises like shrinking the first and business class cabins. They will seriously lose out in the long term.

#6269. Tracing Wild Horse Nine's Route Through Chile—From Santiago to Rapa Nui

Within a few minutes of arriving at archaeological site Ahu Tongariki in Rapa Nui, where 15 gargantuan moai statues stand with their backs to the sea, my guide Gina’s phone lights up with the words “Tsunami Alert.” I ask her if this is a relatively normal occurrence on the island. “No… Although there was one [tsunami] in 1960 that washed several of these away towards the hill,” she says, gesturing towards the large sacred monolithic heads carved from volcanic stone, the Pacific Ocean sitting vast and blue behind them. The alert was later lifted, but I still felt a sense of impending doom as I posed for a photo in front of the moai.

Martin McDonagh's new film, starring Sam Rockwell and John Malkovich, follows two CIA agents through Chile.

Flirting with one’s own mortality at the edge of the world sits right at the heart of Wild Horse Nine, a new film written and directed by Martin McDonagh and filmed partially on Rapa Nui. Starring Sam Rockwell and John Malkovich, the dark comedy charts the journey of two CIA agents in Chile as they travel from their station in Santiago to the Polynesian island for a week-long vacation. Their trip also happens to be just before the country’s 1973 military coup, which would oust socialist president Salvador Allende and install dictator General Augusto Pinochet—an event that, for those at all familiar with the history of American foreign policy in Latin America, these two agents have clearly meddled in as operatives. I’d come to Chile to follow in the film's wake—to trace the real-life locations and history behind the silver-screen fiction.

The film’s characters Chris Carlisle (Malkovich) and Lee Chesterfield (Rockwell) form the kind of acerbic buddy duo that’s become associated with McDonagh films like In Bruges. The older, brasher Chris, now in the waning years of his spy career, considers their trip to Rapa Nui his final act following a terminal cancer diagnosis, bullishly demanding to see “the big heads” in reference to the moai. Lee, meanwhile, functions as exasperated colleague, grieving friend, and increasingly, minder, as his mentor’s memory begins to slip, sometimes returning loudly in moments of unguarded truth—or perhaps deathbed confessions. (One such example: a monologue where he cheerily reminisces about other elected governments he’d helped overthrow on the job.)

Chris and Lee are an uncurious pair of travelers, bristling at polite requests to educate themselves about Rapa Nui's Indigenous culture, and showing little interest in taking its history seriously. (“Why are you here if you’re just going to make fun of the place?” a fellow tourist asks Chris.) They play the part of ugly American tourists astutely—and yet, it’s largely through their eyes that we see both a 1970's Santiago and Rapa Nui on the screen.

Chris Carlisle (Malkovich) and Lee Chesterfield (Rockwell) travel from Santiago to Rapa Nui once character Chris receives a teminal diagnosis.

The rising interest in traveling to film locations is why tour operator Abercrombie & Kent has launched a 9-day itinerary, which allows guests to chase Wild Horse Nine's trail. I traveled to Chile to road-test the new offering. And like the characters of Carlisle and Chesterfield, I begin my trip in Santiago.

Unlike in the movie, the city is experiencing an unseasonable amount of rain on the morning I arrive. The Andes, which usually loom imposingly over the skyline, are concealed behind thick clouds, and the Mapocho River, which cuts through the city like an artery, is close to bursting its banks. But the 19th-century architecture of bohemian Barrio Lastarria is much more familiar. I’m met outside my hotel by my guide Lisette Matamala, who will spend the next couple of days introducing me to the fraught political history that serves as the backbone of Wild Horse Nine’s suspenseful plot.

The rain is lashing down, but we forge ahead on foot to nearby Plaza de la Constitución, and stand under comically sized umbrellas to have a look at La Moneda Palace. The seat of the Chilean president, this palace was bombed during the coup, resulting in one of the most memorable images from that day. In the movie, viewers see the regal structure, still intact, glimpsed through the office window of cranky CIA bureau chief MJ (Steve Buscemi), a key player in orchestrating the chaos. According to production designer Denis Schnegg, who I will speak to later on the phone, the team filmed that scene in an office opposite the palace that really had been used by the CIA during that time: “To stand in that room and look out at the palace, knowing how these people had been orchestrating it from their window, that the whole thing was planned—it's quite chilling.”

Santiago's presidential palace La Moneda in the aftermath of the 1973 coup d'etat led by Commander of the Army General Augusto Pinochet.

The consequences of their work are etched within the Salvador Allende Museum of Solidarity, a contemporary art museum in the historic neighborhood of Barrio República that has lived several lives: First, as an affluent mid-20th-century family home; then a left wing exhibition space founded in 1971 by a group of creative intellectuals; and, later, as a detention center and listening station operated by Pinochet’s Directorate of National Intelligence (DINA). It has since returned to its original form as a museum, resurrected after the return to democracy in 1990.

While not a Wild Horse Nine filming location, it’s an important stop to help place the film within the context of these very real historical events. “This house has a lot of layers of history and meaning,” museum director María José Lemaitre tells me as we walk down a flight of wide, winding wooden stairs. “And also, darkness.” When the art was reinstalled, secrets were uncovered within the bones of the building: transcriptions of tapped phone calls were hidden by DINA in the ceilings, and phone-tapping equipment sat in the basement.

Lemaitre and her colleague, museum curator Caroll Yasky, bring me to see the latter, housed in a dusty, windowless subterranean room. We linger over the handwritten names and phone numbers of families the DINA had spied on—tangible evidence of the horrors enacted by the history driving McDonagh’s plot. “The museum may show the past, but what is important is the future,” says Yasky as we walk back upstairs into the daylight.

The fingerprints of Pinochet’s regime are never far away in Santiago. I spend a pisco sour-filled evening dining with a university professor whose father had been one of the dictator's driver—a role that, he suggests, haunted his father so deeply he had a stroke to forget it. (It's an anecdote I can’t help but thread back to Chris’ struggles with redemption in Wild Horse Nine, which we often see him exploring in misguided attempts to write a memoir that he plans to leave behind following his imminent death.)

Much of Rapa Nui feels—and appears in the film—as though it sits on the edge of the world.

Another afternoon, we visit Villa Grimaldi, a once-notorious detention center on the outskirts of the city that now serves as a memorial. Two of its survivors are Alvaro Ahumada and Ignacio Puelma, smartly dressed and in their early 70s, who meet us under the trees near the entrance for a tour. We pass sobering remnants of the detention center’s structures, but also clusters of fragrant roses, colorful mosaics, and water features. “We didn’t want to have a horror museum,” says Ahumada, who is also the president of the foundation. “Instead, we wanted to wash away what happened here.”

The pair, I realize, would have been around the same age as the character of a young, optimistic left-wing student in the film named Monica, played by Mariana di Girolamo. These two were both members of the student-led Movement of the Revolutionary Left, and at just 19 and 21 at the time, they had been transferred from Villa Grimaldi to the same concentration camp where they connected over music, even forming a band during their imprisonment. “Our bond is very deep,” says Puelma, as a flock of squawking parakeets fly over us. “We were both rockers, so we had a lot to talk about,” adds Ahumada. “Helping each other, and looking after each other, was an act of resistance.”

Their story evokes a poignant scene in Wild Horse Nine, when they later reach Rapa Nui, during which Chris meets up with Monica at a low-lit, moody bar. As the ill-fated folk singer Victor Jara (Aron Hernandez) performs on stage, Chris tells her with disturbing frankness that he is not just a CIA agent, but one who has come down to Chile to “destabilize your democracy,” a direct reference to the United States’ involvement in installing Pinochet.

In one of the film's scenes, young Chileans are confronted by Chris's character, who tells them he has come to Chile to “destabilize your democracy.”

McDonagh’s decision to depict Jara, who was murdered by members of Pinochet's regime, is yet another reminder that beyond the buffoonery of Chris and Lee, lie the stories of real people like Ahumada and Puelma. Some of the film’s cast still feel its impact, too. “Monica [is based on] a real character: Comandante Tamara, a left-wing student and [guerilla leader] who attempted to assassinate Pinochet. And, of course, we know what happened to Victor Jara, the singer who is playing a Violeta Parra song in that bar,” di Girolamo tells me after the trip. “I was born in the first year of democracy, but my parents were students in school in ‘73. [This history] is just something you grow up with, and it's still an open wound for us.”

I arrive in Rapa Nui the same way Chris and Lee do: on vacation, via the one daily flight from Santiago, landing at a thatched airport where ukulele music wafts through the air and chickens toddle around baggage claim. Gina Pakarati, who was born and raised on the island, picks me up outside in her white Suzuki Jimny, and we set off to visit the same moai sites that, in the film, Chris tells Lee he wants to see before he dies. In fact, it’s when they first reach the island that it’s revealed to viewers that Chris has asked Lee to put a gun to his head and end things right here on Rapa Nui.

Wild horses run across the open, lush green plains of Rapa Nui island.

Pakarati, who knows the island like the back of her hand, blasts local Polynesian folk-country band Topatangi as we trace the rugged coastal drive captured in the film, past swathes of electric-green grassland and black volcanic rock. We pause for herds of the same chestnut-brown wild horses McDonagh frequently turns his camera to.

I wind my window down, and the air smells sweet yet woody. There is a surreal, heavenly quality to being here. At one point, Pakarati pulls over and plucks a small guava off a tree, so ripe that she can pull it apart with her hands, for us to eat at the side of the road.

As we drive up towards Ahu Akivi, one of several imposing moai sites on the island, small groups of tourists are milling around, some of whom I recognize. (Given the island’s size, you tend to cross paths with the same visitors fairly quickly.) Just like Chris and Lee, we’ve all come here for the same once-in-a-lifetime experience—albeit without a Super 8 camera and guns in holsters. But finally laying eyes on the moai feels like seeing a myth come to life. Pakarati, who is 43 and comes from a long lineage of Rapa Nui people, explains to me that of all the ceremonial platforms here, this one is particularly special because its seven statues are “looking towards Polynesia, the land where they came from.”

Towering moai made from volcanic stone—which Malkovich's character refers to as “the big heads”—are a living piece of ancient Polynesian history on Rapa Nui.

She recalls playing among the statues as a child (an activity now deterred by a rope) and hearing her grandfather’s stories of helping the visiting archeologist William Mulloy with their restoration in the 1960s. Thanks largely to Mulloy, that period drew more attention to the island and, after the first commercial flight arrived in 1967, ushered in the first real wave of tourism. Though it is a territory of Chile, life on Rapa Nui felt awfully far away from the coup, I'm told. Hotels began opening, more cars appeared on the roads, and in 1993, the first Hollywood film crew arrived. Despite the fact that the subsequent Kevin Costner-produced movie Rapa Nui was a widely criticized box-office flop, Pakarati says, economically everything changed after it, due to how many jobs were created—and she suggests that the spotlight of Wild Horse Nine might prompt another such wave of activity.

That initial Hollywood-driven boom on the island inspired hospitality ventures like still-operating, family-run Iorana Hotel. It’s an eccentric ocean-view property just outside of town that opened in the 1990s but feels frozen in the '70s. So much so that, in Wild Horse Nine, Chris and Lee both stay there, picking fights with unsuspecting tourists and waving their guns around in the rooms. Cars from the era were temporarily shipped over to drive past the property in certain shots, says Schnegg, but when it came to the interiors, which feature floor-to-ceiling wood paneling, tiki-style floral-patterned upholstery, and buttercup-yellow room doors, little was changed. (“The hotel is actually sort of disconnected from [town], which is probably why it's a bit stuck in time,” Schnegg notes.) One addition, however, were the protagonist’s rooms, which were specially built for the film. The owners plan to keep the set and turn it into a tourist attraction. “The last night [of filming] we were set up until 7 a.m. and then had a huge celebration in the morning,” says the owners' daughter, Carolina, as we take a look at the set. “I think this film will be good for the island.”

The family-run Iorana Hotel transports visitors—and viewers—straight to the 1970s.

We watch Chris and Lee ramble around many of the moai sites, but the one that stuns me most in its scale and beauty is the quarry at Rano Raraku, where hundreds of moai protrude at different levels from the hillside of an extinct volcano. Many lie solemnly in situ among the grass, while others now stand, having been hauled up into a standing position by archeologists in the ‘70s. Some are massive, and others unfinished. A view towards the coastline offers a spectacular vantage point of the fifteen statues of Ahu Tongariki, which all look back upon the quarry where they were created.

In Wild Horse Nine, we witness Chris and Lee unravel at this very site in a dramatic final shootout. I, in contrast, sit on a bench with Pakarati, the breeze making the grass shimmer (nowhere else have I been so astounded by the green of the grass), as she explains how these mammoth works were constructed and moved around the island by her ancestors. It may be a thrill to stand where the actors of Wild Horse Nine stood, but there’s much more gravity in knowing that I’m treading the same soil as those who carved the hulking statues before me. These days, Rapa Nui's archaeological sites can only be entered with an authorized guide—and I’m grateful for it as Pakarati shares her stories.

Rapa Nui provides a pensive setting for the film's character's, particularly Chris who knows his days are numbered.

Toward the film's end, Chris, death knocking on his door, describes isolated Rapa Nui as a lonely place. But I find it to be quite the opposite. On my final morning, we wake early and drive back over to Ahu Tongariki to watch the sun rise. The atmosphere is similar to gathering in anticipation of an eclipse. Locals and tourists alike set up camping chairs and drink coffee out of flasks as the sky changes hue: deep purple merging into soft blues, followed by shades of pink, ochre, and yellow bursting from behind the silhouettes of the moai.

Standing in the early dawn light, it’s easy to understand why such an epic natural landscape was used as a burial ground on ancient Rapa Nui—and why McDonagh thought a CIA agent like Chris, dying and trying to seek redemption from his darkened memories, may want to swagger over to such a place before his morally disreputable life comes to an end. Even with his internal struggle, does he have the right to such a bucket list? “When I read the script for the first time, I felt a little guilty about laughing [while they do] these terrible things,” di Girolamo had told me during our conversation. “Yet I’d felt empathy for these agents. I cried.”

The sun fixes itself high above the moai and we all clap. Another new day at the edge of the world.

Wild Rapa Nui is a 5.5-hour flight from Santiago, and feels a world away.

I flew direct from New York City to Santiago, before catching the 5.5-hour flight to Rapa Nui on LATAM Airlines—currently the only commercial flight to get you there. My itinerary was booked through tour operator Abercrombie & Kent, which has crafted an exclusive Wild Horse Nine trip tailored to the movie locations, while also connecting travelers with the real-life Chileans who lived under the Pinochet regime and want to share their stories.

Santiago: I spent three nights at the Singular Hotel, a boutique property in the center of artsy Barrio Lastarria. Rooms are spacious and comfortable, but the real winner here is the buzzy rooftop bar serving excellent pisco sours. It’s also walking distance from La Moneda Palace and the must-visit Chilean Museum of Pre-Columbian Art, which features several artifacts from Rapa Nui.

Rapa Nui: While there is an Explora property further inland, most hotels are clustered in and around the sole town of Hanga Roa, a laid-back, sunny community lined with seafood restaurants, surf shops, and cafes and bars wafting ukulele music. Check into Nayara Hangaroa for oceanfront rooms, a pool set upon volcanic rocks, and a concierge to assist with arranging excursions. Rumor has it that John Malkovich stayed here while filming Wild Horse Nine.

La Moneda Palace: A 15-minute walk from the Singular Hotel, Chile’s presidential palace is worth a pause as you pass through downtown. Buttressed by the Plaza de la Constitución and the Plaza de la Ciudadanía, it’s a largely civic area, but it’s hard not to be stirred by the location knowing, as Schnegg noted, that everything that took place here.

In Wild Horse Nine, the still-operating Municipal Theatre of Santiago is turned into an upper-class restaurant.

Municipal Theatre of Santiago: “For a pivotal scene with Chris and Lee, we turned the opera house into a sort of upper-class restaurant where [you’d imagine] the political elite would meet,” says Schnegg of the Municipal Theatre of Santiago, a beautiful, fully operational theater in the center of the city. Buy tickets for a performance to see its grand 19th-century interiors, or do as I did and request Abercrombie & Kent arrange a tour for a behind-the-scenes glimpse.

Museum of Memory and Human Rights: While not a location in Wild Horse Nine, this museum is an essential stop to confront Chile’s recent history and understand the lasting trauma of the Pinochet dictatorship. “It's an open wound for us because we didn't have justice,” says di Girolamo. “There are still mothers looking for their sons.” Set within a brutalist building near Quinta Normal Park, the museum displays testimonials from survivors, preserved artifacts, memorials to the missing, and government documents from the time—including several declassified CIA documents revealing its role in the 1973 coup.

Iorana Hotel: One of the main locations in Wild Horse Nine, this family-owned property overlooking the ocean is fully in operation and taking bookings. With furniture clad in tiki prints, retro wood paneling, and palm trees swaying outside the windows, it’s also a fun place just to snap a couple of photos. Ask to see the set that still remains—just watch out for the grumpy resident dog, who is best admired from afar.

Anakena Beach is a scenic tourist site on Rapa Nui, and actor Mariana di Girolamo's favorite filming location.

Anakena Beach: “My favorite location in the movie is Anakena Beach,” says di Girolamo of the scene where she and Chris strike up a brief, unlikely friendship at the Rapa Nui tourist spot, where a bar serving piña coladas sits side by side with the Ahu Nau Nau moai. “That beach is so beautiful, but I was also able to go to a very special place nearby that you can only visit with someone local: the Cave of the Virgins [or Ana o Keke] set inside a cliff.”

Ahu Tongariki and Rano Raraku: These two moai sites are within short driving distance of each other (as are most sites on Rapa Nui) and make frequent appearances in the movie. Book a local authorized guide to visit them, or arrange a guided excursion through Nayara Hangaroa. And don’t rush, either: the statues and the landscape look vastly different throughout the day as the light changes. “We were filming there for weeks on end, just living with the sky and the wind and the water and the sounds and the horses,” says Schnegg. “I’d just think, is this real?”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6268. United’s Premium Boeing 787s With New Cabins: Which Routes Do They Fly?

We recently saw United Airlines introduce its long awaited new Boeing 787-9s, featuring all-new cabins, which are being branded as United Elevate. This represents the evolution of the carrier’s long haul experience, including all-new Polaris business class seats.

Of course one common question is which routes actually feature these new planes. So in this post, I’d like to go over that — which planes have the new cabins, and which routes do they fly? The airline is flying these planes on an increasing number of routes out of two hubs, so there are more opportunities to try this product.

Prior to 2026, United already had over 80 Boeing 787 Dreamliners in its fleet, split between the 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10 variants. However, United is now taking delivery of another 71 Boeing 787-9s, which recently started to be delivered (in addition to 56 Boeing 787-10s, which will be delivered as of 2028).

What’s exciting about these planes is that they feature an all-new passenger experience, and are in an ultra premium configuration. The planes feature just 222 seats, compared to the 257 seats you’ll find on all the previous 787-9s.

If you want to actually fly a United Boeing 787-9 with the new United Elevate interiors, what are your best odds of getting on one of these? The good news is that they’re consistently scheduled on certain routes.

As it currently stands, United has 16 of these 787s in its fleet, with several more expected to be delivered in the coming months. United plans to have 33 of these jets by 2028, so the airline is taking delivery of an average of around one of these per month (though the pace has been even faster in the first several months).

When you go to book a ticket, the best way to tell if a flight is operated by the new plane is whether you see “Polaris Studio available” listed under the United Polaris fare options (assuming those seats are for sale). Otherwise there are no obvious indicators, other than looking at the seat map.

We recently saw the IATA winter season kick off, and with that, we’re seeing the plane based out of both Houston (IAH) and San Francisco (SFO).

You’ll currently find the 787 with Elevate interiors scheduled to fly to the following destinations out of San Francisco:

You’ll then find the 787 with Elevate interiors scheduled to fly to the following destinations out of Houston:

Let me emphasize that schedules are always subject to change (especially when Boeing delivery delays are a potential factor), and the above is just how things currently stand. I’m also not including flights between San Francisco and Houston, which sometimes see the plane so that it can be rotated between hubs, but obviously that route doesn’t feature the true Polaris soft product.

In recent months, we’ve seen United start to take delivery of its brand new Boeing 787-9s, featuring a more premium layout, plus new cabins. These are exciting planes for passengers, as they feature a much improved onboard experience. They’re also great in terms of upgrade and award availability, given the number of premium seats.

If you want to fly United’s new 787s, you’ll currently find them flying out of Houston and San Francisco. Out of Houston, they’re primarily flying to London, Sao Paulo, Sydney, and Tokyo, while out of San Francisco, they’re primarily flying to London and Singapore. It’s great to see the pace at which United is taking delivery of these planes.

I look forward to trying the new interiors, though I’m hoping to wait until these planes have Starlink installed, since I think that really completes the experience.

What do you make of United’s new Boeing 787-9s, and the routes they’re flying?

#6267. The Airlines Offering Premium Economy On Airbus A380 Flights

Brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age. He became involved in the flight simulator and VATSIM communities, which sparked his interest in aviation and eventually led him to earn his private pilot license. Outside of work, he continues to build flight hours, explore new airports, and stay involved in the aviation community.

Six of the 10 airlines still flying the Airbus A380 offer a premium economy cabin on the type. British Airways will shortly have the largest at 84 seats, following the retrofit announced on October 5, 2026, which also gives its aircraft the highest premium ratio of any A380 at roughly 48%. All Nippon Airways (ANA) follows at 73 seats, then Qantas at 60, Emirates at 56, Lufthansa at 52, and Singapore Airlines at 44.

The four without it are Qatar Airways, Etihad, Korean Air and Asiana. Qatar's layout of 8 first, 48 business and 461 economy produces a premium ratio of around 11%, the lowest among A380 operators. Where the cabin exists, the experience varies considerably. Emirates won the Skytrax award for best premium economy seat in 2026 and is adding the cabin to 68 A380 routes. ANA fits 73 premium economy seats against only 56 in business and flies them on a single route between Tokyo Narita International Airport (NRT) and Honolulu (HNL).

British Airways announced a full retrofit of its Airbus A380 fleet on October 5, 2026, and the new layout puts World Traveller Plus at 84 seats. That is the largest premium economy cabin on any A380 operating anywhere. The refurbished configuration runs 12 First, 106 Club Suites, 84 World Traveller Plus and 215 World Traveller for a total of 417 seats, down from 469 in the current layout. Economy absorbs the entire reduction, falling by 88 seats, while premium economy grows by more than half.

The proportions are what make the aircraft unusual. Head for Points calculated that the new layout gives British Airways 202 premium seats, roughly 48% of the aircraft, which is the highest premium ratio of any A380 operator by a wide margin. Emirates and Qantas are the next closest at around 30%, and both carry at least 56 fewer premium seats than the refurbished BA aircraft will. Since the A380 is the largest passenger aircraft ever built, that also gives British Airways the highest absolute number of premium seats on any single aircraft in service.

The timing matters for anyone trying to book. The first refurbished aircraft is expected in service within months, with the program running into 2027 and 2028, which means the 84-seat cabin will exist alongside the older 55-seat World Traveller Plus layout across the fleet for an extended period. British Airways operates 12 A380s to a small number of destinations from London Heathrow Airport (LHR), so the chance of drawing a refurbished aircraft on any given booking depends on how far along the program the fleet has progressed.

Emirates won the Skytrax award for the best premium economy seat in 2026, finishing ahead of Cathay Pacific and EVA Air, and The Points Guy named it Best International Premium Economy for a second consecutive year. AirlineRatings.com's passenger-voted Flyers' Choice Awards also named Emirates the preferred premium economy. The airline ranks second overall for premium economy with Skytrax and first for both the seats and the catering.

The A380 cabin seats 56 passengers within a four-class layout of 14 first, 76 business, 56 premium economy and 341 economy, giving the aircraft 146 premium seats and a premium ratio of around 30%. The seats are leather with adjustable headrests, calf rests, and footrests, and Emirates serves multicourse meals on china tableware with stainless steel cutlery, which is closer to a business class service pattern than most premium economy products attempt.

Scale is the other factor. Emirates operates roughly half the world's A380 fleet, with 116 aircraft, about 100 of which are active, and premium economy is arriving through the carrier's retrofit program rather than on new deliveries. The cabin joined Dubai to Milan on A380 services from November 10, 2025, alongside New York routes, and Emirates confirmed plans to offer premium economy on 68 routes by March 2026. Given the size of the fleet receiving it, a passenger searching for premium economy on a superjumbo will find more Emirates departures than from any other operator.

The cost of the world's longest A380 premium economy fares typically range within the $2,000-2,500, although this varies by discounts and season.

Qantas carries 60 premium economy seats on its A380s within a four-class layout of 14 first, 70 business, 60 premium economy and 341 economy, totaling 485 seats. That gives the aircraft 144 premium seats and a premium ratio of around 30%, effectively matching Emirates. The seats offer more width and legroom than economy, with adjustable headrests, footrests, storage and charging ports, and the fare includes priority check-in, priority boarding, upgraded meals, noise-canceling headphones and an amenity kit. Qantas operates 10 A380s, with around eight active, on routes from Sydney and Melbourne to London, Los Angeles, Dallas and Singapore.

Lufthansa fits 52 premium economy seats into a 509-seat A380 alongside 8 first, 78 business and 371 economy. The carrier operates eight aircraft and has committed to the type while retiring other quadjets, with summer 2026 routes including Los Angeles, Boston, Denver, Washington and Delhi, plus a new Munich to Mumbai service from July 2026. Lufthansa's premium economy ranks seventh overall in Skytrax's 2026 assessment and fifth for the seat specifically, though its highest-rated version is the Allegris cabin on the A350 and 787-9 rather than the A380.

Singapore Airlines has the smallest premium economy cabin on the type at 44 seats, in a 471-seat aircraft carrying 6 suites, 78 business and 343 economy. That is a premium ratio of around 27%, the lowest of the three. The product itself rates highly, placing third overall with Skytrax for premium economy and fourth for the seat, with calf and footrests, personal storage, charging ports and large entertainment screens. Premium economy passengers also get the Book the Cook service, allowing a main course to be reserved before departure, alongside priority check-in, boarding and baggage handling. The carrier operates 12 A380s across eight major routes from Changi for summer 2026.

All Nippon Airways carries 73 premium economy seats on its A380s, which ANA's own fleet material confirms in a 520-seat layout of 8 first, 56 business, 73 premium economy and 383 economy. That makes it the second-largest premium economy cabin on any A380, and Simple Flying reported it as the largest premium economy cabin across ANA's entire fleet. The seats sit at the rear of the upper deck behind first and business, arranged 2-3-2.

The aircraft itself is unlike any other A380 operation. ANA has three, each painted in a different sea turtle livery, and every scheduled A380 flight operates between Narita and Daniel K. Inouye International Airport (HNL) in Honolulu. No other operator confines the type to a single route. The aircraft entered service in May 2019 and continues to fly Narita to Honolulu year-round, with ANA adjusting frequencies seasonally. The third airframe only entered commercial service in late 2023 after an extended period in storage during the pandemic.

The configuration reflects who the aircraft carries. ANA built it around the Hawaii leisure market, and the cabin mix shows it, with 73 premium economy seats against 56 in business. The economy deck includes ANA COUCHii, where groups of three or four seats convert into a sofa-style space with raisable leg rests for an additional fee, which Airport Spotting described as aimed at families traveling with young children. For a passenger wanting premium economy on an A380, ANA offers one of the largest cabins available and the only route where you can find it.

A pro-Russian Serbian politician has allegedly caused a jet to return to Belgrade after dodging security

Four airlines fly the A380 with no premium economy cabin. Qatar Airways configures its aircraft with 8 first, 48 business and 461 economy seats across 517 total, giving it 56 premium seats and a premium ratio of around 11%, the lowest of any A380 operator by a substantial margin. Simple Flying excluded Qatar entirely from an earlier comparison of premium economy fares on the world's longest A380 routes, noting the airline does not offer the cabin on the type.

Etihad, Korean Air and Asiana complete the group. Etihad operates nine A380s and Asiana six, with Asiana running a three-class layout that includes 104 upper deck economy seats arranged 2-4-2. Those Asiana aircraft are also on borrowed time. Simple Flying reported that following the Korean Air merger, both carriers were expected to retire the type as part of fleet optimization.

The division is not a straightforward premium versus budget split. Qatar Airways has one of the most highly regarded business class products in the industry in Qsuite, yet its A380 carries the smallest proportion of premium seating of any operator of the type. A passenger wanting more than economy on a Qatar A380 has to buy business outright, with no intermediate option. Across the roughly 10 airlines still operating the A380, six offer premium economy and four do not, meaning the cabin is available on most superjumbo flights but not all of them.

#6266. Air India CEO Wants ‘More Widebody Aircraft’

Air India is looking to buy more widebody jets as it expands overseas and works to return to profitability.

“We want more widebody aircraft,” CEO Tewolde Gebremariam said Tuesday at the Aviation India and South Asia summit in New Delhi, according to Reuters. The carrier has held talks with both Airbus and Boeing. Gebremariam did not say how many aircraft Air India might buy.

The airline’s most recent Boeing order, announced in January, was for 30 narrowbodies: 20 737 MAX 8s and 10 MAX 10s.

The carrier is also updating the widebodies it already flies. In April, Air India took delivery of the first of 26 older Boeing 787-8s slated for cabin retrofits. The aircraft went from two cabins to three with the addition of premium economy.

Gebremariam, who previously led Ethiopian Airlines, described high operating costs as a “major concern” but said he expects Air India to return to profitability “very soon.”

Air India Group lost S$3.56 billion in the fiscal year ended March 31, according to financial disclosures from Singapore Airlines, which owns a 25% stake in the group. The loss came as the carrier dealt with disruption from the war in Iran and Pakistan’s closure of its airspace to Indian airlines.
