#6230. The GOP’s midterm plan: Make America hate Muslims again

With less than a week to go before the midterms, the Republicans’ desperation is becoming obvious. Donald Trump is stumping in Mississippi, where Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is locked in a tight race, and half the Cabinet is running around giving speeches to people who don’t know who they are. But the biggest sign of the GOP’s anxiety is the resurrection of a tried-and-true tactic: racism.

Only months ago, the party went all-in on red-baiting, accusing mainstream Democrats of being communist sympathizers, a reaction to the 2025 victory of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the primary wins of a few democratic socialist candidates. This came alongside the now perennial attacks on transgender Americans, led by the president who continues to insist that elementary schools are performing gender-affirming surgeries in the nurse’s office without parental consent.

We knew they would rely on xenophobia, which has  been the central organizing principle of Trump’s decade of political dominance. He may not have kept most of his promises, such as “no new wars” and “bringing prices down on day one,” but he has delivered magnificently on his pledge to incarcerate and deport as many immigrants, undocumented and otherwise, as humanly possible. In fact, he’s even exceeded expectations.

Since they make up the largest share of immigrants, Latinos have been hit the hardest by this cruel policy, and Trump has long asserted that they are all violent criminals. But as we were warned in the 2024 presidential campaign, Haitians have also been among the top immigrant groups targeted by MAGA leaders, with Vice President JD Vance homing in on the racist right-wing id by declaring that these Black immigrants were eating the household pets of their Real American white neighbors.

For a moment, there seemed to be a new target when a social media post by Bo French, the GOP’s nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner, went viral, exposing a growing conservative antipathy to Indian Americans. This was somewhat surprising since Vance, one of the party’s leading race-baiters, is married to the daughter of Indian immigrants, and Vivek Ramaswamy, another child of Indian immigrants, is Ohio’s Republican nominee for governor.

But none of these attacks and lies has gotten the traction they were hoping for, so the party has gone back to the deep well to draw up a big bucket of Islamophobia.

In the wake of 9/11, some in the GOP became infected by a strain of anti-Arab bigotry that, to his credit, George W. Bush attempted to fight. It waxed and waned as the attacks grew more distant. Then came Trump, whose demonization of Muslims goes back to the 2016 campaign. At that time, the U.S. was in the midst of an outbreak of “lone-wolf” terrorist attacks, and his violent rhetoric really got the crowds going.

Trump famously said he wanted to take up waterboarding “and worse,” and told lurid stories about dipping bullets in pigs blood to scare terrorists. Declaring that he would ban all Muslims from coming to America “until we can figure out what the hell is going on,” he executed his infamous “Muslim ban” days after taking office in 2017, an order that became the focus of legal challenges and, after some re-tooling by the administration, was ultimately upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018.

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has long been a particular focus of Trump’s ire. As a progressive, she has been a fierce critic of the administration, but no more than most other Democrats. But she’s a Black woman, an immigrant and a Muslim who wears a hijab. Omar, who fled Somalia with her family at eight and lived for years in a Kenyan refugee camp, represents Minnesota, which became one of Trump’s bete noirs after Kamala Harris chose the state’s governor, Tim Walz, as her running mate. Trump began attacking Minnesota’s community of Somali Americans with some of the most bigoted comments in American history, and that’s saying something.

Somalia, he said, is “garbage, a “sh*thouse country” that “stinks.” He has even claimed that 98% of Somali immigrants don’t work and that they are all criminals driving around in Mercedes-Benz and BMWs. Reprising his role as inciter-in-chief, the president called for (white) Minnesotans to “fight back” against the state’s Somali population, writing that they “view you as weak and stupid people.”

Another target of MAGA’s anti-Muslim bigotry is Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan-born Democratic nominee for the Senate. Earlier this week, Vance referred to him as “very, very evil,” a “psychopath” who pushes “anti-white racial hatred.” This charge of reverse racism is one of the favorite tropes of the modern right, guaranteed to draw cheers at a MAGA rally. Trump called El-Sayed a violent jihadist, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. expanded the attacks, saying that the one billion Muslims worldwide contribute nothing to society, having never won the Nobel Prize or any other prestigious awards, an easily disprovable lie.

The blatant bigotry of these latest attacks is enough to take your breath away, not because they are unprecedented; this is America, after all, and racism is one of our “exceptional” characteristics. But until the last decade, Republicans had learned that it was far better for them to obscure their racism with dog whistles and code words so as not to scare the suburban white people.

The blatant bigotry of these latest attacks is enough to take your breath away, not because they are unprecedented; this is America, after all, and racism is one of our “exceptional” characteristics. But until the last decade, Republicans had learned that it was far better for them to obscure their racism with dog whistles and code words so as not to scare the suburban white people. The famous quote from the notorious GOP strategist Lee Atwater, who recommended referring to “welfare” and “busing” to stand in for overtly racist language, held true for years.

Republicans stuck with that tactic for decades, starting with Richard Nixon, who used the term Trump thinks he invented, “law and order,” as a code word for cracking down on Black protests in inner cities. Ronald Reagan famously talked about “welfare queens” during his 1976 primary bid for president, and four years later he opened his presidential campaign by declaring his belief in states’ rights — another dog whistle — in Mississippi, near the spot where white civil rights workers were killed. Three decades later, Trump turned even more creative with his “birther” campaign against President Barack Obama, combining the party’s burgeoning Islamophobia with classic All-American racism. To this day, Trump refers to Obama using his full name — Barack Hussein Obama — with a childish glee.

I don’t think claiming that a whole African country is a “sh*thouse” or saying that Black immigrants are barbecuing their neighbors’ cats for dinner is the kind of subtlety Atwater was talking about. In fact, I will not be surprised to see Trump, who has lost virtually all rhetorical restraint, drop the ugliest epithets of all someday soon. It’s just a matter of time. And if he does, I’m sure JD Vance and all the rest of MAGA’s staunchest loyalists will find a way to rationalize it as something the other side is responsible for.

Tripadvisor is cutting jobs in its legacy hotel metasearch business under a global restructuring, and both CEO Matt Goldberg and CFO Michael Noonan are leaving. Goldberg said the decision to combine the Viator and Tripadvisor experiences teams "hasn't proved out as we expected," a judgment backed by the numbers: third-quarter experiences revenue fell 3% and adjusted EBITDA in the segment fell 27%. Total revenue dropped 11% to $436.4 million, and the company posted a net loss of $316.9 million against net income of $48.5 million a year earlier. Goldberg said Viator and B2B2C experiences bookings grew in the low teens while the Tripadvisor channel declined by high single digits, citing SEO headwinds, weakness in the North America to Europe corridor, and execution problems. The restructuring shifts product engineering and data analytics roles into experiences and is expected to deliver $40 million in gross annualized savings. Tripadvisor said it will keep investigating strategic alternatives and will use the $685 million from the sale of TheFork to American Express to pay down debt. Goldberg leaves February 16, 2027; Noonan departs December 31, with Chief Strategy and Operations Officer Kristen Dalton stepping in as interim CFO.

But New York calculates sales tax on the full taxable purchase price. And the surcharge is just a hidden part of the price. I’ve written about airports allowing surcharges as an end-run around their own pricing rules. The Port Authority of New York New Jersey is clear on this. Its regulation generally caps prices at 15% above comparable street prices, but expressly allows an additional employee wage and benefit fee of up to 3%. The regulation also excludes the employee fee from gross receipts under agreements where the Port Authority collects a share of concession revenue. I covered the same 3% employee benefit and retention charge at a Newark self-checkout last year. The Port Authority tells merchants to add the fee, and incentivize them to do it – moving part of the price into fees means they get to keep more of the money. Philadelphia authorized a similar 3% add-on while retaining its street price cap. There it was expressly a way to let merchants charge passengers more and circumvent the cap. Minneapolis prefers a 4.5% hospitality charge with signage explaining it wasn’t a tip and didn’t go to the people providing the hospitality. The employee fee on this book isn’t a tip, but airport machines have been demanding those, too. In Austin, I couldn’t pay for a bottle of water without entering a tip. The terminal rejected $0.00. Staff confirmed it, and the transaction only went through when I entered a penny. Earlier this year I also flagged an Austin airport self-checkout that defaulted to an 18% tip while adding a card processing surcharge. One commenter asked about the JFK airport charge, “Since I would be paying the employee retention fee, do i get a say which employees stay or go?” I’d retain the scanner, but put whomever programmed the surcharge on a performance improvement plan. #6226. “Chaos” in the air: Five ways voting could be disrupted on Election Day

This article originally appeared on ProPublica.

As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday, voting experts are watching to see how the Trump administration’s unprecedented efforts to assert more federal control over elections will play out.

Since President Donald Trump retook the White House, his administration has tried to force states to turn over their unredacted voter rolls and to restrict mail-in voting. The Department of Homeland Security has used its resources to identify and prosecute noncitizen voters, an effort that has unfolded alongside the agency’s massive crackdown on immigrants.

The president has justified these steps by claiming, without evidence, that American elections are beset by fraud and that illegal voting is tipping the scales in favor of Democrats.

Courts have thwarted most of the administration’s plans to date, but Trump and his top deputies have kept up the pressure. Most recently, they’ve threatened to prosecute election officials who don’t reject ballots from people that the federal government has identified as likely noncitizens.

The administration hasn’t explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to the polls or seizing ballots or voting machines.

Election experts say the cumulative effect has been to ramp up anxiety about the midterms and to erode voters’ trust in the system.

“The administration has been creating a lot of noise, a lot of confusion, a lot of doubt,” said Ben Hovland, whom Trump fired as a commissioner for the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission earlier this year. He said he worries that this will make voters “sit it out” and “throw their hands up.”

In an emailed response to questions, a DHS spokesperson said Immigration and Customs Enforcement “is not planning operations targeting polling locations,” adding that the agency would only arrest people at the polls to address a safety threat as part of “intelligence-driven targeted enforcement.”

The DHS and the Justice Department “are laser focused on identifying, prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens,” the spokesperson added. “Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences — including criminal charges and deportation.”

Before and on Election Day, it’s typical for the major political parties to mount poll-watching operations, but both Democrats and Republicans say they’ve expanded these activities in this pressurized midterm.

Republicans will focus on issues such as voter eligibility and voter-roll accuracy, according to Ally Triolo, the Republican National Committee’s election integrity communications director. Democrats will concentrate on voter intimidation and other hurdles to voting, Angelo Fernández Hernández, a Democratic National Committee spokesperson, said.

Here are five issues that voting rights experts say they’re watching as this year’s election unfolds:

An incident in Leon County, in the Florida Panhandle, illustrates the widespread anxiety about law enforcement at the polls.

Mark Earley, the county’s supervisor of elections, told ProPublica he was “furious” when two marked U.S. Customs and Border Protection vehicles parked outside the county’s busiest early voting location last month, after he’d been repeatedly reassured by the administration that agents would not do this.

He reported the sighting to the FBI, then learned that the agents, who were headed out of state, had just stopped by to try to vote themselves. The episode generated a flurry of news coverage.

“Given the negative media coverage regarding federal agents at the polls, it shows pretty bad judgment that they showed up in their official vehicles,” Earley said.

It’s against the law for federal law enforcement to be near polling places.

Nick Brown, Washington’s attorney general, leads a group of Democratic state officials and voting rights advocates who have been planning how to respond if, indeed, there is real federal interference. The group has “war-gamed” how to react if government agents attempt to commandeer voting equipment or ballots.

“We’ve seen the tension and chaos that’s in the air,” Brown said. He called the federal government “the biggest challenge to smooth elections right now, which is not the way it’s supposed to be.”

A DOJ spokesperson said “the best preparation for any election official is following federal law.”

It’s routine for DOJ monitors to watch over polling places, and the agency has assured states that, in the midterms, its observers will follow the law and not interfere with voting or election administration. Still, state officials remain concerned. During Wyoming’s primary election, poll workers said they felt uneasy when DOJ monitors asked about their training and to inspect voting systems. The state’s governor criticized these actions as “a bit aggressive” and “irregular.”

The Trump administration’s multipronged effort targeting alleged noncitizen voters has already led to eligible voters being improperly removed from the rolls. Voting rights groups fear this will block some U.S. citizens from being able to vote when they show up on Tuesday.

Federal officials have made clear they plan to go after anyone they think is committing voter fraud.

On the first day of early voting in Texas, Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, posted a YouTube video announcing his intentions. “If you violate federal election law,” he warned, “I will hunt you down and prosecute you.”

This threat came days after the DOJ sued California, seeking to block the state from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 voters it claims are “likely” noncitizens. The administration had obtained the state’s public voter rolls, which the DHS had blended with its own immigration information and third-party data.

In a court filing, California called the claim that there are 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls “specious.” Los Angeles County analyzed a sampling of the likely noncitizen voters that the federal government claimed were registered there. Many weren’t registered in the county or had never voted, the analysis showed. Some said on their voter registration forms that they were born in the United States.

Asked about the case, the DOJ told ProPublica, “Federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections, and the Department has a duty to enforce it.”

A federal judge has rejected the DOJ’s motion for an emergency order that would have barred California from counting the 20,000 voters’ ballots. (A federal appeals panel later backed that decision.) On Thursday, the administration sent grand jury subpoenas to California officials demanding records about their response to allegations of noncitizens on the state’s rolls. Late Friday, a federal judge issued a restraining order blocking the DOJ’s demands, calling them an “intimidation plan” that would interfere with legal voting.

Last week, the DOJ wrote a letter threatening to sue Washington state if officials there refused to review a list of 400 voters it believes to be noncitizens within 24 hours. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters late last month that the department was considering additional actions, saying there were “a number of states that we’re looking at.”

In a letter responding to the DOJ, Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs called the government list of 400 names “not reliable,” saying it included U.S. citizens, people who aren’t registered to vote and duplicate entries. “Time and time again,” Hobbs wrote, “DHS claims about noncitizen voter registration turn out to be greatly exaggerated or false.”

Sam Trepel is Rule of Law program director at States United Democracy Center and a former attorney for the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division. She said the agency’s actions involving California and Washington were a “disturbing use of prosecutorial authority.”

Trepel worries that the DOJ may try to seize ballots cast by voters identified as likely noncitizens, before or after the election, which would “put their votes at risk and undermine trust more broadly.”

Voting rights advocates also worry that the government’s efforts to target noncitizen voters could frighten eligible voters to the point that they won’t show up.

A federal judge recently put limits on a multistate effort by the DHS to go door-to-door in search of suspected noncitizen voters, at least through Election Day, saying it was illegally intimidating legal voters.

“A voter could say, ‘Well, maybe I don’t want to put myself on the target list here, maybe I won’t register, or maybe I won’t vote,’” said David Janovsky, acting director of The Constitution Project at the watchdog group Project on Government Oversight.

States often change laws and rules related to voting.

Since 2024, Republican-led states have taken a number of steps that experts say will make it more difficult for some of their residents to cast ballots and have them count.

A North Carolina law, for example, requires voters to provide proof of identification when sending mail-in ballots. Under new rules, ballots now come with two envelopes, both of which must be sealed. Ballot rejections have skyrocketed, Democracy Docket reported, because voters aren’t sealing the inner envelope.

Texas and other states have cut back on the number and location of polling places, especially in areas favoring Democrats. In hotly contested Tarrant County, which includes Fort Worth, the number of polling sites was slashed by almost a third. This could increase the risk of long lines and voter confusion on Election Day.

Voting rights groups such as the Texas Civil Rights Project are tracking two issues involving the state’s voter registration systems. A software error at the Texas Department of Public Safety stopped several hundred thousand new voter registrations from being forwarded to local election officials, preventing them from being added to the rolls. A separate state system for updating registration information wasn’t processing changes for several weeks, leading to more backlogs. Counties say they’ve been able to address these problems.

Every election features some issues with voting equipment.

So far, there have been isolated complaints involving touch-screen voting machines — including one from Dolly Parton’s sister in Tennessee — spawning fears that machines have been “rigged” to switch votes.

ES&S, the company that makes the machines garnering the complaints, told ProPublica that the company hadn’t received widespread reports. Election experts say occasional problems with touch-screen machines don’t signify tampering or manipulation. Any attempt to tamper with programming would surface during testing by election officials and be corrected, they said.

Incidents in the run-up to the midterms have ratcheted up election officials’ concerns about the potential for both cyber and physical attacks.

Last month, officials in several states, including Arizona, received envelopes with an unknown white powder. Arizona eventually deemed the material nontoxic, but Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said “the fear it caused was real.”

In 2024, false bomb threats, thought to be from foreign actors, caused widespread evacuations of vote-counting sites across the country. The disruptions were brief, however, in part because a message board funded by the federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, alerted election officials that the FBI had deemed the threats not credible.

Trump, however, has dismantled CISA since retaking the presidency, leaving states and local election officials to grapple with both physical and cyber threats on their own. Election nonprofits have stepped up to try to fill the gap, and states, with CISA’s help, have enhanced their own cyber defenses.

Derek Tisler, counsel and manager for the elections and government program at the Brennan Center for Justice, said the federal government’s absence has weakened the defenses.

“States acting on their own just do not have the same power,” he said.

Election lawyers fear that actions by the Trump administration in the run-up to the midterms suggest the government will aggressively pursue postelection challenges if the results are not to the president’s liking.

Late last month, the DOJ sued Alaska, seeking to block the state from certifying the result of its Senate race if the Republican incumbent doesn’t win. A federal judge threw out that lawsuit on Sunday, but the administration is expected to appeal.

Trump has said he personally ordered the lawsuit to be filed. It claims the system is unfairly rigged against Sen. Dan Sullivan, because another Alaska man named Dan Sullivan also qualified for the general election ballot. The New York Times reported last week that campaign aides to Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola orchestrated the candidacy of the second Dan Sullivan after a monthslong, statewide search to recruit someone with the same name.

Nonetheless, the DOJ’s case is unusual, both because federal law prohibits the government from interfering with an active election and because challenges typically come after voting is complete. Postelection challenges are most often brought by losing candidates in state courts.

“This is using the federal government to interfere with our election process in a way that I think is pretty troubling on multiple levels,” said Brown, the Washington attorney general.

In response to ProPublica’s questions, the DOJ pointed to Blanche’s statement about the lawsuit on social media, which said the agency “does not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaska’s election.” (The lawsuit calls it “vital” that the state not certify “any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion” and asks the judge to prevent Alaska from doing this.)

Some election lawyers have suggested that if the GOP suffers significant losses, Trump could try to pressure Republicans in Congress to block new members from being seated. Several lawyers, including Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, say that the incoming Democratic majority would be able to fend off such an effort; courts, too, are likely to stymie it, though it might cause a short delay, according to Muller.

Brown said he and other attorneys general are also planning how to respond if local election officials or boards refuse to certify election results, based on their own claims of fraud or claims by the administration.

“I worry tremendously about what they might do,” Brown said.

#6225. Bomb Hoaxes Test Europe’s Airlines as Geopolitical Pressures Mount

Photo Credit: Flight disruption has impacted many airlines.  Wizz AIr

None of this week’s threats has proved real, but each one still cost a diversion, a search and a rebuilt schedule. Whoever sent them, the hoaxes have added to a list of disruptions, from conflict-driven fuel costs to closed airspace, that is making routine flying in Europe ever more challenging.

Bomb threats disrupted at least 27 flights across Europe on Thursday, the second wave this week. No explosives have been found.

French fighter jets intercepted Aer Lingus flight EI402 from Dublin to Rome, carrying more than 150 passengers, and escorted it to the Évreux air base in Normandy. The French prime minister’s office said the pilot had not cooperated as expected, without giving more detail. Bulgaria’s air force escorted three airliners to the ground. In Madrid, Air Europa and Iberia aircraft were halted, emptied and searched after Spanish authorities received three emailed threats in less than 20 minutes, the Associated Press reported. At least 27 flights across Europe were disrupted Thursday by bomb threats, the second wave in a week, and no explosives were found in any case. French fighter jets intercepted an Aer Lingus Dublin–Rome flight carrying more than 150 passengers and escorted it to an air base in Normandy, Bulgaria's air force escorted three airliners to the ground, and Madrid authorities searched Air Europa and Iberia aircraft after receiving three emailed threats in under 20 minutes. Earlier threats on Monday and Tuesday hit flights operated by Wizz Air, Ryanair, LOT, and Scandinavian Airlines, plus a cruise ship in Greece. No government has said who is responsible, and Bloomberg reported no pattern in the carriers or routes targeted. Matthew Borie of Osprey Flight Solutions told the AP the threats could be copycats, a single person or group, or "hybrid warfare" by state actors, and pointed to a possible Russian link; Moscow has denied European accusations of sabotage this year. The operational math is the problem: each threat an airline acts on means a diversion or stopped departure, a full search, often a replacement aircraft, crews timing out, and passengers rebooked — and Skift has reported that insurance typically doesn't cover those commercial losses. The hoaxes arrive while European carriers are already absorbing jet fuel prices that have more than doubled year over year, Middle East airspace closures that lengthen Asia routes, and drone incursions at airports.

#6222. Black voters could sway the midterms in surprising places

Loss aversion is a phenomenon in psychology and behavioral economics. Defined simply, it means that the pain experienced from a loss is felt twice as much as winning. In politics, that intensity manifests itself in motivation. If you take something away from people, they are going to feel it more acutely than promising them something, and the theft produces a backlash.

That’s what appears to be happening right now with Black voters. Across the country, they have been lining up to vote early, presumably against Donald Trump and the Republican Party’s MAGA agenda, in astonishing numbers, particularly in the South. That this comes only six months after the Supreme Court gutted the Voting Rights Act in Louisiana v. Callais should not come as a surprise.

In the Trump era, Republicans have become experienced at taking rights away from the American people. For women, it was the roll back of their constitutional rights when the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, sparking a backlash in that year’s midterm elections. Since Trump returned to office in January 2025, immigrants have come under assault from a xenophobic administration intent on carrying out mass deportations via masked, secret police rampaging through neighborhoods. The LGBTQ+ community, and trans people in particular, have seen their rights stripped away.

To many Black Americans, the GOP’s agenda and behavior will not have come as a surprise. After all, it’s been at the core of their history going back to before the country’s founding.

These policies have come as a shock to some Americans who never thought Trump would go there, and they have also opened the eyes of others to the cruelty at the heart of MAGA, overseen by the highest court of the land. But to many Black Americans, the GOP’s agenda and behavior will not have come as a surprise. After all, it’s been at the core of their history going back to before the country’s founding.

Black Americans know what it means to have their civil rights taken away from them. They understand fully the fear of being targeted by brutal, marauding gangs of armed men. In the decade following the Civil War and the passage of the 14th and 15th Amendments, Black people began to participate fully in civil society. Mississippi elected two Black U.S. senators and a lieutenant governor, and former slaves and their offspring enjoyed freedom of speech, movement and opportunity. But the white members of Southern society would not let that stand, and as soon as the federal government withdrew its troops, they stepped in with legal and social barriers to deny Black Americans their rights, this time backed by vigilante and state violence that became Jim and Jane Crow.

Almost a century had passed by the time Lyndon Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act in 1964 and the Voting Rights Act in 1965, a period characterized by subjugation and violence by the white majority. But Black America kept fighting, against all odds, until they won.

This year, we have seen yet another attempt by reactionary politicians and judges to turn back the clock. After the Callais decision, several Southern states reverted immediately to form and radically redrew their congressional districts to favor the white majority, making it much more difficult for voters to elect a Black federal and state representatives.

They may come to regret that decision. This isn’t 1955 (or 1855) anymore, as much as Donald Trump would like to make it so, and the Black community is once again mobilizing. According to experts, early voting data is showing something unexpected: The vote is being driven by young voters rather than just those who went through the earlier battles. It’s muscle memory for the Black community.

After 2024, when Trump won a surprising 15% of the Black vote — nearly doubling his share of 8% in the 2020 election — Republicans thought they were defying history to make great inroads within the community. Then, incredibly, the administration began attacking Black America. The result is what some politicos are calling a “Blacklash,” and it could very well be decisive in some places where nobody expected the Democrats to do well. And even if it doesn’t result in flipping seats, it’s a shot across the bow.

In Mississippi, prosecutor and former judge Scott Colom, who is Black, is running an excellent race against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, the GOP incumbent. Colom has made some very clever advertisements which have garnered a lot of national attention, but Republicans and Democrats alike had largely ignored the race until just a couple of months ago. Polling has tightened, and the GOP has dispatched an influx of luminaries, including Trump himself. For the first time in years, Democrats from Bill Clinton to Kamala Harris, along with a long line of senators, have descended on the state to support Colom. Former President Barack Obama even cut an ad for him. Mississippi has the largest population of Black voters of any state in the country. If Colum gets a big Black turnout with just enough disaffected whites, he could win.

Louisiana, after giving birth to the case that saw the Supreme Court’s conservative majority gut the Voting Rights Act, has been winnowed down to one majority Black district in a state that is one-third African-American. But there has been a surge in Black participation akin to what is seen in presidential years, which could prove decisive in a race for Louisiana’s open Senate seat that has been a sleeper until the last couple of weeks. According to a recent poll, Republican Julia Letlow and Democrat Jamie Davis are tied. Among voters who have already cast their ballot, Davis — who is Black — holds a six-point advantage, and 34% of early votes have been cast by Black Louisianans.

Then there’s South Carolina, which has seen Trump make three desperate appearances to shore up Darline Graham’s torpid campaign. The endangered incumbent, foisted upon South Carolina Republicans by the president himself following the sudden death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, is not getting the job done. As numbers cruncher Nate Silver pointed out, a recent New York Times poll showing the race essentially tied is not an outlier; she is in deep trouble. As of late October, the Times reports, “Black voters accounted for around 28 percent of early votes, while making up around 20 percent of the overall electorate in recent cycles. The trend is not unlike what we’re seeing in Georgia and North Carolina thus far.” If that holds true through Election Day, we could see the biggest upset of the whole campaign, largely due to Black South Carolinians saying “Enough is enough.”

In a few short hours, all the ads, mailers, signs and rallies will mercifully come to an end. I am cautiously optimistic, but like many, I’ll never celebrate prematurely again. There is good reason, though, to feel more positive than we have in a long time. Trump and his acolytes have overreached. Opting for the big tech credo of “move fast and break things,” they vastly overestimated their abilities — and the American people’s tolerance.

They have also aroused a group of Americans who know what it is to lose their rights and privileges. With all that history and so many battles, Black Americans have shown what it takes to never give up.

Delta Air Lines and American Express offer seven cobranded cards for everyone from occasional Delta flyers to frequent travelers.

Depending on the card and the offer you qualify for, you could earn up to 125,000 bonus SkyMiles.

Here’s how the current offers compare and what to consider before applying.

*Bonus value is based on TPG’s November 2026 valuations and is not provided or reviewed by the issuer.

American Express has a few eligibility rules to keep in mind before applying for one of these cards. For starters, Amex typically only allows a person to earn one welcome bonus per card in their lifetime. That means you'll want to prioritize applying when a card offers an elevated, limited-time offer, such as the ones all but one of these cards have right now.

You also may not be eligible for a welcome bonus on a personal Delta Amex card if you have or previously had a higher-tier Delta Amex card. For example, if you have or previously had the Delta Reserve Amex, you may not be eligible for the welcome offers on the Delta Blue, Delta Gold or Delta Platinum.

Delta's business Amex cards are not subject to this same "family rule."

Amex may consider other factors when determining your eligibility, including your income, credit score and history with the issuer. Fortunately, you'll generally find out whether you're eligible for a welcome offer before accepting the card.

Delta offers four personal cards. The card that is right for you depends on how frequently you fly with Delta and how much you’re willing to pay for an annual fee.

Let’s take a look at what differentiates each of the Delta SkyMiles personal cards.

Best for: Delta loyalists or those who want Sky Club access (subject to limitations)

The Delta SkyMiles Reserve is ideal for hardcore Delta fans and frequent flyers.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 125,000 bonus miles after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers may vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

This bonus is worth up to $1,500 per our valuations.

If you qualify for the full 125,000 miles, this is an excellent time to apply. It matches the highest mileage bonus we’ve seen on the card and requires $1,000 less spending than the previous 125,000-mile offer with the lowest spending requirement.

Key benefits: Delta’s premium consumer credit card offers a range of valuable perks. For loyal Delta flyers who enjoy visiting the Sky Club, this card can pay for itself through lounge access, spending boosts and other benefits.

With this card, you’ll earn 3 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline. Plus, you'll enjoy a slew of Delta-related perks, including:

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Reserve.

Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Reserve American Express Card

If you fly frequently with Delta but can’t justify the pricier Delta SkyMiles Reserve, the Delta SkyMiles Platinum is worth considering.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 90,000 bonus miles after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers may vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

Per TPG's valuations, this bonus is worth up to $1,080.

If you qualify for the full 90,000 miles, this is a strong offer for $3,000 in spending. We’ve seen offers with more miles or a statement credit, though they required more spending.

Key benefits: This card is a good option if you fly Delta regularly and want to earn miles on purchases and reach elite status. However, even if you aren’t pursuing status, the companion certificate alone can make the annual fee for this card worth it.

With this card, you’ll earn 3 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline.

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Platinum.

Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Platinum American Express Card

Best for: Occasional Delta flyers or those test-driving a Delta card

If you want to take advantage of a welcome bonus but don’t fly Delta frequently, the Delta SkyMiles Gold is a strong option.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 80,000 bonus miles after spending $2,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers may vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

TPG's valuations place this bonus at up to $960.

If you qualify for the full 80,000 miles, now is a good time to apply. However, we have seen up to 90,000 miles — as well as up to 80,000 miles plus a statement credit — offered before.

Annual fee: $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150

Key benefits: This card is ideal for occasional Delta flyers seeking a few extra perks when flying with the airline.

With this card, you’ll earn 2 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline.

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Gold.

Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Gold American Express Card

If you want an entry-level card to start earning SkyMiles and fly less frequently with Delta, then Delta SkyMiles Blue is the card for you.

Current welcome offer: Earn 10,000 bonus miles after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership.

According to TPG’s valuations, these miles are worth $120. The SkyMiles Blue typically doesn't receive an elevated offer, so we recommend applying whenever you're ready.

Key benefits: As a no-annual-fee card, it offers fewer benefits than the others. Still, there are some simple perks for cardmembers.

With this card, you’ll earn 2 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline.

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Blue.

Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Blue American Express Card

If you own a small business or have a side hustle through which you pay business expenses, one of these offers may be a great addition to your work wallet.

Best for: Business owners who fly Delta frequently and want lounge access

As the most expensive business card Delta offers, the Delta SkyMiles Reserve Business comes packed with great perks for Delta loyalists.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 125,000 bonus miles after spending $15,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers may vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

Per TPG's valuations, this bonus is worth up to $1,500.

If you qualify for the full 125,000 miles, this clears our usual threshold. The highest offer we’ve seen was 200,000 miles after $20,000 in spending, compared with $15,000 for this offer.

Key benefits: This card offers a range of useful perks for Delta-loyal small-business owners.

With this card, you’ll earn 3 miles per dollar spent on purchases made directly with Delta.

Its suite of Delta-related benefits includes:

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Reserve Business.

Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Reserve Business American Express Card

Best for: Business owners who fly frequently with Delta

Business owners who are looking for a good mid-tier airline business card should consider the Delta SkyMiles Platinum Business for its earnings potential and benefits.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 100,000 bonus miles after spending $10,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers may vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

According to TPG's valuations, this offer is worth up to $1,200.

The full 100,000-mile bonus matches the highest mileage offer we’ve seen, though previous offers awarded the same bonus after $8,000 in purchases. If you already have $10,000 in eligible business spending planned and want the card now, this is a good offer. If you’re flexible on timing, we’d consider waiting for the same bonus with a lower spending requirement.

Key benefits: This is a solid mid-tier option for business owners who travel with Delta semi-frequently.

With this card, you’ll earn 3 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline.

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Platinum Business.

Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Platinum Business American Express Card

Best for: Business owners who fly occasionally with Delta

The Delta SkyMiles Gold Business is ideal for smaller businesses or business owners who aren’t Delta loyalists.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 85,000 bonus miles after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers may vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

The bonus is worth up to $1,020 when factoring in TPG's valuations.

If you qualify for all 85,000 miles, this is a good time to apply. It’s just 5,000 miles shy of the highest offer we’ve seen, which also required $6,000 in purchases. If the card already fits your business, we’d take the full offer.

Annual fee: $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150

Key benefits: Even if they don't fly Delta often, small-business owners can still benefit from this card's perks.

With this card, you’ll earn 2 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline.

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Gold Business.

Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Gold Business American Express Card

With a full lineup of Delta cards, you may wonder how to pick the best offer for your needs. While it might be tempting to go with the highest offer, you should also consider its long-term value to your wallet.

The good news is that many of these offers can be a great fit, depending on your travel habits. As a round-up:

Related: Why the Delta SkyMiles Reserve card is still one of the best cards I’ve added to my wallet

Delta and American Express offer a wide range of cobranded cards, whether you fly with the airline occasionally or are a frequent Delta loyalist.

Just remember that American Express has a once-per-card, per-lifetime rule for welcome offers. If you've had a particular Delta Amex before, or, in some cases, a higher-tier personal Delta card, you may not be eligible for that card's welcome offer.

Welcome offers vary, so check the bonus you’re offered and make sure you can meet the spending requirement with purchases you already plan to make.

#6220. American Airlines Has Reopened Its Exclusive LAX Dining Room After 6 Years—Here’s How To Get In

Last Wednesday I wrote exclusively American Airlines would reopen its Flagship Dining inside the business class lounge at LAX this week. Now it’s officially open. What was First Class Dining has been closed since March 2020, and when it returns, qualifying American business class passengers will be able to use it with their tickets, and there are other paths to entry too. That’s great news. When it was open previously it was fantastic. Flagship First Dining was a restaurant inside the Flagship Lounge. There were tables, booths, a bar and a window looking out toward the aircraft. The room had 59 seats, but when I visited there were never more than two other passengers at once. The food was excellent, too. I especially liked the miso black cod, and the pork belly came with cauliflower tempura that I still remember. American has since dropped “First” from the name. As the airline removes international first class from its Boeing 777-300ERs and replaces its three cabin Airbus A321Ts, they’ve opened the dining rooms to a much larger group instead of doing away with them. Since September 15, qualifying Flagship Business and Flagship Business Plus passengers have been able to use Flagship Dining in Dallas and Miami. Los Angeles is next. Access covers qualifying American Airlines long haul international, premium transcontinental and Flagship Hawaii itineraries. That includes eligible Flagship flights between Los Angeles and New York JFK, though an ordinary domestic first class ticket doesn’t get you in. The qualifying flight must be marketed and operated by American. Business class access doesn’t include a guest. Getting into the Flagship Lounge based on AAdvantage or oneworld status doesn’t get you into the separate dining room. Eligible partner first class access continues, and there’s also a way in with miles. AAdvantage Platinum Pro members can redeem 25,000 miles and Executive Platinum members can redeem 20,000 miles for a Flagship Dining pass. It includes the member and their immediate family or up to two guests on an eligible same day American or oneworld flight, even when flying coach. It includes the Flagship Lounge, too. I’ve thought this was one of the best uses of miles when traveling as a family. American has introduced a new dining menu and a wine and chocolate pairing featuring KHK Hillside Cabernet Sauvignon and K+M chocolate, co-founded by chef Thomas Keller. The cabernet retails for about $125 a bottle. Here’s American’s photo of the pairing. The new Dallas wine list also includes Bollinger La Grande Année, which retails for around $200 a bottle. American even listed it as an ingredient in a cranberry orange spritz. That seems like an expensive way to make it harder to taste the champagne. I’d ask for it in a separate glass. And the food has improved in the broader Flagship lounges, not just in the separate dining rooms. On a recent visit to the Dallas Flagship Lounge, I found a better buffet, a staffed charcuterie station and an improved chef station. I ordered from the lounge’s menu using a QR code, and the food arrived at my table in four minutes. It was a relatively quiet Tuesday evening, but I was impressed. That menu ordering is available in Los Angeles, too. When I last wrote about the rollout, the QR codes were in the theater seating and across from the secondary beverage station. Delta still offers the more ambitious food. It now has two Delta One lounges at LAX, with table service throughout, while United’s Polaris Lounge has a sit down restaurant. I’d still put the food in American’s main Flagship Lounge behind Delta, even though the gap has narrowed. But American makes the larger Flagship Lounge available to many more passengers, including eligible elites traveling in coach. And now a regular qualifying Flagship Business fare comes with the separate dining room. United’s base Polaris fares don’t include Polaris Lounge access. Delta’s Basic Business fares will lose Delta One lounge access for travel beginning January 19, 2027. At this point Americna’s three Flagship Dining locations really close a gap and even start to offer a competitive advantage for some. The tradeoff is that First Dining was so special because almost nobody was there. Opening it to business class is a big improvement for those passengers, but it also means many more people competing for a table. American uses an electronic waitlist when the dining room is full. If you’re traveling before a busy departure period, I’d check in with the host when you first arrive. What was First Class Dining has been closed since March 2020, and when it returns, qualifying American business class passengers will be able to use it with their tickets, and there are other paths to entry too. That’s great news. When it was open previously it was fantastic.

Flagship First Dining was a restaurant inside the Flagship Lounge. There were tables, booths, a bar and a window looking out toward the aircraft. The room had 59 seats, but when I visited there were never more than two other passengers at once.

The food was excellent, too. I especially liked the miso black cod, and the pork belly came with cauliflower tempura that I still remember.

American has since dropped “First” from the name. As the airline removes international first class from its Boeing 777-300ERs and replaces its three cabin Airbus A321Ts, they’ve opened the dining rooms to a much larger group instead of doing away with them.

Since September 15, qualifying Flagship Business and Flagship Business Plus passengers have been able to use Flagship Dining in Dallas and Miami. Los Angeles is next.

Access covers qualifying American Airlines long haul international, premium transcontinental and Flagship Hawaii itineraries. That includes eligible Flagship flights between Los Angeles and New York JFK, though an ordinary domestic first class ticket doesn’t get you in. The qualifying flight must be marketed and operated by American. Business class access doesn’t include a guest.

Getting into the Flagship Lounge based on AAdvantage or oneworld status doesn’t get you into the separate dining room. Eligible partner first class access continues, and there’s also a way in with miles.

AAdvantage Platinum Pro members can redeem 25,000 miles and Executive Platinum members can redeem 20,000 miles for a Flagship Dining pass. It includes the member and their immediate family or up to two guests on an eligible same day American or oneworld flight, even when flying coach. It includes the Flagship Lounge, too. I’ve thought this was one of the best uses of miles when traveling as a family.

American has introduced a new dining menu and a wine and chocolate pairing featuring KHK Hillside Cabernet Sauvignon and K+M chocolate, co-founded by chef Thomas Keller. The cabernet retails for about $125 a bottle. Here’s American’s photo of the pairing.

The new Dallas wine list also includes Bollinger La Grande Année, which retails for around $200 a bottle. American even listed it as an ingredient in a cranberry orange spritz. That seems like an expensive way to make it harder to taste the champagne. I’d ask for it in a separate glass.

And the food has improved in the broader Flagship lounges, not just in the separate dining rooms. On a recent visit to the Dallas Flagship Lounge, I found a better buffet, a staffed charcuterie station and an improved chef station. I ordered from the lounge’s menu using a QR code, and the food arrived at my table in four minutes. It was a relatively quiet Tuesday evening, but I was impressed.

That menu ordering is available in Los Angeles, too. When I last wrote about the rollout, the QR codes were in the theater seating and across from the secondary beverage station.

Delta still offers the more ambitious food. It now has two Delta One lounges at LAX, with table service throughout, while United’s Polaris Lounge has a sit down restaurant. I’d still put the food in American’s main Flagship Lounge behind Delta, even though the gap has narrowed.

But American makes the larger Flagship Lounge available to many more passengers, including eligible elites traveling in coach. And now a regular qualifying Flagship Business fare comes with the separate dining room.

United’s base Polaris fares don’t include Polaris Lounge access. Delta’s Basic Business fares will lose Delta One lounge access for travel beginning January 19, 2027. At this point Americna’s three Flagship Dining locations really close a gap and even start to offer a competitive advantage for some.

The tradeoff is that First Dining was so special because almost nobody was there. Opening it to business class is a big improvement for those passengers, but it also means many more people competing for a table. American uses an electronic waitlist when the dining room is full. If you’re traveling before a busy departure period, I’d check in with the host when you first arrive.

I’m personally excited to try this out. I have 4 Flagship Business flights through LAX booked over the next 12 months, so I will definitely make use during my layovers (though the first two are long-haul so I do want to visit the Qantas First Lounge for one of those trips, if it’s open).

Nat and Heather are the dream team making AA great again.

Finally. Routing through there soon. Looking forward to this.

July 22, 2018 I was flying back from Sacramento to Dallas via LAX. I was CK and either got it or burned a pass for dining. Went in and thought I was the only person in there. Heard some faint talking. Positioned myself to see who was talking because I thought I recognized the voice. He hung up his call, so I made my move once I realized who it was. Former VP Joe Biden. Literally all by himself and making calls to thank people for attending an event the day before. He was not a presidential candidate (until April 2019). He was so gracious and invited me to sit with him for a bit and asked me where I was coming from and where I was going. Shared I was heading home from a 40-man golf tournament of high school friends (g.1989). I asked if it would be okay for a picture I could share with friends, he said of course. Enjoyed a brief 1:1 with future President of the United States. Btw – there was no Secret Service, he was Joe-citizen and hadn’t declared.

So the Flagship Dining at LAX is a special place in my heart.

Wow, its a wow moment for me! I like the sound of all this new details and would love to dine here. Hopefully I have enough time to sit and relax. Great job AA. See you soon!!
